title: Progress in visible-light-activated photocatalytic coatings to combat implant-related infections: From mechanistic to translational roadmap

sections.heading: Synthesis strategies for constructing photocatalytic coatings targeting biomedical implant application
sections.text: 4.1 Synthesis strategies for constructing photocatalytic coatings targeting biomedical implant application Effective photocatalyst development requires a comprehensive understanding of synthesis procedures and the characterization of physicochemical properties essential for their performance under light. Notably, achieving an optimal balance among critical properties, including surface area, wettability, stability, and reusability, is crucial when designing reliable photocatalytic coatings. This is because a larger surface area provides more active sites for photocatalytic reactions, enhancing the chances of successful organic compound degradation or other desired reactions. In addition, proper wettability ensures uniform reactant contact with the photocatalytic surface, optimizing reaction efficiency. At the same time, stability and reusability contribute to long-term and sustainable performance, enhancing the cost-benefit of the approach. Importantly, the chosen synthesis technique significantly influences all these essential factors. Consequently, researchers have delved into a wide array of coating fabrication methods, selecting the most appropriate based on their specific objectives. These methods encompass various wet chemical approaches, including sol-gel, hydrothermal, and solvothermal processes, as well as plasma-assisted methods, all employed to engineer both doped and undoped photocatalytic coatings tailored to meet diverse application requirements ( Fig. 7 ). Fig. 7 Technological approaches for constructing photocatalytic coatings.  Recent advancements in materials science and nanotechnology have revolutionized surface treatment and coating techniques, enabling the fabrication of efficient photocatalytic coatings with tailored properties. Key techniques include: a) sol-gel synthesis, a chemical process that involves hydrolysis and polycondensation reactions to produce metal oxide gels, allowing precise control of material composition and structure, making it ideal for fabricating thin, uniform coatings with customizable properties, a’) Spin-coating of a thin TiO 2  film prepared by sol-gel chemistry. Reproduced with permission [ 221 ]. Copyright 2024, American Chemical Society. b) Anodization method, conducted in an electrolytic solution under constant voltage potential; this method promotes crystallization when submitted to annealing at high temperatures, enabling the growth of nanoscale coatings with enhanced photocatalytic and structural properties directly on substrates that can be easily decorated with nanoparticles using hydrothermal treatment. b’) Au-decorated nanoparticles on TiO 2  nanotubes. Reproduced with permission [ 222 ]. Copyright 2020, MDPI. (c) Magnetron sputtering, a physical vapor deposition technique that bombards a target material with energetic particles at a low deposition rate, expelling atoms that condense into a thin, uniform film on a substrate, producing high-purity, adherent coatings with precise control over thickness and composition. c’) Ag nanoparticle-impregnated N-doped titania film. Reproduced with permission [ 223 ]. Its high surface area, hydrophilicity, and ability to incorporate chemical elements also enhance its effectiveness for photocatalytic coatings. d’) TiO 2  nanoceramic coating. Fig. 7 4.1.1 Sol-gel synthesis Sol-gel methods are widely used for the synthesis of photocatalysts, making these valuable for nanoscale TiO 2  material production ( Fig. 7 a). They involve two main stages: hydrolysis and polycondensation. During hydrolysis, metal alkoxides break down in either water or alcohol, with the choice of reaction medium leading to either an “aqueous” or “non-aqueous” route [ 224 ]. Polycondensation follows, involving the bonding of neighboring molecules, forming metal oxide bonds and polymer networks. This process increases the system's viscosity, resulting in a porous gel structure while maintaining a liquid phase, in which the size and cross-linking of colloidal particles depend on the precursor and pH [ 225 ]. Then, substrates are often immersed in the reaction mixture during hydrolysis or condensation, followed by aging, drying, thermal treatments, or a combination to promote crystallization and adhesion. By using such methods, thin films with thicknesses spanning 50–500 nm can be fabricated using diverse coating techniques, such as dip-coating, spin-coating, spray-coating, flow-coating, and capillary-coating [ 225 ]. For instance, aiming to enhance the photocatalytic properties of spin-coated sol-gel anatase-type TiO 2 , Tsuji et al. [ 226 ] implanted Ag-negative ions at different energies and doses to these coatings, followed by annealing. The treated samples demonstrated improved photocatalytic efficiency, where Ag nanoparticles (AgNPs), located at a shallow depth in the coating, significantly improved the photocatalytic efficiency, surpassing that of rutile single crystal TiO 2  due to a lower bandgap. Corroborating such results, Khitous et al. [ 221 ] demonstrated a simple, low-cost method that combines asymmetrically shaped AuNPs, formed via thermal dewetting, with a TiO 2  sol-gel layer applied by spin-coating, enhancing visible-light photocatalysis through improved reaction kinetics and hot electron lifetimes ( Fig. 7 a’). In addition, as an example that the method of synthesis can completely change the photocatalytic efficiency, in a study conducted by Asadi et al., [ 227 ] nitrogen and sulfur co-doped TiO 2  nanoparticles were synthesized through a combination of sol-gel and hydrothermal methods. Their results revealed that materials prepared using the sol-gel approach exhibited significantly enhanced photocatalytic activity compared to the hydrothermal one, probably due to the particle size and surface area differences, making them a promising option for practical applications. Nevertheless, a disadvantage of such a method for biomedical implant application relies on its poor adhesion to metallic substrates, thereby needing special attention towards physical or chemical modification of the substrate to enhance the adhesion strength at the coating-substrate interface [ 228 ]. 4.1.2 Anodization method The anodization method is commonly conducted in an electrolytic solution under constant voltage potential, facilitating the growth of nanostructure surfaces such as nanotubes ( Fig. 7 b). Highly ordered TiO 2  nanotube arrays (TNTAs), prepared via electrochemical anodization, have gained interest due to their aligned porosity, high crystallinity, and oriented nanotubular morphology, which enhance light absorption and charge separation. Considering this, Xiao et al. [ 229 ] constructed a hierarchically ordered Au x /NP-TNTA heterostructure, fabricated through two-step anodization and electrostatic self-assembly, with versatile photocatalytic properties, including pollutant degradation, with enhanced photosensitization from glutathione-capped Au x  clusters (i.e., atomically precise thiolate-protected gold clusters) and elucidated mechanisms offering insights for novel metal-cluster/1D semiconductor applications. Targeting implant applications, Moon et al. [ 222 ] prepared TiO 2  nanotubes (NTs) via anodization followed by crystallization through heating at 400 °C for 3 h in air. Then, to extend the photocatalytic activity of titania beyond the UV range into the visible light spectrum, the authors decorated the NTs with Au ( Fig. 7 b’) or Pt by ion plasma sputtering. Such doping can also be performed by hydrothermal treatment (HT). Typically, the synthesis of photocatalytic coatings using HT occurs by introducing the sample into the vessel containing a liquid medium, followed by annealing at high temperatures and subsequent cooling, allowing for the growth of a coating onto the substrate. Zhang et al. [ 230 ] recently reported on successfully constructing a TiO 2  nanostructure on a Ti surface by HT growth using NaOH solution. Interestingly, to achieve photocatalytic activity under visible light, the authors synthesized a TiO 2 /MoS 2  coating in two HT steps: the first one with NaOH and the second one with MoS 2 , which effectively killed  S. aureus  in vitro and in vivo within 10 min of irradiation. 4.1.3 Magnetron sputtering Photocatalytic coatings can also be produced using magnetron sputtering, offering precise control over plasma parameters and the desired properties ( Fig. 7 c). Sputtering is a well-established process that involves expelling atoms from a target surface when bombarded by energetic particles, leading to the formation of thin films on a substrate [ 231 ]. The ejected atoms have high energy, which enhances their ability to condense and adhere to the substrate. Wong et al. [ 223 ] developed TiO 2 (N)/Ag/TiO 2 (N) sandwich films via magnetron sputtering, embedding an Ag layer between two N-doped TiO 2  layers using two Ti and one Ag target ( Fig. 7 c’). Microbiological experiments showed that in the absence of Ag, microbial cells preserved their integrity with smooth surface morphology, regardless of visible light exposure. However, when Ag was incorporated into the films, it induced roughening of the bacterial surface in the dark, likely due to interactions between Ag and the bacterial cell wall. Upon exposure to visible light, these surfaces underwent more pronounced structural changes, including the development of distinct cracks. In another report, Ueda et al. [ 232 ] deposited pure gold (Au) and a titanium-gold (Ti-Au) alloy film (60 mol% Ti, 40 mol% Au) onto Ti substrates using sputtering, followed by thermal oxidation to create TiO 2  layers. These layers were evaluated for their antibacterial properties against  Escherichia coli , cytotoxicity, and bonding strength to Ti substrates. The most promising results in terms of antibacterial activity under visible-light exposure were achieved with a 38 nm thick sputtered film made of pure Au, evidencing an R-value of 1.8, corresponding to approximately 98 % reduction in  E. coli  viability. Interestingly, Ratova et al. evaluated the photocatalytic and antimicrobial performance of bismuth oxide, bismuth tungstate, and titanium dioxide coatings deposited on glass beads via reactive magnetron sputtering, followed by annealing [ 233 ]. Bismuth oxide coatings showed superior dye degradation and complete inactivation of  E. coli  under visible light within 48 h, attributed to their low bandgap and stable hydrophobic surface, offering both disinfection and antifouling advantages. Nevertheless, bismuth oxide coatings may not present ideal mechanical and chemical stability for implant applications. In contrast, titanium dioxide is widely used in biomedical implants due to its excellent biocompatibility and long-term stability, but it requires modification to be activated under visible light—making doping with Bi 2 O 3  a promising strategy to combine the robustness of TiO 2  with the visible-light responsiveness of bismuth-based systems. 4.1.4 Plasma electrolytic oxidation Plasma electrolytic oxidation (PEO) utilizes a powerful electrical discharge within a system comprising a cathode (a cooled vessel), a working substrate immersed in an electrolyte serving as the anode, and a power supply ( Fig. 7 d). This method offers a cost-effective alternative to vacuum-based plasma technologies and is particularly advantageous for creating robust, uniform coatings on complex-shaped metallic objects, such as biomedical implants and devices, without exposing the entire substrate to high temperatures or requiring sophisticated equipment. Unlike other coating processes, PEO results from a substrate conversion process in tandem with deposition. Its core advantage lies in the generation of high-voltage plasma discharges around substrates of varying shapes, enabling the doping of diverse chemical elements in a single step. This capability allows for the production of biofunctional coatings characterized by thickness, roughness, porosity, and crystallinity, which are beneficial for photocatalytic activity and implant-bone integration. Wu et al. [ 185 ] synthesized TiO 2  porous nanoceramic coatings on titanium substrates using the PEO process that presented photocatalytic activity due to a disordered outer layer with oxygen vacancies, effectively degrading methylene blue, rhodamine B, and lipopolysaccharide (LPS) under visible light ( Fig. 7 d’). Although the authors claimed that the coating could improve Ti implant decontamination, light irradiation of biofilm formed onto the developed coating was not evaluated. On the other hand, we [ 19 ] employed the PEO technique to develop a Bi-doped TiO 2  coating suitable for biomedical and dental implant applications. This coating demonstrated enhanced photocatalytic activity, attributed to Bi doping, resulting in the effective reduction of  S. sanguinis  and  Actinomyces naeslundii  dual-species biofilm, with visible light further amplifying its antibacterial properties, holding potential for peri-implant infection control.

sections.heading: Substrates and synthesis methods
sections.text: 5.1 Substrates and synthesis methods Among the metallic substrates tested ( Fig. 11 c), pure Ti was used most frequently (47 %), followed by titanium-aluminum-vanadium (Ti–6Al–4 V; 8 %) and stainless steel (SS; 8 %). Glass, poly(vinyl chloride), polypropylene, silica wafer, and composites were also used. It is worth noting that while many studies claim the potential suitability of their developed coatings for biomedical implant applications, some have opted for non-metallic substrates like glass or silica. These choices are often made due to the inertness and transparency of such substrates, which makes them appropriate model surfaces as they minimize their influence on the outcomes and expand the potential applications across various fields. However, it is crucial to acknowledge that while these substrates offer advantages for studying general photocatalytic antimicrobial coatings, researchers should carefully assess the specific requirements of their individual studies and applications. Given that the chosen method can substantially influence the properties of the resulting coatings—especially in subtractive techniques—researchers are encouraged to thoroughly examine how their developed coatings perform on substrates pertinent to their intended applications. This is particularly important for materials like Ti and its alloys, which are commonly used for biomedical implant applications. Regarding the synthesis methods ( Fig. 11 d), hydrothermal treatment emerged as the most frequently employed fabrication technique in the reported studies, accounting for 11 % of the cases. It was followed by magnetron sputtering (8 %) and immersion techniques (8 %). Additionally, various other methods such as anodization, electrodeposition, electromagnetic deposition, electrophoretic deposition, plasma spray, pulsed-pressure-metal-organic chemical vapor deposition (pp-MOCVD), spray methods, and plasma-based techniques (e.g., ion plasma, plasma electrolytic oxidation, pulsed DC plasma) were utilized. In certain cases, two-step deposition methods were employed, primarily involving a combination of heat/annealing treatment with other technologies. Overall, it is possible to observe a common factor uniting all the methods employed in these processes: temperature. The structural attributes of semiconductor materials, particularly crystallinity, hold a pivotal role in dictating their photocatalytic efficacy [ 245 ]. The achievement of such properties can be pursued through diverse techniques, with high temperature representing one viable approach. Specifically, crystallinity significantly influences the separation and mobility of charge carriers (electrons and holes) generated during photocatalysis [ 301 ]. In crystalline structures, electrons and holes exhibit greater freedom of movement, reducing the likelihood of recombination, where they combine and neutralize each other's effects. This heightened charge separation substantially enhances the material's effectiveness in initiating and sustaining photocatalytic reactions. In this view, Krumdieck et al. [ 275 ] focused on developing a high-performance, nanostructured TiO 2  coating using an up-scalable pulsed-pressure metal-organic chemical vapor deposition (pp-MOCVD) process, producing the anatase-rutile-carbon (NsARC) composite with enhanced functionality ( Fig. 12 a). By integrating single-crystalline anatase nanostructures, rutile-anatase heterojunctions, and amorphous carbon, the coating achieves superior surface area, effective charge separation, and visible-light activation. The nanomorphology includes segmented mille-feuilles structures of anatase and strobili-like dendritic rutile optimized for visible-light-driven photocatalytic activity ( Fig. 12 b). The proposed mechanism suggests that high precursor flux, rapid pyrolysis, and carbon formation induce the unique mille-feuille anatase structure by stabilizing unstable crystal step edges, while dendritic rutile strobili are formed through fast crystal growth and potential carbon involvement, resulting in polycrystalline branching ( Fig. 12 c and d). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and Raman analysis showed the presence of amorphous carbon and carboxylate groups, with no carbon doping of the TiO 2  matrix, while the anatase phase displayed a rare (220) texture, and the rutile phase was identified as phase-pure. Unlike conventional TiO 2 , NsARC's black coloration, derived from carbon capping, extending light absorption while reducing electron-hole recombination, ultimately demonstrating antimicrobial performance, achieving up to a 99.99 % reduction in viable  E. coli  under UV, 3 to 4-log under visible light, and a 2-log reduction in darkness via carbon-centered radicals, ROS generation, and membrane disruption, highlighting its potential for scalable antimicrobial applications ( Fig. 12 e and f). Fig. 12 Influence of crystallinity and nanostructure on antimicrobial and visible-light-driven photocatalytic properties of an anatase-rutile-carbon (NsARC) TiO 2  coating.  a) As-deposited NsARC TiO 2  coating on a stainless-steel substrate, 10 μm thick, with scanning electron microscopy (SEM) micrographs revealing mille-feuilles and strobili structures and strong z-orientation in the fracture cross-section. b) SEM micrographs showing the NsARC morphology with a high specific surface area. c) Proposed nanostructure development mechanism illustrating rapid anatase crystal growth with carbon capping at step edges. d) SEM micrograph of one strobili and two mille-feuilles columns. e) Efficiency of plating (EOP) determined through colony-forming unit counts. f) Schematic depicting the antimicrobial activity mechanisms involving light absorption by carbon and TiO 2 , ROS generation and diffusion, and bacterial membrane damage. Reproduced with permission [ 275 ]. Copyright 2019, Springer Nature (open access). Fig. 12

methods_paragraphs.text: 4.1.1 Sol-gel synthesis Sol-gel methods are widely used for the synthesis of photocatalysts, making these valuable for nanoscale TiO 2  material production ( Fig. 7 a). They involve two main stages: hydrolysis and polycondensation. During hydrolysis, metal alkoxides break down in either water or alcohol, with the choice of reaction medium leading to either an “aqueous” or “non-aqueous” route [ 224 ]. Polycondensation follows, involving the bonding of neighboring molecules, forming metal oxide bonds and polymer networks. This process increases the system's viscosity, resulting in a porous gel structure while maintaining a liquid phase, in which the size and cross-linking of colloidal particles depend on the precursor and pH [ 225 ]. Then, substrates are often immersed in the reaction mixture during hydrolysis or condensation, followed by aging, drying, thermal treatments, or a combination to promote crystallization and adhesion. By using such methods, thin films with thicknesses spanning 50–500 nm can be fabricated using diverse coating techniques, such as dip-coating, spin-coating, spray-coating, flow-coating, and capillary-coating [ 225 ]. For instance, aiming to enhance the photocatalytic properties of spin-coated sol-gel anatase-type TiO 2 , Tsuji et al. [ 226 ] implanted Ag-negative ions at different energies and doses to these coatings, followed by annealing. The treated samples demonstrated improved photocatalytic efficiency, where Ag nanoparticles (AgNPs), located at a shallow depth in the coating, significantly improved the photocatalytic efficiency, surpassing that of rutile single crystal TiO 2  due to a lower bandgap. Corroborating such results, Khitous et al. [ 221 ] demonstrated a simple, low-cost method that combines asymmetrically shaped AuNPs, formed via thermal dewetting, with a TiO 2  sol-gel layer applied by spin-coating, enhancing visible-light photocatalysis through improved reaction kinetics and hot electron lifetimes ( Fig. 7 a’). In addition, as an example that the method of synthesis can completely change the photocatalytic efficiency, in a study conducted by Asadi et al., [ 227 ] nitrogen and sulfur co-doped TiO 2  nanoparticles were synthesized through a combination of sol-gel and hydrothermal methods. Their results revealed that materials prepared using the sol-gel approach exhibited significantly enhanced photocatalytic activity compared to the hydrothermal one, probably due to the particle size and surface area differences, making them a promising option for practical applications. Nevertheless, a disadvantage of such a method for biomedical implant application relies on its poor adhesion to metallic substrates, thereby needing special attention towards physical or chemical modification of the substrate to enhance the adhesion strength at the coating-substrate interface [ 228 ].

methods_paragraphs.text: 5.1 Substrates and synthesis methods Among the metallic substrates tested ( Fig. 11 c), pure Ti was used most frequently (47 %), followed by titanium-aluminum-vanadium (Ti–6Al–4 V; 8 %) and stainless steel (SS; 8 %). Glass, poly(vinyl chloride), polypropylene, silica wafer, and composites were also used. It is worth noting that while many studies claim the potential suitability of their developed coatings for biomedical implant applications, some have opted for non-metallic substrates like glass or silica. These choices are often made due to the inertness and transparency of such substrates, which makes them appropriate model surfaces as they minimize their influence on the outcomes and expand the potential applications across various fields. However, it is crucial to acknowledge that while these substrates offer advantages for studying general photocatalytic antimicrobial coatings, researchers should carefully assess the specific requirements of their individual studies and applications. Given that the chosen method can substantially influence the properties of the resulting coatings—especially in subtractive techniques—researchers are encouraged to thoroughly examine how their developed coatings perform on substrates pertinent to their intended applications. This is particularly important for materials like Ti and its alloys, which are commonly used for biomedical implant applications. Regarding the synthesis methods ( Fig. 11 d), hydrothermal treatment emerged as the most frequently employed fabrication technique in the reported studies, accounting for 11 % of the cases. It was followed by magnetron sputtering (8 %) and immersion techniques (8 %). Additionally, various other methods such as anodization, electrodeposition, electromagnetic deposition, electrophoretic deposition, plasma spray, pulsed-pressure-metal-organic chemical vapor deposition (pp-MOCVD), spray methods, and plasma-based techniques (e.g., ion plasma, plasma electrolytic oxidation, pulsed DC plasma) were utilized. In certain cases, two-step deposition methods were employed, primarily involving a combination of heat/annealing treatment with other technologies. Overall, it is possible to observe a common factor uniting all the methods employed in these processes: temperature. The structural attributes of semiconductor materials, particularly crystallinity, hold a pivotal role in dictating their photocatalytic efficacy [ 245 ]. The achievement of such properties can be pursued through diverse techniques, with high temperature representing one viable approach. Specifically, crystallinity significantly influences the separation and mobility of charge carriers (electrons and holes) generated during photocatalysis [ 301 ]. In crystalline structures, electrons and holes exhibit greater freedom of movement, reducing the likelihood of recombination, where they combine and neutralize each other's effects. This heightened charge separation substantially enhances the material's effectiveness in initiating and sustaining photocatalytic reactions. In this view, Krumdieck et al. [ 275 ] focused on developing a high-performance, nanostructured TiO 2  coating using an up-scalable pulsed-pressure metal-organic chemical vapor deposition (pp-MOCVD) process, producing the anatase-rutile-carbon (NsARC) composite with enhanced functionality ( Fig. 12 a). By integrating single-crystalline anatase nanostructures, rutile-anatase heterojunctions, and amorphous carbon, the coating achieves superior surface area, effective charge separation, and visible-light activation. The nanomorphology includes segmented mille-feuilles structures of anatase and strobili-like dendritic rutile optimized for visible-light-driven photocatalytic activity ( Fig. 12 b). The proposed mechanism suggests that high precursor flux, rapid pyrolysis, and carbon formation induce the unique mille-feuille anatase structure by stabilizing unstable crystal step edges, while dendritic rutile strobili are formed through fast crystal growth and potential carbon involvement, resulting in polycrystalline branching ( Fig. 12 c and d). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and Raman analysis showed the presence of amorphous carbon and carboxylate groups, with no carbon doping of the TiO 2  matrix, while the anatase phase displayed a rare (220) texture, and the rutile phase was identified as phase-pure. Unlike conventional TiO 2 , NsARC's black coloration, derived from carbon capping, extending light absorption while reducing electron-hole recombination, ultimately demonstrating antimicrobial performance, achieving up to a 99.99 % reduction in viable  E. coli  under UV, 3 to 4-log under visible light, and a 2-log reduction in darkness via carbon-centered radicals, ROS generation, and membrane disruption, highlighting its potential for scalable antimicrobial applications ( Fig. 12 e and f). Fig. 12 Influence of crystallinity and nanostructure on antimicrobial and visible-light-driven photocatalytic properties of an anatase-rutile-carbon (NsARC) TiO 2  coating.  a) As-deposited NsARC TiO 2  coating on a stainless-steel substrate, 10 μm thick, with scanning electron microscopy (SEM) micrographs revealing mille-feuilles and strobili structures and strong z-orientation in the fracture cross-section. b) SEM micrographs showing the NsARC morphology with a high specific surface area. c) Proposed nanostructure development mechanism illustrating rapid anatase crystal growth with carbon capping at step edges. d) SEM micrograph of one strobili and two mille-feuilles columns. e) Efficiency of plating (EOP) determined through colony-forming unit counts. f) Schematic depicting the antimicrobial activity mechanisms involving light absorption by carbon and TiO 2 , ROS generation and diffusion, and bacterial membrane damage.
