1 Introduction Biomedical and dental implants have revolutionized medicine and dentistry, yet they also pose a high risk of infections, contributing to 25.6 % of healthcare-associated infections in the United States [ 1 , 2 ]. In particular, implants that breach the natural barrier between the internal and external environment—such as percutaneous devices and dental implants—are especially vulnerable, as bacteria can colonize the implant surface and bypass host defenses. This vulnerability arises because the implant-tissue interface weakens local immune responses, allowing even less virulent pathogens to establish infections [ 3 ]. While long-term or life-supporting implants near vital organs pose the greatest health risks, all surgically invasive devices, especially those in contact with the bloodstream, can potentially lead to sepsis [ 3 , 4 ]. Within the oral microenvironment, for example, which houses over 700 bacterial species and experiences a constant flow of physiological fluids at the implant-tissue interface, the incidence of infections around dental implants has shown a marked increase. As such, the prevalence of peri-implantitis has been reported to be around 20 % at the patient level and 13 % at the implant level [ 5 ]. Implant infections typically arise from the accumulation of biofilms on the implant surface, involving complex interactions between the infectious microorganisms, the properties of the biomaterial, and the response of the host's immune system to both the pathogens and the implant material itself [ 3 ]. Biofilms are microbial communities protected by a self-produced matrix of extracellular polymeric substances (EPS), making it challenging for antimicrobial agents to penetrate while also leading to antibiotic resistance impairing the effectiveness of supplementary local or systemic therapies [ 6 ]. Particularly in the case of dental implants, the presence of complex geometry and inaccessible areas in the screw threads pose a significant challenge, diminishing the efficiency of current mechanical debridement therapy [ 7 ]. In this context, urgent solutions are required to overcome biofilm resistance and adapt the distinctive characteristics of the peri-implant environment, especially soft tissue loss [ 8 ], emphasizing the necessity for innovative approaches. Stimuli-responsive smart biomaterials–from nanoparticles to hydrogels and coatings–[ [9] ,  [10] ,  [11] ,  [12] ] have emerged as a promising approach to combat biomedical and oral biofilms. For instance, these smart biomaterials can have advanced surfaces that can perform multiple functions during bacterial infections and activate bactericidal responses based on environmental cues, such as changes in chemicals, pH, light, and temperature [ 13 , 14 ]. The feasibility of using smart surfaces to alter the pH of the peri-implant microenvironment over a wide range or achieving rapid temperature changes with temperature-responsive materials may be limited, as demanding precise coordination with the biological system's timing is necessary for effective functionality [ 14 ]. In contrast, light, as a stimulus, is an appealing option for controlling biomaterial properties and function due to its wide availability, easy controllability, and compatibility with various biological and chemical processes, offering precise control without unwanted side effects in medical devices [ 14 , 15 ]. Light-based decontamination relies on specific wavelengths of light, from ultraviolet (UV) to near-infrared, to activate photoresponsive materials, leading to the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) or hyperthermic conditions for rapid pathogen eradication [ 16 ]. This approach encompasses diverse therapeutic strategies like photothermal therapy (PTT), photodynamic therapy (PDT), photocatalysis, photobiomodulation (PBM), and optogenetic therapy, all related to light-induced photochemical and/or biological reactions, as well as heat production [ 16 , 17 ]. Particularly among these, photocatalysis stands out in the biomedical field for its effective ROS generation, eliminating the need for photosensitizers and avoiding unwanted hyperthermia effects, hence making it a valuable approach for the local elimination of pathogenic bacteria [ 14 , 18 , 19 ]. Photocatalysis is a phenomenon that uses solid photocatalysts, often semiconductors, to instigate chemical reactions at the interface of solid-liquid or solid-gas phases by absorbing light and prompting electron migration when excited by energy from light irradiation at specific wavelengths [ 20 , 21 ]. Semiconductors like TiO 2  and ZnO find common use as photocatalysts in the management of bacterial infections by producing ROS through photoexcitation [ 16 , [22] ,  [23] ,  [24] ]. Nonetheless, their efficacy is hindered in specific human health applications due to the limited absorption in the UV spectrum, owing to the broad bandgap energy [ 25 ]. To address the issue of light attenuation within the human body, the biomaterials field is investigating innovative approaches, including implant coating designs that enable photoactivation in the visible light spectrum. This spectrum is less affected by tissue absorption, offers higher photon energy, produces fewer thermal effects, and is more cost-effective compared to near-infrared and UV light [ 26 , 27 ]. Hence, several strategies have been employed to enhance the semiconductors’ light absorption to the visible light spectra, including elemental doping, introduction of oxygen vacancies, alterations in size and structure, and the combination with other semiconductor materials [ 25 ]. A comprehensive overview of visible-light-triggered photocatalysis has been extensively covered in previous reviews, providing valuable insights into the strategies and mechanisms behind this technology, which in turn facilitates the design of advanced materials in the engineering field [ [27] ,  [28] ,  [29] ,  [30] ,  [31] ]. Moreover, significant progress has been reported in the realm of visible-light-triggered photocatalysis for antimicrobial purposes, encompassing various materials from small molecules to nanomaterials and addressing diverse environmental concerns, including air pollution, water purification, paints, and the improvement of personal protective or medical equipment [ 18 , 25 , [32] ,  [33] ,  [34] ,  [35] ,  [36] ,  [37] ]. Nevertheless, limited attention has been directed towards designing solutions tailored to the specific requirements and multifunctional demands of biomedical implant contexts. For instance, the introduction of this technology in the dental implant field has only been reported since 2019 [ 19 ], when our group highlighted the use of visible-light-triggered photocatalytic coatings that serve as versatile surfaces. These coatings demonstrated potential advantages not only for the initial stages of implant rehabilitation but also for antibacterial action against oral-related bacteria, which is potentiated by light activation to release ROS locally and “on-demand”, presenting a novel therapeutic approach for managing peri-implant diseases [ 19 ]. With the recent emergence of photocatalytic coatings for addressing biofilm-related implant infections and their rapid advancement in the field, we are now in a position to delve into a deeper comprehension of the mechanisms and challenges associated with visible-light-activated photocatalytic coatings for biofilm eradication to biomedical implants, and especially the complex and diverse oral biofilms. This comprehensive review aims to summarize the latest design principles for visible-light-triggered photocatalytic antibacterial coatings, emphasizing physicochemical modifications and surface property optimizations and introducing novel research concepts ( Fig. 1 ). An overview of the properties influencing implant biofilm formation and current antimicrobial strategies is followed by examining light-based therapies and their underlying ROS-based mechanisms. The review then delves into the design and mechanistic principles for visible-light-triggered antibacterial photocatalytic coatings, further supported by an evidence-based assessment of recent developments. Variations in methodology, protocols, dopants, and other factors affecting microbiological and cellular responses are considered, along with exploring future challenges in the field. Fig. 1 Schematic overview of the scope of the current review paper.  This review focuses on the development of photocatalytic coatings to mitigate implant-related infections through light-activated mechanisms. These coatings depend on a light source with a wavelength compatible with the band gap of the semiconductor photocatalysts, facilitating the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) upon irradiation, which can damage bacterial components, ultimately leading to cell death. Emphasis is placed on engineering semiconductor materials to achieve visible-light photocatalytic activity, optimizing their physicochemical properties and performance. The review incorporates an evidence-based systematic search to summarize findings on the applicability of these coatings for (biomedical) implants. By leveraging interdisciplinary approaches from engineering, biomedical sciences, and chemistry, this work highlights the integration of material design, biological validation, and technological innovation, providing a foundation for advancing photocatalytically-active coatings into clinical practice. Fig. 1

2 The key role of biofilm in implant infection Implant-related infections, primarily associated with titanium (Ti)-based implants, pose a significant challenge in the biomedical field due to their chronic nature, complex biofilm structures, and resistance to antimicrobial treatments, resulting in substantial societal and economic burdens for healthcare systems worldwide [ 38 ]. In the first section of this review, the complex process of biofilm formation on implanted devices, encompassing stages of development, microbial involvement, and healthcare challenges, is introduced. It also explores the interactions between implant surfaces, host tissues, and microorganisms, shedding light on the current implications for infection prevention and treatment approaches in healthcare settings. A summary of all these issues is shown in  Fig. 2 . Fig. 2 Schematic representation illustrating the stages of biofilm formation on implant surfaces, key factors driving biofilm accumulation and pathogenesis, and antimicrobial strategies designed to overcome these processes.  (a) The main phases of biofilm formation and spread include protein adsorption, microbial adhesion, biofilm development, maturation, and dispersal. Environmental conditions, such as reduced oxygen levels, availability of nutrients, metabolite accumulation, and mass transport mechanisms, can trigger microbial dysbiosis. This imbalance ultimately drives the transition from health to disease. (b) In parallel, several factors intrinsic to the material's surface influence microbial attachment and pathogenesis, further contributing to this shift. These surface-specific properties, including roughness, polarity charge, and electrochemical behavior, can create conditions conducive to bacterial colonization, thereby promoting adhesion and biofilm formation. Moreover, individual host responses, systemic conditions, and patient-specific habits can modulate the microbial profile and play a significant role in the progression of the pathogenesis process. (c) To address these challenges, antimicrobial surface mechanisms have been proposed, including contact-killing, antifouling, and releasing strategies. These mechanisms aim to either eliminate bacteria upon contact, prevent their adhesion, or release antimicrobial agents to inhibit microbial activity. (d) Among current antimicrobial strategies, surface modifications, antimicrobial coatings, superhydrophobic properties, and antibiotic-loaded surfaces have shown potential for inhibiting bacterial growth and preventing colonization on implant surfaces. By combining these approaches, it is possible to create more effective solutions to combat biofilm-related infections and improve implant longevity. Fig. 2 2.1 Unraveling the biofilm formation process on implant surfaces Biofilm development is an intricate, multi-step process involving multiple bacterial species. These biofilms are composed of microbial communities enclosed within an extracellular matrix, forming a highly organized structure [ 39 , 40 ]. This matrix consists of exopolysaccharide (EPS), lipids, nucleic acids, and other biomolecules essential for the biofilm's biochemical properties and nutritional needs [ 40 , 41 ]. The EPS and its singular architecture serve dual functions: they provide a survival mechanism that protects bacteria from host immune defenses and external agents such as antibiotics while also acting as a platform for surface attachment. This enables bacterial species to adhere to surfaces, facilitating growth and acting as a virulence factor in implant infections [ 42 ]. Biofilm formation typically unfolds in several stages, including protein adsorption, microbial attachment (reversible and irreversible), maturation, and dispersion/detachment ( Fig. 2 a) [ 43 , 44 ]. In a nutshell, throughout the biofilm formation process, multiple factors from both the microbial cells and the surface drive the initial adhesion, involving polarity, London-van der Waals forces, and hydrophobic interactions [ 45 ]. During this phase, numerous bacteria adhere to the protein-coated surface, initiating attachment and triggering biofilm formation. Although this stage is initially reversible because of the weak interactions between the bacteria and implant, it transitions to an irreversible phase if the attractive forces outweigh the repulsive ones. In such cases, certain bacteria that were loosely attached become firmly fixed, resulting in the formation of a strongly adhered monolayer [ 46 ]. During the maturation stage, the adhered bacteria on the implant surface grow and interact through the secretion of autoinducer signals, activating genes specifically associated with biofilm formation [ 39 , 44 ]. This phase is characterized by the production of EPS, chemical signaling interactions, and the transformation of microcolonies into macrocolonies protected by the extracellular matrix barrier [ 3 ]. Environmental conditions such as oxygenation, pH, nutrient supply, metabolic byproducts, and mass transport mechanisms can induce microbial dysbiosis [ 42 , 43 ]. This dysbiosis drives the shift from a healthy state to a disease. Once the biofilm reaches maturity, microbial cells from the biofilm migrate due to the depletion of nutrients. To sustain growth and access new resources, these cells disperse to other zones of the implant as a strategy to continue another biofilm life cycle, spreading infection and hindering the effectiveness of antimicrobial therapies [ 40 , 47 ]. 2.2 Influential factors determining microbial attachment The biofilm attachment is a multifactorial process influenced by the site-specific microbiota and surface characteristics, including surface roughness, surface-free energy and wettability, charge, and electrochemical behavior ( Fig. 2 b) [ 48 , 49 ]. One of the key factors influencing microbial colonization on implants during the initial stages of adhesion is surface roughness. On moderately rough surfaces (Sa = 1.0–2.0 μm) and rough surfaces (Sa >2.0 μm), microorganisms benefit from greater protection against shear forces, favoring their adhesion and proliferation due to the increased contact area between the cells and surface [ 50 ]. However, it is essential to emphasize that the relationship between surface roughness and biofilm formation is complex and depends on several environmental conditions and, at present, there is no universally ideal roughness capable of inhibiting the adhesion of all bacterial species [ 51 , 52 ]. Evidence suggests that an average roughness value of 0.2 μm may serve as a threshold below which bacterial adhesion is unlikely to be further reduced [ 50 , 53 ]. Nevertheless, the applicability of this standard to the implant body surface remains questionable since research has shown that moderate roughness is essential to suitable osteoblastic cell adhesion and the osseointegration process, improving the success rate and secondary stability of the implant [ [54] ,  [55] ,  [56] ,  [57] ,  [58] ]. When considering the influence of surface properties on biofilm development, it is unreliable to assess each property separately. Despite surface roughness being considered a singular feature, its nature may impact other properties, such as wettability [ 59 ]. For instance, evidence suggests that surfaces with a higher roughness exhibit increased hydrophobicity, which may decrease initial bacterial adhesion [ 60 , 61 ]. However, the impact of surface hydrophobicity on bacterial adhesion is multifaceted, as it can either promote or inhibit adhesion depending on the specific conditions. In our previous work, a rough superhydrophobic surface created through plasma technology and chemical modification was demonstrated to reduce bacterial adhesion and biofilm proliferation concurrent with a shift in the microbial profile to a more host-compatible or symbiotic composition [ 61 ]. Furthermore, various bacterial species exhibit distinct preferences for surface hydrophobicity. For instance, the hydrophobic  Streptococcus sanguinis  adheres better to saliva-coated pure Ti and Ti alloy than the hydrophilic  Streptococcus constellatus  [ 62 ]. Another research also demonstrated that the adhesion of  Streptococcus gordonii , a primary colonizer of oral surfaces, varies depending on the physical-chemical properties of different dental materials. Yet, none of the tested materials entirely inhibited bacterial attachment [ 63 ]. Among the relevant factors related to microbial adhesion to implants, surface charge significantly influences the binding force between bacteria and surfaces, and its impact on biofilm development has been recognized inside the biomedical field [ 64 ]. Given that most microbial cells carry a negative charge at neutral pH, positively charged surfaces tend to favor bacterial adhesion, while negatively charged surfaces tend to resist it [ 51 , 65 ]. Beyond charge, the electrochemical behavior of the surface provides an essential role in the integrity of the metallic implants [ 61 ]. From the bio-tribological perspective, which considers the synergistic effect between wear and corrosion under biological conditions, microbiologically induced corrosion significantly influences the fate of implanted materials, particularly in the complex oral environment [ 66 , 67 ]. For example, acidic metabolites generated by the bacteria can lower the pH at the biofilm-implant interface, triggering the diffusion of salivary fluoride ions through the biofilm matrix. This process accelerates metal degradation, increasing the release of Ti ions and particles [ 68 ]. The effect of these metallic ions and particles is species-dependent, potentially altering the biofilm composition and generating dysbiosis by favoring the overgrowth of certain bacterial species [ 69 ]. As a negative consequence, this complex process can disrupt the structure and microbiome profile of the peri-implant region, generating an inflammatory response and compromising the electrochemical stability of the material [ 67 , 69 , 70 ]. 2.3 Pathogenesis factors driving disease progression Although the factors that affect the shift from a health-associated to a disease-associated microbiome are not fully understood, there is consensus that relevant conditions such as host inflammatory response [ 71 ], systematic conditions of patients [ 72 ], and critical habits [ 73 ] may contribute to the microbial composition and influence the pathogenesis process [ 74 ]. The host immune response is a complex mechanism that responds not only to the bacteria that cover the implant but also recognizes the biomaterial surface as a foreign body. This recognition triggers an inflammatory response involving the blood coagulation cascade and immune cells, especially neutrophils [ 75 , 76 ]. For this reason, the individual host response to the microbiological profile has a significant role in the progression of peri-implant disease and in microbial dysbiosis that is directly affected by inflammatory tissue breakdown products generated during infection [ 3 ]. Drawing from this concept, molecules within the peri-implant sulcus fluid have been investigated for their association with inflammatory patterns and proteolytic activity [ 76 ]. The increased MMP-8 levels and decreased expression of MMP blockers, for example, lead to tissue damage, attracting active osteoclasts and stimulating bone resorption [ 77 ]. MMP-8 triggers the breakdown of type I collagen, abundant in periodontal and peri-implant regions, and is notably evident in patients with peri-implantitis [ 78 ]. Studies have linked higher MMP-8 levels in peri-implantitis sites to clinical disease signs, and its reduction post-treatment suggests its potential as a biomarker for diagnosing peri-implant health or disease [ 79 , 80 ]. Furthermore, the state of macrophage polarization within peri-implantitis lesions represents a significant signaling pathway. In general, M1 macrophages drive a pro-inflammatory response stimulated by bacterial cues, whereas M2 macrophages are essential in resolving inflammation and hence aid tissue repair. In this sense, the balance and expression of M1/M2 macrophages potentially affect the immune response quality and the extent of tissue damage [ 81 , 82 ]. Similarly, each subject exhibits distinct biological factors that impact peri-implant disease initiation, development, and worsening [ 83 ]. Despite the lack of a direct association of diabetes as a critical condition for peri-implantitis development, it is generally assumed that diabetes induces a negative influence on inflammatory mechanisms and apoptosis, leading to an insufficient host response and impairing tissue healing [ 72 , 84 ]. Studies show that the inflammatory process is significantly increased in a chronic hyperglycemia condition. The classical expression of proinflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α and interleukin (IL)-6, as well as certain chemokines, like C–C chemokine receptor (CCR)-2 and monocyte chemotactic protein (MCP)-1 can be confirmed in peri-implant biopsies of diabetic individuals [ 85 , 86 ]. As expected, the level of these mediators is directly related to the peri-implantitis severity and is more prominent in patients with poorly controlled diabetes [ 72 ]. On the other hand, maintaining proper glycemic control reduces implant failure rates and mitigates the hyperinflammatory state often observed in peri-implantitis regions, highlighting the importance of glycemic regulation in promoting effective healing and long-term stability of implants [ 87 ]. In the same way that systemic conditions may negatively interfere with implant survival rates, chronic smoking seems to be associated with the severity of peri-implant disease [ 73 ]. Like co-morbidities, tobacco products can alter the host response by affecting antibody production and the secretion of immunoinflammatory mediators, including pro-inflammatory cytokines [ 88 ]. Furthermore, evidence shows that smokers exhibit an abundant pathogen-rich anaerobic microbiome, resembling a community associated with disease [ 89 ]. Interestingly, this dysbiosis condition exists even in periodontally healthy individuals and remains evident even after treating the disease, creating an environment prone to harm and at risk of potential inflammation in the future [ 90 ]. Occasionally, bacterial infection following bone implant surgery is another critical issue when considering these patients, and the development of multifunctional scaffolds capable of preventing infection while supporting bone regeneration has been reported to be a potential treatment strategy [ 91 ]. Considering the aspects mentioned, one of the main strategies to prevent biofilm accumulation is oral hygiene practices [ 92 ]. Regular maintenance and proper oral hygiene decrease the development of peri-implantitis, playing an essential role in preventing the shifts in the microbiota profile to a dysbiotic condition [ 93 ]. However, in addition to systemic diseases and critical habits, real conditions such as a patient's motor abilities, frequent carbohydrate consumption, and lack of cooperation during follow-up appointments represent a clinical challenge in preventing and treating implant-related infections [ 94 , 95 ]. For these reasons, the development of advanced implant surface strategies has become a focal point, offering a targeted local approach to minimize biofilm formation and reduce the risk of implant-related infections, particularly in patients where conventional preventive measures fall short. 2.4 Touchpoints in antibacterial surface design strategies Surface properties of implants have been shown to directly impact the biofilm formation. Hence, anti-biofilm strategies for biomedical implants are mostly focused on surface treatments and antimicrobial coatings to improve the functional features of devices without disturbing the intrinsic properties of the (mostly metallic) material [ 59 , 96 ]. These strategies achieve antimicrobial effects through several mechanisms, including contact-killing, antifouling, and release mechanisms ( Fig. 2 c) [ 49 , 59 , 61 ]. Nowadays, surface modifications of implanted devices have proven to be a powerful approach for reducing the incidence of implant-associated diseases [ 97 ] ( Fig. 2 d). Basically, this process can be carried out at the molecular, atomic, or textural level to precisely modify the surface topography, altering its micro- or nano-structural features and tuning the physicochemical and biological properties of the substrate [ 98 ]. The effectiveness of these surfaces in inhibiting microbial growth is influenced by specific characteristics, such as the size and shape of the nanostructures (e.g., diameter of pits or height of pillars) and their wettability (the ability of the surface to repel or attract water), which collectively determine their interaction with microbial cells [ 98 ]. Additionally, physicochemical processes like silanization have proven effective in functionalizing implants with bioactive and antimicrobial molecules, including peptides, polymers, and proteins [ 98 , 99 ]. Nevertheless, a notable drawback of such surface modification techniques lies in the unpredictability of their antimicrobial effect; that is, the surface does not result in the eradication of the biofilms [ 64 ]. This is because even though microbial cells may have died, they remain attached to the implant and may serve as binding sites for other pathogens, contributing to the proliferation of microorganisms [ 98 ]. The ability of the immunological system to ‘clean’ the surface by removing the dead bacteria from the functional surface is to be proven. In addition to micro- or nano-structuring of a metallic surface, the deposition of antimicrobial coatings represents an alternative for enhancing implant performance and preventing infections [ 100 ]. Coatings involve applying or spreading a substance onto a surface, forming an additional external layer. This may be achieved through several techniques, including electrochemical reactions, immersion, covalent binding of functionalized polymeric films, drop-casting methods, and other advanced processes [ 101 ]. These methods enable surface functionalization with a wide range of antimicrobial agents—such as compounds, molecules, biopolymers, drugs, metallic ions, and peptides—onto metallic surfaces to effectively reduce viable microorganisms in biofilms developing on the substrate [ 102 ]. For instance, Cordeiro et al. demonstrated that copper-containing coatings produced via plasma electrolytic oxidation provided robust antimicrobial activity while improving cell responses [ 103 ]. Coated implants containing antibacterial agents are, in fact, a widely recognized strategy to prevent the initial adhesion of planktonic cells to the implant surface [ 43 , 49 , 98 , 104 , 105 ]. However, the mechanical stresses that the surface undergoes during implant placement can present significant challenges in developing durable coatings [ 98 ]. If the bond between the coating and the implant surface weakens, the coating may deteriorate or peel off, exposing the bare implant. This degradation could create a more favorable environment for microbial colonization, increasing the risk of peri-implant diseases. An approach to overcome this issue is to build a highly hydrophobic coating, as most of the degrading agents for these coatings are water and water-borne [ 106 ]. In general, surface treatments, coatings, or their combination provide targeted antimicrobial mechanisms to combat bacterial adhesion and biofilm formation. The contact-killing mechanism exerts a bactericidal effect through nature-inspired surface designs or by immobilizing antimicrobial agents that leverage their charges to disrupt bacterial cell membranes or impede normal bacterial metabolic functions, resulting in the rupture of bacterial cell membranes or inhibiting bacterial growth and reproduction [ 107 , 108 ]. Similarly, the antifouling mechanism seeks to impede bacterial attachment by altering bonding forces using polymers or modifying the physical properties of the surface. For instance, the design of a superhydrophobic surface may repel microbial cells during the initial adhesion stage [ 61 ]. Certain polymers, such as surfactants, hyaluronic acid, and alginic acid, also offer antifouling effects [ 108 ]. Regarding drug delivery systems, antimicrobial surfaces rely on bactericidal agents, such as antibiotics, to release and effectively prevent microbial proliferation after implant placement [ 109 ]. Nevertheless, the overuse of antibiotics has accelerated the rise of drug-resistant bacterial strains, posing significant challenges [ 110 ]. In this context, while antibiotic-loaded coatings can help inhibit bacterial growth to some extent, challenges remain. One issue is the difficulty in accurately quantifying the necessary amount of drug to incorporate into the coating. Additionally, the lack of a strong bond between the surface and the bactericidal agent and/or the rapid degradation of the coating material can lead to a rapid, uncontrolled drug release (a.k.a. burst release) within a short period. While several studies have aimed to control this burst release, the chronic nature of peri-implant diseases makes it unlikely that such coatings will maintain an adequate, sustained drug release over months or years [ 109 , 111 ]. As a detrimental consequence, this can lead to suboptimal drug concentrations, which may contribute to the development of microbial resistance. Ultimately, the extracellular DNA released from lysed, antibiotic-sensitive microbial cells can trigger the expression of virulence-related genes and promote the proliferation of resistant microorganisms [ 43 ].

2.1 Unraveling the biofilm formation process on implant surfaces Biofilm development is an intricate, multi-step process involving multiple bacterial species. These biofilms are composed of microbial communities enclosed within an extracellular matrix, forming a highly organized structure [ 39 , 40 ]. This matrix consists of exopolysaccharide (EPS), lipids, nucleic acids, and other biomolecules essential for the biofilm's biochemical properties and nutritional needs [ 40 , 41 ]. The EPS and its singular architecture serve dual functions: they provide a survival mechanism that protects bacteria from host immune defenses and external agents such as antibiotics while also acting as a platform for surface attachment. This enables bacterial species to adhere to surfaces, facilitating growth and acting as a virulence factor in implant infections [ 42 ]. Biofilm formation typically unfolds in several stages, including protein adsorption, microbial attachment (reversible and irreversible), maturation, and dispersion/detachment ( Fig. 2 a) [ 43 , 44 ]. In a nutshell, throughout the biofilm formation process, multiple factors from both the microbial cells and the surface drive the initial adhesion, involving polarity, London-van der Waals forces, and hydrophobic interactions [ 45 ]. During this phase, numerous bacteria adhere to the protein-coated surface, initiating attachment and triggering biofilm formation. Although this stage is initially reversible because of the weak interactions between the bacteria and implant, it transitions to an irreversible phase if the attractive forces outweigh the repulsive ones. In such cases, certain bacteria that were loosely attached become firmly fixed, resulting in the formation of a strongly adhered monolayer [ 46 ]. During the maturation stage, the adhered bacteria on the implant surface grow and interact through the secretion of autoinducer signals, activating genes specifically associated with biofilm formation [ 39 , 44 ]. This phase is characterized by the production of EPS, chemical signaling interactions, and the transformation of microcolonies into macrocolonies protected by the extracellular matrix barrier [ 3 ]. Environmental conditions such as oxygenation, pH, nutrient supply, metabolic byproducts, and mass transport mechanisms can induce microbial dysbiosis [ 42 , 43 ]. This dysbiosis drives the shift from a healthy state to a disease. Once the biofilm reaches maturity, microbial cells from the biofilm migrate due to the depletion of nutrients. To sustain growth and access new resources, these cells disperse to other zones of the implant as a strategy to continue another biofilm life cycle, spreading infection and hindering the effectiveness of antimicrobial therapies [ 40 , 47 ].

2.2 Influential factors determining microbial attachment The biofilm attachment is a multifactorial process influenced by the site-specific microbiota and surface characteristics, including surface roughness, surface-free energy and wettability, charge, and electrochemical behavior ( Fig. 2 b) [ 48 , 49 ]. One of the key factors influencing microbial colonization on implants during the initial stages of adhesion is surface roughness. On moderately rough surfaces (Sa = 1.0–2.0 μm) and rough surfaces (Sa >2.0 μm), microorganisms benefit from greater protection against shear forces, favoring their adhesion and proliferation due to the increased contact area between the cells and surface [ 50 ]. However, it is essential to emphasize that the relationship between surface roughness and biofilm formation is complex and depends on several environmental conditions and, at present, there is no universally ideal roughness capable of inhibiting the adhesion of all bacterial species [ 51 , 52 ]. Evidence suggests that an average roughness value of 0.2 μm may serve as a threshold below which bacterial adhesion is unlikely to be further reduced [ 50 , 53 ]. Nevertheless, the applicability of this standard to the implant body surface remains questionable since research has shown that moderate roughness is essential to suitable osteoblastic cell adhesion and the osseointegration process, improving the success rate and secondary stability of the implant [ [54] ,  [55] ,  [56] ,  [57] ,  [58] ]. When considering the influence of surface properties on biofilm development, it is unreliable to assess each property separately. Despite surface roughness being considered a singular feature, its nature may impact other properties, such as wettability [ 59 ]. For instance, evidence suggests that surfaces with a higher roughness exhibit increased hydrophobicity, which may decrease initial bacterial adhesion [ 60 , 61 ]. However, the impact of surface hydrophobicity on bacterial adhesion is multifaceted, as it can either promote or inhibit adhesion depending on the specific conditions. In our previous work, a rough superhydrophobic surface created through plasma technology and chemical modification was demonstrated to reduce bacterial adhesion and biofilm proliferation concurrent with a shift in the microbial profile to a more host-compatible or symbiotic composition [ 61 ]. Furthermore, various bacterial species exhibit distinct preferences for surface hydrophobicity. For instance, the hydrophobic  Streptococcus sanguinis  adheres better to saliva-coated pure Ti and Ti alloy than the hydrophilic  Streptococcus constellatus  [ 62 ]. Another research also demonstrated that the adhesion of  Streptococcus gordonii , a primary colonizer of oral surfaces, varies depending on the physical-chemical properties of different dental materials. Yet, none of the tested materials entirely inhibited bacterial attachment [ 63 ]. Among the relevant factors related to microbial adhesion to implants, surface charge significantly influences the binding force between bacteria and surfaces, and its impact on biofilm development has been recognized inside the biomedical field [ 64 ]. Given that most microbial cells carry a negative charge at neutral pH, positively charged surfaces tend to favor bacterial adhesion, while negatively charged surfaces tend to resist it [ 51 , 65 ]. Beyond charge, the electrochemical behavior of the surface provides an essential role in the integrity of the metallic implants [ 61 ]. From the bio-tribological perspective, which considers the synergistic effect between wear and corrosion under biological conditions, microbiologically induced corrosion significantly influences the fate of implanted materials, particularly in the complex oral environment [ 66 , 67 ]. For example, acidic metabolites generated by the bacteria can lower the pH at the biofilm-implant interface, triggering the diffusion of salivary fluoride ions through the biofilm matrix. This process accelerates metal degradation, increasing the release of Ti ions and particles [ 68 ]. The effect of these metallic ions and particles is species-dependent, potentially altering the biofilm composition and generating dysbiosis by favoring the overgrowth of certain bacterial species [ 69 ]. As a negative consequence, this complex process can disrupt the structure and microbiome profile of the peri-implant region, generating an inflammatory response and compromising the electrochemical stability of the material [ 67 , 69 , 70 ].

2.3 Pathogenesis factors driving disease progression Although the factors that affect the shift from a health-associated to a disease-associated microbiome are not fully understood, there is consensus that relevant conditions such as host inflammatory response [ 71 ], systematic conditions of patients [ 72 ], and critical habits [ 73 ] may contribute to the microbial composition and influence the pathogenesis process [ 74 ]. The host immune response is a complex mechanism that responds not only to the bacteria that cover the implant but also recognizes the biomaterial surface as a foreign body. This recognition triggers an inflammatory response involving the blood coagulation cascade and immune cells, especially neutrophils [ 75 , 76 ]. For this reason, the individual host response to the microbiological profile has a significant role in the progression of peri-implant disease and in microbial dysbiosis that is directly affected by inflammatory tissue breakdown products generated during infection [ 3 ]. Drawing from this concept, molecules within the peri-implant sulcus fluid have been investigated for their association with inflammatory patterns and proteolytic activity [ 76 ]. The increased MMP-8 levels and decreased expression of MMP blockers, for example, lead to tissue damage, attracting active osteoclasts and stimulating bone resorption [ 77 ]. MMP-8 triggers the breakdown of type I collagen, abundant in periodontal and peri-implant regions, and is notably evident in patients with peri-implantitis [ 78 ]. Studies have linked higher MMP-8 levels in peri-implantitis sites to clinical disease signs, and its reduction post-treatment suggests its potential as a biomarker for diagnosing peri-implant health or disease [ 79 , 80 ]. Furthermore, the state of macrophage polarization within peri-implantitis lesions represents a significant signaling pathway. In general, M1 macrophages drive a pro-inflammatory response stimulated by bacterial cues, whereas M2 macrophages are essential in resolving inflammation and hence aid tissue repair. In this sense, the balance and expression of M1/M2 macrophages potentially affect the immune response quality and the extent of tissue damage [ 81 , 82 ]. Similarly, each subject exhibits distinct biological factors that impact peri-implant disease initiation, development, and worsening [ 83 ]. Despite the lack of a direct association of diabetes as a critical condition for peri-implantitis development, it is generally assumed that diabetes induces a negative influence on inflammatory mechanisms and apoptosis, leading to an insufficient host response and impairing tissue healing [ 72 , 84 ]. Studies show that the inflammatory process is significantly increased in a chronic hyperglycemia condition. The classical expression of proinflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α and interleukin (IL)-6, as well as certain chemokines, like C–C chemokine receptor (CCR)-2 and monocyte chemotactic protein (MCP)-1 can be confirmed in peri-implant biopsies of diabetic individuals [ 85 , 86 ]. As expected, the level of these mediators is directly related to the peri-implantitis severity and is more prominent in patients with poorly controlled diabetes [ 72 ]. On the other hand, maintaining proper glycemic control reduces implant failure rates and mitigates the hyperinflammatory state often observed in peri-implantitis regions, highlighting the importance of glycemic regulation in promoting effective healing and long-term stability of implants [ 87 ]. In the same way that systemic conditions may negatively interfere with implant survival rates, chronic smoking seems to be associated with the severity of peri-implant disease [ 73 ]. Like co-morbidities, tobacco products can alter the host response by affecting antibody production and the secretion of immunoinflammatory mediators, including pro-inflammatory cytokines [ 88 ]. Furthermore, evidence shows that smokers exhibit an abundant pathogen-rich anaerobic microbiome, resembling a community associated with disease [ 89 ]. Interestingly, this dysbiosis condition exists even in periodontally healthy individuals and remains evident even after treating the disease, creating an environment prone to harm and at risk of potential inflammation in the future [ 90 ]. Occasionally, bacterial infection following bone implant surgery is another critical issue when considering these patients, and the development of multifunctional scaffolds capable of preventing infection while supporting bone regeneration has been reported to be a potential treatment strategy [ 91 ]. Considering the aspects mentioned, one of the main strategies to prevent biofilm accumulation is oral hygiene practices [ 92 ]. Regular maintenance and proper oral hygiene decrease the development of peri-implantitis, playing an essential role in preventing the shifts in the microbiota profile to a dysbiotic condition [ 93 ]. However, in addition to systemic diseases and critical habits, real conditions such as a patient's motor abilities, frequent carbohydrate consumption, and lack of cooperation during follow-up appointments represent a clinical challenge in preventing and treating implant-related infections [ 94 , 95 ]. For these reasons, the development of advanced implant surface strategies has become a focal point, offering a targeted local approach to minimize biofilm formation and reduce the risk of implant-related infections, particularly in patients where conventional preventive measures fall short.

2.4 Touchpoints in antibacterial surface design strategies Surface properties of implants have been shown to directly impact the biofilm formation. Hence, anti-biofilm strategies for biomedical implants are mostly focused on surface treatments and antimicrobial coatings to improve the functional features of devices without disturbing the intrinsic properties of the (mostly metallic) material [ 59 , 96 ]. These strategies achieve antimicrobial effects through several mechanisms, including contact-killing, antifouling, and release mechanisms ( Fig. 2 c) [ 49 , 59 , 61 ]. Nowadays, surface modifications of implanted devices have proven to be a powerful approach for reducing the incidence of implant-associated diseases [ 97 ] ( Fig. 2 d). Basically, this process can be carried out at the molecular, atomic, or textural level to precisely modify the surface topography, altering its micro- or nano-structural features and tuning the physicochemical and biological properties of the substrate [ 98 ]. The effectiveness of these surfaces in inhibiting microbial growth is influenced by specific characteristics, such as the size and shape of the nanostructures (e.g., diameter of pits or height of pillars) and their wettability (the ability of the surface to repel or attract water), which collectively determine their interaction with microbial cells [ 98 ]. Additionally, physicochemical processes like silanization have proven effective in functionalizing implants with bioactive and antimicrobial molecules, including peptides, polymers, and proteins [ 98 , 99 ]. Nevertheless, a notable drawback of such surface modification techniques lies in the unpredictability of their antimicrobial effect; that is, the surface does not result in the eradication of the biofilms [ 64 ]. This is because even though microbial cells may have died, they remain attached to the implant and may serve as binding sites for other pathogens, contributing to the proliferation of microorganisms [ 98 ]. The ability of the immunological system to ‘clean’ the surface by removing the dead bacteria from the functional surface is to be proven. In addition to micro- or nano-structuring of a metallic surface, the deposition of antimicrobial coatings represents an alternative for enhancing implant performance and preventing infections [ 100 ]. Coatings involve applying or spreading a substance onto a surface, forming an additional external layer. This may be achieved through several techniques, including electrochemical reactions, immersion, covalent binding of functionalized polymeric films, drop-casting methods, and other advanced processes [ 101 ]. These methods enable surface functionalization with a wide range of antimicrobial agents—such as compounds, molecules, biopolymers, drugs, metallic ions, and peptides—onto metallic surfaces to effectively reduce viable microorganisms in biofilms developing on the substrate [ 102 ]. For instance, Cordeiro et al. demonstrated that copper-containing coatings produced via plasma electrolytic oxidation provided robust antimicrobial activity while improving cell responses [ 103 ]. Coated implants containing antibacterial agents are, in fact, a widely recognized strategy to prevent the initial adhesion of planktonic cells to the implant surface [ 43 , 49 , 98 , 104 , 105 ]. However, the mechanical stresses that the surface undergoes during implant placement can present significant challenges in developing durable coatings [ 98 ]. If the bond between the coating and the implant surface weakens, the coating may deteriorate or peel off, exposing the bare implant. This degradation could create a more favorable environment for microbial colonization, increasing the risk of peri-implant diseases. An approach to overcome this issue is to build a highly hydrophobic coating, as most of the degrading agents for these coatings are water and water-borne [ 106 ]. In general, surface treatments, coatings, or their combination provide targeted antimicrobial mechanisms to combat bacterial adhesion and biofilm formation. The contact-killing mechanism exerts a bactericidal effect through nature-inspired surface designs or by immobilizing antimicrobial agents that leverage their charges to disrupt bacterial cell membranes or impede normal bacterial metabolic functions, resulting in the rupture of bacterial cell membranes or inhibiting bacterial growth and reproduction [ 107 , 108 ]. Similarly, the antifouling mechanism seeks to impede bacterial attachment by altering bonding forces using polymers or modifying the physical properties of the surface. For instance, the design of a superhydrophobic surface may repel microbial cells during the initial adhesion stage [ 61 ]. Certain polymers, such as surfactants, hyaluronic acid, and alginic acid, also offer antifouling effects [ 108 ]. Regarding drug delivery systems, antimicrobial surfaces rely on bactericidal agents, such as antibiotics, to release and effectively prevent microbial proliferation after implant placement [ 109 ]. Nevertheless, the overuse of antibiotics has accelerated the rise of drug-resistant bacterial strains, posing significant challenges [ 110 ]. In this context, while antibiotic-loaded coatings can help inhibit bacterial growth to some extent, challenges remain. One issue is the difficulty in accurately quantifying the necessary amount of drug to incorporate into the coating. Additionally, the lack of a strong bond between the surface and the bactericidal agent and/or the rapid degradation of the coating material can lead to a rapid, uncontrolled drug release (a.k.a. burst release) within a short period. While several studies have aimed to control this burst release, the chronic nature of peri-implant diseases makes it unlikely that such coatings will maintain an adequate, sustained drug release over months or years [ 109 , 111 ]. As a detrimental consequence, this can lead to suboptimal drug concentrations, which may contribute to the development of microbial resistance. Ultimately, the extracellular DNA released from lysed, antibiotic-sensitive microbial cells can trigger the expression of virulence-related genes and promote the proliferation of resistant microorganisms [ 43 ].

3 Fundamental mechanisms of photoresponsive biomaterials Currently, although the abovementioned strategies assisted by surface modification and antimicrobial-loaded coatings have been demonstrated to effectively reduce biofilms, the necessity for high antimicrobial doses (e.g., antimicrobial metals) to prevent and control infection can lead to elevated concentrations that might induce toxicity and adverse effects. This scenario may easily induce bacterial resistance and diminish the surface's effectiveness in antimicrobial action over time. For all these reasons, researchers have undertaken the development of coatings and alternative techniques that allow smart and controlled drug release to provide a suitable antimicrobial effect. Thus, ideally, these technologies should be cautious when using antibiotics. Among antibiotic-free technologies, light-based approaches, such as PTT, PDT, and photocatalysis, stand out as highly attractive options due to their rapid response, straightforward control through user-friendly devices, and reduced risks of developing antibacterial resistance ( Fig. 3 ). Fig. 3 Schematic illustration of light-based approaches towards biofilm eradication.  Photodynamic therapy (PDT), photothermal therapy (PTT), and photocatalysis each employ distinct antibacterial mechanisms but share the common principle of utilizing light to target and eliminate biofilms. PDT relies on a photosensitizer that, upon light activation, generates reactive oxygen species (ROS), leading to bacterial membrane damage and cell death. PTT leverages photothermal agents that absorb light and convert it into heat, raising the local temperature to induce bacterial destruction. This effect can be enhanced by plasmonic nanomaterials, which exhibit localized surface plasmon resonance, amplifying light absorption and heat generation. Photocatalysis, in turn, involves semiconductor materials that, upon light irradiation, generate electron-hole pairs, initiating oxidative reactions and ROS generation that kill bacteria. These techniques have been widely explored for medical and environmental applications, offering promising strategies for biofilm eradication. Fig. 3 3.1 Photothermal therapy PTT is based on the local increase of temperature to induce bacterial death, relying on two essential components: (i) a light source with an appropriate wavelength and (ii) a photothermal agent (PTA). The most frequently employed light spectrum for PTT is near-infrared (NIR), wherein the first NIR window (NIR-I) spans wavelengths from 700 to 1000 nm, and the second NIR window (NIR-II) ranges from 1000 to 1700 nm [ 112 ]. The utilization of NIR light is primarily attributed to its enhanced penetration into tissues and diminished absorption by water and blood components, such as hemoglobin, facilitating superior biomedical applications. The second pivotal component for PTT is a PTA, which, when exposed to light, can convert light energy into heat through various mechanisms depending on the type of PTA [ 113 ]. The primordial characteristics of PTAs for biomedical applications include higher photothermal conversion efficiency (PCE), photostability, excellent biocompatibility, rapid clearance from the body after use, and facile synthesis and modification [ 114 ]. Among the myriad PTAs reported in the literature, four main types can be identified: noble metals, semiconductors, polymers, and organic molecules. Each PTA employs a distinct mechanism of heat generation [ 113 ]. Noble metal materials, such as gold (Au), silver (Ag), and platinum (Pt), commonly in nanoparticle form, serve as photothermal agents due to the photophysical phenomenon known as local surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) [ 115 ]. In LSPR, light irradiation induces the excitation of free electrons on the metallic surface, leading to the collective oscillation of electrons in the CB. The non-radiative decay process, via intra- and interband transitions, results in the formation of energetic and hot electrons, with particle heating attributed to the phonon-phonon scattering process [ 116 ]. Nevertheless, the photothermal action of noble metallic nanoparticles is intrinsically linked to factors such as size, shape, dielectric constant, wavelength, and light intensity. Semiconductors, including molybdenum disulfide (MoS 2 ), manganese dioxide (MnO 2 ), and titanium dioxide (TiO 2 ), constitute the second class of PTAs capable of generating heat. Here, this process occurs through the generation and relaxation of electron-hole pairs. Light irradiation of semiconductors with energy equal to or greater than the band gap causes electron excitation, leading to their migration to the CB. Subsequently, electronic vacancies or holes are formed in the VB. The non-radiative relaxation of electrons allows the liberated energy, in the form of heat, to affect the crystal structure of the semiconductor [ 117 ]. Consequently, the crystal's thermal energy increases, promoting temperature rise and distribution. In addition to metals and semiconductors, polymers (e.g., polyaniline [ 118 ], poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) [ 119 ] and carbon-based nanomaterials [ 120 ]) are extensively investigated as PTAs due to their advantageous properties, such as biodegradability and high PCE, respectively. Polymers and carbon-based materials as PTAs induce a temperature increase through molecular orbital migration. PTA's electrons in the ground state, within the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO), undergo excitation upon light irradiation, migrating to a higher energy orbital, the lowest occupied molecular orbital (LOMO) [ 121 ]. This transition, coupled with a relaxation process, facilitates energy transfer from the excited electron to the atomic lattice, increasing the material's temperature [ 115 ]. Yet, more recently, small organic molecules have emerged as a new generation of PTAs. For instance, cyanine-based dyes (indocyanine green [ 122 ], Prussian blue [ 123 ], red phosphorous [ 124 ]) offer cost-effectiveness and purportedly higher biocompatibility. For example, Shim et al. [ 125 ] demonstrated that indocyanine green, combined with NIR light (801 nm) for 12 s (24 J cm −2 ), induced a 96.8 % reduction in  Streptococcus gordonii  biofilms cultivated on zirconia disks. Nevertheless, the low PCE, poor photostability, and lack of an in vivo assay remain significant drawbacks to further applications of this PTA class in the prevention and treatment of infections associated with zirconia dental implants. Regardless of the mechanism, the antimicrobial effect induced by PTAs under irradiation is directly correlated with the biological effects of increased temperature. Since human infections are primarily caused by mesophile microorganisms, i.e., organisms that thrive at approximately 37 °C, temperatures exceeding this threshold are regarded to cause cell damage [ 126 ]. PTT-induced damage in microbial cells is intrinsically associated with the denaturation of bacterial cell walls, proteins, and enzymes, culminating in the leakage of cell components and DNA/RNA inactivation [ 127 ]. This effect is primarily attributable to alterations in protein/nucleic acid structure, induced spatial dissociation/rearrangement of protein subunits, or the disruption of chemical interactions between amino acid side chains [ 128 ]. Behzadpour et al. [ 129 ] demonstrated that polypyrrole core–carbon-coated nanostructures increased on average 20 °C within 20 min of exposure to 808 nm wavelength light. The temperature increase resulted in an approximately 80 % reduction in colony-forming units (CFU) of methicillin-resistant  Staphylococcus aureus  ( S. aureus ) (MRSA), with protein and nucleic acid leakage assessed by the Bradford method. Also, Shi et al. [ 130 ] revealed that molybdenum disulfide nanodots, combined with erythrocyte membrane fragments, can alter bacterial morphology. However, just as bacteria are prone to heat damage, host cells are also susceptible. Considering this, Hu et al. [ 131 ] developed a surface charge-adaptive gold nanoparticle (AgNP) capable of adhering and accumulating preferentially in biofilms. The PTT effect in MRSA resulted in a robust bactericidal effect, and in rabbits, the same antimicrobial effect was observed, with minimal heat spreading to healthy tissues and less pronounced inflammatory infiltration after 7 days of treatment. Addressing the need for implants capable of sequentially regulating antibacterial activity and promoting osteogenesis, Chen et al. developed a micropatterned graphene oxide nanocomposite coating on titanium implants [ 132 ]. In vitro, the coating exhibited potent antibacterial effects under NIR light, reducing  E. coli  and  S. aureus  by 96.9 % and 98.6 %, respectively, due to its photothermal effect (reaching 54.3 °C within 10 min) while its micropatterned surface supported cell adhesion, guided growth, and enhanced osteogenic differentiation in the absence of light. This dual-functional design offers a promising strategy for antibacterial implants that effectively combat infection and support bone integration—two critical challenges in long-term implant success. Similarly, to overcome persistent bacterial infections on titanium implants, a multifunctional coating composed of Cu 2-x S and graphene oxide (TGC) was developed, enabling synergistic photothermal and chemodynamic antibacterial action under NIR-II irradiation [ 133 ]. In vitro, the coating exhibited strong photothermal behavior and generated hydroxyl radicals (·OH) via Fenton-like reactions in the presence of H 2 O 2 , leading to 99.2 % and 99.4 % bacterial reduction against  E. coli  and  S. aureus , respectively. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis revealed severe morphological damage and membrane rupture in bacteria exposed to the TGC coating under NIR light. In vivo, the coating maintained photothermal performance and significantly reduced bacterial load in an implant-associated infection model, with 98.75 % inhibition of  S. aureus  and decreased IL-6 expression in peri-implant tissues, indicating effective infection control and attenuation of inflammation. Certain metal ions, such as Cu 2+ , have demonstrated antibacterial properties and the ability to induce chemodynamic therapy (CDT) effects (i.e., ROS generation via a catalytic mechanism). For example, Mei et al. [ 134 ] developed copper-doped polyoxometalate nanoclusters (Cu-POM) as a multifunctional strategy to eradicate biofilm-associated infections on implant surfaces through synergistic chemodynamic and mild PTT ( Fig. 4 a). In vitro, Cu-POM combined with NIR irradiation generated ROS and hydroxyl radicals via Fenton-like reactions, as confirmed by methylene blue oxidation and electron paramagnetic resonance ( Fig. 4 b). This treatment also caused lipid peroxidation, DNA degradation, and up to 53.6 % bacterial death, altering biofilm metabolism with thousands of metabolites upregulated or downregulated ( Fig. 4 c). Beyond direct antibacterial effects, Cu-POM + NIR stimulated macrophage polarization toward the pro-inflammatory M1 phenotype via ROS-mediated pathways. In vivo, the Cu-POM + NIR-treated group exhibited effective temperature rise (∼45 °C), complete wound healing, reduced biofilm burden, suppressed inflammation, and elevated expression of CD86 and iNOS, confirming the reactivation of local innate immunity. Further, to tackle implant-associated infections and promote bone integration, a multifunctional titanium implant (Ti-TF-acBSP) was developed by co-functionalizing the surface with photothermal FeIIITA nanoparticles and immunomodulatory acetylated Bletilla striata polysaccharide (acBSP) ( Fig. 4 d–g) [ 135 ]. In vitro, under NIR irradiation, the coating achieved ∼80 % reduction of  S. aureus  through hyperthermia-induced bacterial membrane disruption, confirmed by morphological deformation, ONPG hydrolysis, and DNA leakage assays. Beyond direct antibacterial effects, acBSP induced macrophage polarization toward the M1 phenotype, enhancing pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion, bacterial phagocytosis, and promoting the secretion of osteoinductive factors such as OSM and VEGF, which stimulated osteogenic differentiation of MSCs. In vivo, the Ti-TF-acBSP coating exhibited excellent photothermal activity, significantly reduced bacterial colonization in a rat femur infection model, suppressed inflammation, and improved new bone formation and implant-bone contact.
