Fig. 4 As demonstrated, PTT offers several advantages, including a broad antimicrobial spectrum of action, a relatively brief treatment duration, a low likelihood of bacterial resistance, and effective antibiofilm activity. However, PTT presents some limitations, including potential undesired cytotoxicity to host cells in the vicinity [ 136 ], which is dependent on the temperature attained during the treatment protocol, and a restricted or insufficient investigation efficacy against mature multispecies biofilms. Consequently, photothermal biomaterials have frequently been developed and explored with other antimicrobial strategies, primarily photodynamic therapy—a second type of therapy based on light exposure. 3.2 Photodynamic therapy PDT constitutes an antimicrobial approach reliant on the generation of ROS through the interaction of a photosensitizer with light of a compatible and specific wavelength [ 137 ]. This process aims to induce damage and subsequent death in microbial cells. In contrast to PTT, PDT offers the flexibility to utilize various wavelengths of light, depending on the photosensitizer. However, not all wavelengths are suitable for clinical applications. For instance, exposure to UV light (λ < 400 nm) can instigate oxidative stress in host cells, potentially leading to apoptosis [ 138 ] and, in severe cases, a mutagenic and oncogenic effect [ 139 ]. The utilization of clinical blue light (400 < λ < 490 nm) remains a subject of debate, with certain studies suggesting cytotoxicity [ 140 ]. Nevertheless, the detrimental effects are believed to be linked to light fluence [ 141 ], defined as the energy received per unit area and per unit time. Consequently, most PDT studies are focused on higher wavelengths, notably around 630 nm. The preference for higher wavelengths aligns with the optical window concept [ 142 ], suggesting that these higher wavelengths can mitigate two principal optical phenomena limitations. The first phenomenon is light scattering, whereby biological tissues with diverse components, such as macromolecules, cell organelles, and interstitial layers, scatter light, resulting in light dispersion and loss of directionality [ 142 ]. Light scattering serves as the primary limiting factor for light penetration [ 143 ]. Consequently, longer wavelengths exhibit reduced scattering. Although less significant, the second phenomenon is light absorption by tissue chromophores, primarily hemoglobin, myoglobin, melanin, and cytochromes [ 144 ]. These endogenous chromophores predominantly absorb light in wavelengths around 400 nm. However, longer wavelengths (≈1300 nm) undergo absorption primarily by water [ 143 ]. At the same time, the photons in these longer wavelengths may not have the required energy to excite the photosensitizer. Therefore, researchers have proposed an optical window ranging from 630 to 850 nm, with an effective average penetration depth of 1–6 mm [ 142 , 145 ]. Considering these photophysics concepts and limitations, adjustments to light parameters can optimize the success of the PDT process. Corrections of light parameters such as fluence, wavelength, and even the angle of incidence can be made using mathematical theorems [ 145 ]. Still, light is not the sole determinant in this process; the photosensitizer also plays a crucial role in PDT. Photosensitizers are substances capable of absorbing and transferring energy, exhibiting specific required characteristics such as low dark toxicity, clinical acceptance of light absorption wavelengths, a high absorption band to minimize the required photosensitizer dose, and painless administration [ 146 ]. Furthermore, for clinical acceptability, photosensitizers must possess a constant composition, extended shelf life, and preferably, be water-soluble with no aggregation in biological environments to maintain photochemical efficiency [ 147 ]. Over the past few decades, numerous photosensitizers have been developed and studied, categorized into different classes [ 137 ]. The tetrapyrrole class is the most utilized and is characterized by chemical compounds featuring four pyrrole aromatic rings [ 148 ]. Each pyrrole ring consists of four carbon atoms and one nitrogen atom, enabling these naturally occurring pigments to exhibit high light absorption at the Soret band (≈400 nm) and peaks at the Q bands (≈620–700 nm) [ 147 ]. Upon irradiation, this class predominantly produces singlet oxygen. Within the tetrapyrroles, well-known and commercially available photosensitizers include porphyrins (e.g., photofrin, chlorins, and phthalocyanines) [ 149 ]. These subclasses are primarily employed with red (≈660 nm) and far-red (>670 nm) light, except for indocyanine green, which is used with near-infrared light [ 137 ]. Another significant photosensitizer class encompasses synthetic dyes, with methylene blue [ 150 ] and toluidine blue [ 151 ] from the phenothiazinium salts subclass being well-known examples, absorbing light around 660 nm wavelength. Another class of photosensitizers comprises natural compounds [ 152 ]. Although still a topic of debate in the literature due to their variable composition and plant-based origin, natural photosensitizers, such as curcumin, have been tested for PDT effects under blue light irradiation [ 153 ]. The amount and type of light the photosensitizer absorbs are pivotal in determining its subsequent activity and efficiency. In cases of excessive light absorption, photosensitizer can undergo the photobleaching phenomenon, which involves the destruction of the photosensitizer molecule, often resulting in diminished PDT effectiveness and reduced ROS production [ 147 ]. The generation of ROS, responsible for antimicrobial effects, is a multifaceted process involving photophysics and photochemistry processes. In its ground state, the photosensitizer possesses two electrons with opposite spins positioned in the lower energy molecular orbital. Upon irradiation, one of these electrons is excited to a higher energy orbital, retaining its ground state spin and forming the first excited singlet state of the photosensitizer with only nanoseconds of life before its energy loss. Three outcomes may occur: (i) fluorescence emission, (ii) conversion of lost energy into heat, or (iii) spin inversion. The spin inversion is mediated by the intersystem crossing process, forming the photosensitizer triplet excited state with a longer lifetime (microseconds) [ 154 ]. The triplet excited state of the photosensitizer can undergo two types of reactions [ 155 ]. In Type I reactions, superoxide anion radicals (O 2 − ), hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ), and hydroxyl radicals (·OH) are produced. O 2 −  is primarily generated through monovalent reduction, wherein the triplet photosensitizer state transfers an electron to an O 2  molecule [ 156 ]. Alternatively, charge transfer from the triplet photosensitizer state to an oxygen molecule may occur. Although O 2 −  does not exhibit high oxidant activity, it plays a crucial role in the production of H 2 O 2 , ·OH, and other ROS. Superoxide anion radicals can undergo dismutation to form hydrogen peroxide and oxygen. Additionally, O 2 −  can donate an electron to metallic ions like Fe 3+ , initiating the Fenton reaction, wherein hydrogen peroxide produces hydroxyl radicals. This reaction breaks down oxygen-oxygen bonds in H 2 O 2 , forming hydroxyl radicals and hydroxide ions. Other potential reactions involve superoxide anions interacting with hydroxyl or nitric oxide (NO) radicals. The interaction between O 2 −  and H 2 O 2 , as well as O 2 −  with NO, results in the formation of singlet oxygen ( 1 O 2 ) and peroxynitrite (OONO − ), respectively. Singlet oxygen is also formed through an alternative route, the Type II reaction, following light irradiation. In this reaction, the excited photosensitizer can directly transfer its energy to an oxygen molecule, generating singlet oxygen [ 154 , 157 , 158 ]. This specific ROS ( 1 O 2 ) has a brief half-life, approximately 40 ns, and a short action radius of around 20 nm. Thus, the presence of oxygen during PDT is imperative for proper ROS generation and, consequently, antimicrobial activity. The antimicrobial effects induced by PDT are directly related to the interaction of ROS with bacteria, fungi cells, and biofilms [ 159 ]. ROS such as H 2 O 2  and ·OH can easily traverse cell membranes, actively participating in enzyme activity and other biological processes [ 154 ]. Within cells, ·OH radicals can initiate chain reactions by adding themselves to organic substrates or oxidizing these substrates through electron subtraction. In both scenarios, the reaction products are radicals that can further interact with other molecules and substrates. This chain reaction primarily contributes to the oxidative damage inflicted by ROS produced from PDT. Targeted sites for chemical oxidation encompass fatty acids, lipids, proteins, and DNA [ 160 , 161 ]. In proteins, amino acid residues such as cysteine, methionine, tyrosine, and histidine are primarily affected. Ene-reactions lead to the oxidation of unsaturated lipids, generating lipid hydroperoxides [ 154 ]. Regarding DNA, two potential targets exist: nucleic acids, with guanine being the most susceptible, and sugars, particularly deoxyribose, which promotes linkage between DNA strands [ 162 ]. Although cells possess mechanisms to repair and rectify certain oxidative damages, PDT can cause extensive damage that surpasses the repair capacity. Consequently, microbial cells may undergo death or incur severe mutations [ 161 ]. Concerns within the scientific community have been raised regarding PDT's potential to induce antimicrobial resistance when complete microbial eradication is not achieved [ 163 ]. Microbial cells employ an enzyme machinery comprising superoxide dismutase, catalase, and peroxidase, among others [ 164 ]. However, these enzymes prove ineffective against ROS generated by PDT, primarily due to the damage occurring in the cell membrane, leading to cell leakage [ 165 ]. Additionally, there is no known enzyme specifically targeting  1 O 2 , possibly because singlet oxygen represents a high-energy form of an oxygen molecule [ 163 ]. Although some concerns exist regarding the possibility of internalized photosensitizers by microbial cells being expelled through efflux pumps, only a select few photosensitizers possess the necessary structure to be substrates for these efflux pumps [ 166 ]. Consequently, PDT stands out as a promising strategy for addressing infections and overcoming antimicrobial resistance. For instance, Dovigo et al. [ 167 ] demonstrated that curcumin-based PDT achieved a ∼5-log reduction in  Candida albicans  and effectively inactivated  S. aureus , with efficacy strongly influenced by photosensitizer concentration, light fluence, and pre-irradiation time. Similarly, Anil et al. [ 168 ] reported that methylene blue-mediated PDT significantly reduced  Tannerella forsythia  and  Porphyromonas gingivalis  on titanium compared to conventional agents without altering surface roughness or energy—preserving implant surface integrity. To address biofilm-related implant infections, a multifunctional titanium implant surface (Ti-M/I/RGD) was developed, integrating mesoporous polydopamine nanoparticles (MPDA) for photothermal conversion, indocyanine green (ICG) for PDT and RGD peptides for enhanced cytocompatibility [ 169 ]. ICG was selected as the photosensitizer due to its strong absorption in the near-infrared (NIR) region. In vitro, the Ti-M/I/RGD substrate exhibited strong NIR-triggered photothermal effects and efficient ROS generation, achieving up to 99.7 %  S. aureus  reduction through the synergistic action of PDT and PTT. The platform effectively disrupted established biofilms by enhancing membrane permeability, promoting DNA degradation, and increasing bacterial susceptibility to lytic enzymes. Notably, RGD-functionalized surfaces maintained mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) adhesion, proliferation, and osteogenic gene expression, even after NIR exposure. In vivo, Ti-M/I/RGD implants demonstrated superior biofilm eradication (∼95.4 % efficiency), suppressed inflammation, and significantly improved bone-implant contact (62.6 %) and new bone formation (56.4 %) in a rat femoral model, representing a clinically relevant advance in the design of antibacterial orthopedic implants. In another study, to address the challenges of hypoxic microenvironments and the structural resistance of biofilms in peri-implantitis, a smart multifunctional implant surface (Ti-U@SnS 2 /I) was developed by integrating upconversion nanoparticles (UCNPs), partially oxidized SnS 2 , and the photosensitizer ICG [ 170 ]. UCNPs convert NIR to visible light, activating SnS 2  for the controlled release of O 2  and CO, while ICG induces aPDT via ROS generation. In vitro and in vivo results demonstrated substantial biofilm eradication (up to 84.7 % in vivo) against  P. gingivalis ,  F. nucleatum , and  S. sanguinis , as well as suppression of NF-κB/p65 signaling and promotion of tissue regeneration, offering a non-antibiotic strategy for managing implant-associated infections. Further, Li et al. developed a magnetron-sputtered MoS 2  with IR780 photosensitizer and RGDC peptide to address persistent implant-associated infections through synergistic PTT and PDT [ 171 ]. In vitro, titanium substrates coated with MoS 2  and loaded with IR780 (Ti–MoS 2 –IPR) exhibited strong absorption in the NIR region and significant photothermal performance, reaching ∼50 °C within 5 min under 0.5 W cm −2  irradiation. Upon NIR exposure, IR780 generated singlet oxygen ( 1 O 2 ), as confirmed by DPBF degradation, while MoS 2  catalyzed glutathione (GSH) oxidation, increasing bacterial susceptibility to heat. The synergistic PTT/PDT effect significantly enhanced  S. aureus  biofilm eradication (97.41 ± 0.46 %) compared to PTT or PDT alone. Mechanistically, ROS-induced membrane damage increased bacterial heat sensitivity and protein leakage, with ONPG and GSH assays confirming compromised membrane permeability and oxidative stress. In vivo, Ti–MoS 2 –IPR achieved a 98.99 ± 0.42 % biofilm reduction within 20 min, with minimal inflammatory infiltration and superior bone integration. Although aPDT is among the most established light-based strategies for infection control, its full clinical integration remains limited by a complex interplay of biological, procedural, and translational reasons. A central obstacle lies in its application against biofilms, which are inherently more resistant to treatment due to their spatial structure, microbial diversity, and protective extracellular matrix [ 172 ]. The penetration of photosensitizers into mature biofilms is often incomplete, potentially limiting ROS-mediated action to superficial layers [ 173 ]. To overcome this, some protocols rely on prolonged photosensitizer pre-incubation and extended irradiation times. While these adjustments may enhance antimicrobial efficacy, they also can increase the risk of adverse effects on host tissues through oxidative stress, phototoxicity, and thermal effects. Also, significant methodological heterogeneity is observed across the aPDT literature regarding photosensitizer composition, concentration, light wavelength, intensity, and whether light delivery is performed with or without surgical access to the infected site. This lack of standardization impedes protocol reproducibility and complicates clinical implementation. Furthermore, the biological relevance of many preclinical models and protocols remains debatable since a large proportion of studies are conducted on planktonic bacteria or simplified mono-species biofilms, often neglecting the polymicrobial complexity and ecological interactions that characterize real clinical infections. Also, regulatory approval remains restricted to a few photosensitizers, and the economic feasibility of implementing aPDT, especially in resource-limited settings, has not been clearly established. As a result, recent attention has shifted toward photocatalytic materials capable of producing reactive oxygen species without exogenous photosensitizers, offering a more autonomous and potentially more practical antimicrobial strategy for clinical use. 3.3 Photocatalysis According to the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry, photocatalysis can be defined as the modification of a chemical reaction rate or initiation under light exposure by the presence of a photocatalyst. The initial reports of photocatalysis date back to the 1920s when it was observed that TiO 2  and other oxides, such as cerium dioxide (CeO 2 ), niobium pentoxide (Nb 2 O 5 ), and tantalum pentoxide (Ta 2 O 5 ), undergo partial reduction after illumination [ 174 ]. Concurrently, researchers speculated on the simultaneous occurrence of reduction and oxidation reactions [ 175 ]. The discussion gained momentum with the observation of exterior paints, particularly those containing TiO 2  [ 174 ]. It was noted that when exposed to intense sunlight, Ti-based exterior paints produced a chalky substance. This chalk resulted from the removal of organic compounds from the paint, leaving behind remnants of exposed TiO 2 -composed paints [ 176 ]. Further interest arose, leading to the evaluation of the photocatalytic effect of TiO 2  associated with light for dye degradation in 1938 [ 175 ]. The absorbance spectrum of TiO 2  powder was also characterized during this period [ 175 ]. Alternatively, in the 1950s, zinc oxide emerged as a promising candidate, proving to be as efficient as TiO 2  [ 174 ]. Yet, Frand & Bard [ 177 ] proposed that illuminating TiO 2  could be utilized for water purification, given its ability to photodecompose water pollutants. Subsequent research revealed that photocatalysis mediated by TiO 2  or other photocatalysts holds promise for environmental, organic synthesis, and biomedical applications. The biomedical interest in photocatalysis soared, particularly following Matsunaga's work in 1985, [ 178 ], which is believed to be the first to demonstrate the antibacterial effects of TiO 2  photocatalysis. Therefore, photocatalysis has garnered interest, particularly for controlling biofilm-related infections, especially the heterogeneous photocatalysis type. Thus, by bridging environmental sustainability with advancements in human and animal health, photocatalysis not only offers practical solutions for pollution control but also could aid in bacterial/microbial infection management. 3.3.1 Integrating photocatalysis into the One Health concept We here present a pioneering perspective by proposing that photocatalysis offers a distinctive and integrative approach within the One Health concept ( Fig. 5 a). This framework recognizes the interconnected health of humans, animals, and the environment, addressing shared global challenges through light-activated antimicrobial and pollutant-degrading technologies. Photocatalysis holds the potential for sustainable and safe interventions across diverse ecosystems, positioning itself as a transformative tool for advancing health on multiple fronts. From an environmental perspective, for example, photocatalysis, particularly under UV light or solar irradiation, has shown significant promise in promoting cleaner and safer ecosystems. Key applications include the development of self-cleaning surfaces, which reduce the persistence of harmful pathogens in public spaces and high-contact environments. Additionally, photocatalytic materials play a critical role in air purification, breaking down airborne pollutants such as volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and nitrogen oxides, thereby improving indoor and outdoor air quality [ 179 , 180 ]. Notably, the use of photocatalysis for water treatment and the degradation of organic and inorganic contaminants in water systems addresses critical issues related to water scarcity and pollution [ 21 ]. By reducing the concentration of emerging contaminants—such as pharmaceuticals and endocrine disruptors—photocatalysis mitigates ecological damage and fosters healthier aquatic ecosystems [ 30 , 179 ]. This cleaner environment, in turn, curbs the spread of environmental pathogens that contribute to zoonotic diseases and antimicrobial resistance. Fig. 5 Schematic illustration proposing the photocatalysis applications within the One Health concept.  a) Photocatalysis leverages different light sources to address environmental, human, and animal health challenges. UV light and solar irradiation are widely applied in living environments, enabling self-cleaning surfaces, air pollutant removal, industrial wastewater treatment, and water purification, contributing to sustainable ecosystems. Visible light is used for medical applications, including antimicrobial therapies, infection control on implant surfaces, and wound healing, ensuring safe and effective treatment strategies while contributing to the prevention of antibiotic resistance. b) When focusing on human health applications, the type of light used becomes critical. UV light, while effective for photocatalysis, poses significant risks to tissues due to its carcinogenic and mutagenic effects, making it unsuitable for direct biomedical or implant dentistry use. Visible light, being safer and non-ionizing, emerges as the optimal choice for health-related photocatalytic applications, balancing efficacy and safety for patients, animals, and medical environments. Fig. 5 In the realm of human health, visible-light-triggered photocatalysis emerges as a safer and more versatile alternative to traditional UV-driven systems. Visible-light-responsive materials not only avoid the adverse effects associated with UV exposure, such as DNA damage and cytotoxicity but also enable practical applications in clinical settings [ 19 ]. These include infection control on implant surfaces, where photocatalytic coatings could provide long-term antimicrobial activity, reducing biofilm formation and implant-related infections without relying on antibiotics ( Fig. 5 b). Photocatalytic treatments under visible light could also serve as effective, non-invasive methods to combat multidrug-resistant microorganisms, offering solutions for chronic infections that are challenging to manage. By addressing these challenges, photocatalysis directly supports the One Health mission of mitigating global health issues through multidisciplinary, sustainable innovations. The reduction in antibiotic reliance is particularly critical, as it combats the growing threat of antimicrobial resistance—a shared concern across human, animal, and environmental health. In this sense, antimicrobial resistance has been called the ‘climate change of health’ as it threatens our worldwide healthcare systems on a daily basis [ 181 ]. Moreover, the ability to degrade environmental contaminants such as pharmaceutical residues, pesticides, and industrial pollutants contributing to antimicrobial resistance demonstrates the cross-disciplinary impact of photocatalytic technologies. 3.3.2 Light in context: translating photocatalytic coatings to clinical practice and beyond conventional antimicrobial surfaces technologies Light-based therapies have emerged as a promising technological approach for clinical applications, particularly in the context of preventing and controlling implant-associated infections. Among currently available light-based antimicrobial therapies, aPDT represents the most clinically established approach and shares mechanistic similarities with photocatalysis, such as ROS generation triggered by light in the presence of a sensitizing/catalyst agent [ 180 , 182 ]. While aPDT has demonstrated effectiveness in controlling a wide range of microorganisms, it relies on the topical application of external photosensitizers [ 183 ], which can limit its practicality in certain clinical contexts. In orthopedic settings, repeated access to deep implant sites for reapplication may require additional clinical interventions, increasing procedural complexity and patient risk [ 184 ]. Photocatalytic coatings may overcome these limitations by permanently integrating into the implant surface, enabling repeated antimicrobial activation solely through controlled light exposure. This built-in functionality minimizes the need for patient compliance and offers clinicians a responsive, surface-bound antimicrobial strategy that can be activated on demand, which is particularly valuable in long-term or recurrent infection scenarios. In addition to their light-activated antimicrobial functionality, photocatalytic coatings represent a highly versatile and tunable surface modification platform. Their performance can be finely tailored through precise control of synthesis parameters, such as the choice of photocatalytic elements (e.g., Ti, Zn, Bi), incorporation of dopants, surface morphology, and annealing conditions, which directly influence key material properties, including crystallinity, hydrophilicity, and bandgap energy [ 18 ]. This tunability allows the adjustment of light responsiveness to specific wavelength ranges, enabling clinical compatibility with different anatomical depths, implant geometries, and light delivery systems. As a result, these coatings can be engineered to meet the requirements of highly specific biomedical scenarios, providing a degree of adaptability that exceeds most conventional antimicrobial surface technologies. Furthermore, many photocatalytic coatings exhibit a multifunctional profile that extends beyond microbial control. Depending on the fabrication approach, these surfaces can simultaneously enhance mechanical durability, corrosion resistance, and cellular compatibility, essential properties for implant osseointegration and long-term clinical performance [ [185] ,  [186] ,  [187] ]. This integrated behavior contrasts with traditional surface treatments that often focus on optimizing a single parameter, frequently at the expense of others, thus limiting their translational potential [ 59 ]. Beyond their inherent versatility, photocatalytic coatings also stand out when compared to other types of stimuli-responsive surfaces. In addition to light-responsive systems, various other smart surfaces have been developed to provide stimulus-triggered antimicrobial responses, including those responsive to pH, temperature, enzymatic activity, or redox gradients [ 59 ]. These technologies represent important advances in the design of dynamically responsive coatings; however, despite their innovation, many of these systems depend on internal physiological cues, such as pH shifts or temperature fluctuations, that can vary considerably between patients, infection stages, and anatomical locations. This variability often hampers the predictability, reproducibility, and clinical standardization of such coatings [ 65 ]. Moreover, their activation is typically passive and self-regulated, operating independently of direct professional intervention, which can limit their applicability in scenarios where targeted, externally controlled antimicrobial action is desired. In contrast, photocatalytic coatings offer distinct advantages in terms of external controllability, temporal precision, and clinical adaptability. Their antimicrobial effect can be selectively and repeatedly activated through non-invasive light exposure, allowing healthcare professionals to initiate treatment at specific time points, such as during routine follow-ups or in response to early signs of microbial recolonization. This responsiveness, driven by an external and tunable stimulus, enables personalized and situation-specific antimicrobial interventions, aligning with the workflow and logic of real-world medical care. Additionally, the use of light as a trigger offers high spatial resolution, minimal systemic impact, and the potential for safe reactivation without the need for chemical replenishment, making photocatalysis a promising strategy for long-term infection control on implantable surfaces. Despite the promising in vitro performance of photocatalytic coatings, their clinical translation remains limited by the scarcity of in vivo investigations. Realistic models are crucial to validate their performance under complex physiological conditions, particularly in anatomically challenging environments such as the oral cavity or deep tissue implant sites, where biofilm formation is both common and clinically problematic [ 65 , 188 ]. In this context, it is important to consider how light-based activation strategies, such as photocatalytic coatings, might be adapted for clinical use. A possible route for application could mirror the established protocols of aPDT, where optical fibers are employed to deliver light directly to the site of interest [ [189] ,  [190] ,  [191] ,  [192] ]. In the context of peri-implant diseases, both non-surgical and surgical treatment protocols may offer clinically viable scenarios for the activation of photocatalytic surfaces. Non-surgical interventions, such as mechanical debridement, are commonly adopted as first-line therapy. Yet, their effectiveness in reducing peri-implant probing depths and inflammatory parameters remains limited in advanced peri-implantitis cases [ 193 ]. In such procedures, photocatalytic activation could potentially be performed adjunctively, complementing the mechanical disruption of the biofilm. In more severe cases where non-surgical therapy fails to reestablish peri-implant health, surgical intervention is indicated, as recommended by the S3 clinical guidelines of the European Federation of Periodontology [ 194 ]. The standard surgical approach involves the elevation of a full-thickness mucoperiosteal flap to allow direct access to the contaminated implant surface, followed by meticulous degranulation and surface decontamination using hand or power-driven instruments [ 195 ]. This procedure phase could provide an ideal opportunity for photocatalytic activation, with light delivery via optical fibers being performed under direct visualization of the implant. Building on this surgical context, the anatomical positioning of the implant represents a critical determinant in selecting the appropriate light delivery strategy for photocatalytic activation and clinical applicability. Superficial implants, such as those placed in subgingival regions, can generally be accessed with visible light sources (e.g., optical fibers). However, for implants situated in deeper anatomical compartments, such as submucosal or orthopedic sites, shorter wavelengths are significantly attenuated by tissue layers. In such cases, light in the red (∼630–700 nm) or near-infrared (∼800–900 nm) range is preferred due to its enhanced tissue penetration capacity, reaching depths of approximately 1.5–2.5 mm in humans [ 196 ]. These characteristics make red and NIR wavelengths particularly relevant for the clinical activation of photocatalytic surfaces in deep-seated implants. In this setting, two interdependent factors must be considered: the bandgap energy of the photocatalytic coating and the spectral and physical properties of the chosen light source. The bandgap defines the minimum photon energy required to promote electron excitation and initiate ROS production; therefore, the selected wavelength must not only penetrate biological tissues effectively but also provide sufficient energy to exceed the bandgap threshold of the material [ 18 ]. The type of light source plays a pivotal role in achieving this balance. Common phototherapeutic sources include lasers, light-emitting diodes (LEDs), and tungsten halogen lamps, each with specific advantages. Lasers offer monochromatic, collimated, and high-intensity beams with excellent spatial precision and deep tissue penetration, making them ideal for targeted intraoperative applications. Although less intense, LEDs are more affordable, offer broader spectral outputs, and are easily integrated into portable or wearable clinical devices. Tungsten halogen lamps provide a broad-spectrum output but often require filtration to isolate the relevant wavelength range for effective photocatalytic activation [ 142 ]. When used in combination with fiber-optic systems, for example, these light sources can be adapted to deliver controlled, site-specific irradiation to the implant surface, enabling the clinical translation of photocatalytic coatings across various anatomical contexts. 3.3.3 Mechanisms of photocatalysis: from electron migration to ROS-induced antimicrobial activity In terms of mechanisms of action, photocatalysis basically involves the presence of a solid photocatalyst, in which reactions occur at the interface between solid/liquid or solid/gas [ 20 , 21 ]. The photocatalyst is a material capable of absorbing light and initiating chemical transformations in other components of the system, predominantly represented by semiconductors with inherently unstable atomic orbitals [ 197 ]. These semiconductors facilitate oxidation reactions when excited by energy delivered through light irradiation [ 198 ]. Light, as an electromagnetic wave, carries energy in photons and induces electron migration within the semiconductor [ 180 ]. Common semiconductors include TiO 2  [ 23 , 174 , 199 , 200 ] and zinc oxide (ZnO) [ 22 , 201 ], along with others such as zinc sulfide (ZnS) [ 202 ] and iron oxide (Fe 2 O 3 ) [ 203 ]. Although TiO 2  provides high photocatalytic efficiency and stability, its absorption is limited to the UV region due to its broad bandgap energy (around 3.2 eV), which depends on its crystalline form [ 25 , 174 ]. Additionally, rapid electron recombination diminishes TiO 2  photocatalytic efficiency [ 27 ]. In response to these limitations, 2D nanomaterials and ZnO emerged as a viable alternative. 2D graphitic carbon nitride/titanium carbide nanocomposites, for instance, have been reported to enhance antibacterial photocatalysis by reducing charge recombination, showing strong antibacterial activity (>90 %), cytocompatibility, and improved mechanical properties [ 204 ]. ZnO, in its crystalline form of wurtzite, exhibits versatile properties, allowing for production in various forms such as nanowires, nanospheres, and nanofibers. However, ZnO is only activated by UV light, which compromises its applicability for biomedical purposes [ 197 ]. One common strategy to overcome this problem is the use of dopants, such as nitrogen, which creates an intragap state close to the VB, reducing the band gap and, therefore, increasing the range of absorbed light wavelengths by the photocatalyst [ 27 , 205 ]. Nonetheless, light-triggered semiconductor electron excitation is a complex process common to all aforementioned semiconductors. In semiconductors, the atomic structure's compactness leads to the overlap of orbitals, forming two bands: the valence band (VB) and the conduction band (CB), with lower and higher energy levels, respectively [ 206 ]. The bandgap, the energetic space between these bands, dictates the energy required for electrons to jump from VB to CB. The bandgap energy can be calculated using the Tauc method and the Planck formula (Eq.  (1) ): (1) E = h v = h c λ where E is photon energy, h is the Planck constant (6.63 × 10 −34  J s −1 ), v is photon frequency, c is the speed of light, and λ is wavelength. Higher-frequency light has a lower wavelength and higher energy [ 207 ]. When delivered energy equals or exceeds the bandgap energy, an electron migrates to the CB, creating an unpaired electron (e − ) in the CB and a hole pair (h + ) in the VB [ 180 ]. This migration converts photon energy to chemical energy through reduction and oxidation reactions at the semiconductor surface, forming ROS [ 16 , 30 ]. The positive electric potential of h +  generates hydroxyl radicals primarily through water photolysis, where h +  removes an electron from H 2 O to generate OH −  [ 198 , 208 ]. Simultaneously, the unpaired electron (e − ) with a negative electric potential promotes the electrochemical reduction of an oxygen molecule to generate the superoxide anion. The remaining H +  ions from water oxidation can react with the produced superoxide anion to form hyperoxide radicals (HO 2 ) [ 208 ]. Both O 2 −  and OH − , along with other ROS, can react with microbial cell organic compounds, degrading them similarly to PDT. For instance, Feng et al. reported that TiO 2 @rGO composites were able to reduce electron-hole recombination and enhance ROS generation for antibacterial activity [ 209 ]. In this system, rGO acted as an electron acceptor, forming Ti–O–C bonds with TiO 2  and facilitating charge separation by transferring photogenerated electrons from TiO 2  to rGO. This suppresses recombination and boosts the production of ·OH and ·O 2 −  radicals, which effectively disrupt bacterial membranes. The interaction of ROS with microbial cells typically initiates externally and progresses internally, targeting metabolic processes and DNA ( Fig. 6 ). The sensitivity of microorganisms to the produced ROS is dictated by their outer layer structure. Bacterial spores, with thicker cell walls rich in proteins, carbohydrates, and lipids, pose more significant challenges for inactivation [ 179 ]. Since microbial cells do not generally take in the photocatalyst, the generated ROS amount must be sufficient for complete inactivation, preventing microbial recovery while avoiding cytotoxic effects on the host tissue. For this, it is important to point out that the preferential susceptibility of bacteria to ROS compared to mammalian cells is attributed to several factors, including structural and biochemical differences. Unlike mammalian cells, which possess enzymatic antioxidant systems (e.g., superoxide dismutase, catalase, and glutathione peroxidase) to neutralize oxidative damage, bacteria—especially anaerobic species—are often less equipped to counteract ROS [ 210 ]. Furthermore, because bacteria lack a nuclear membrane, their DNA is directly exposed to ROS-induced strand breaks and mutations. Nagay et al., [ 19 ], for example, demonstrated that the ROS generated by the photocatalytic activity of Bi-doped TiO 2  coatings were sufficient to kill bacteria while causing no DNA degradation in human gingival fibroblasts. A more in-depth discussion on how light parameters and ROS generation impact biocompatibility is provided in Section  5.4 . Fig. 6 Photocatalytic coatings leverage ROS as their key antimicrobial agents, effectively killing bacteria through oxidative stress and structural disruption.  Upon exposure to light with wavelengths matching the absorption spectrum of the semiconductor photocatalyst, ROS such as hydroxyl radicals, superoxide anions, and hydrogen peroxide are generated. These highly reactive species target and damage bacterial membranes, proteins, and nucleic acids, leading to the breakdown of essential cellular functions and ultimately causing bacterial inactivation. Fig. 6 Overall, three main interactions between the photocatalyst and bacteria influence the efficacy of ROS-induced bacterial killing. The first type of interaction occurs when the photocatalyst is larger than the bacteria, such as in immobilized forms like coatings or thin films, in which the interaction is primarily limited to the bacterial surface. In this scenario, ROS act externally, causing oxidative damage to the bacterial membrane. Hydroxyl radicals play a pivotal role with their high oxidation potential, though their short diffusion potential requires proximity to the membrane for effective action. Additionally, larger photocatalysts may induce some degree of physical stress on the bacterial surface, enhancing the antimicrobial effect. In the second type of interaction, the photocatalyst particles are similar in size to bacteria. This interaction facilitates more localized ROS generation and membrane disruption, often resulting in the leakage of intracellular components. The combined oxidative and physical stresses compromise membrane integrity, amplifying bacterial inactivation. When photocatalyst particles are much smaller than bacteria (∼10–20 nm; third type of interaction), they can penetrate the bacterial cell, enabling intracellular ROS generation. This type of interaction extends the antimicrobial effect beyond the membrane, targeting critical intracellular components such as enzymes and DNA. ROS-induced damage to oxidative stress response enzymes reduces the bacteria's ability to neutralize oxidative damage, while hydrogen peroxide and hydroxyl radicals attack DNA, with guanine bases being particularly susceptible. These intracellular disruptions lead to widespread cell dysfunction and eventual death, making this interaction most comprehensive and lethal. By leveraging these three types of interactions, photocatalysis achieves a multitargeted antimicrobial effect, combining oxidative stress with physical disruption to inactivate bacteria effectively and reduce the risk of resistance development. The growing threat of antimicrobial resistance has become a major public health concern, forcing global organizations such as the World Health Organization (WHO) to advocate for strategies to reduce antibiotic use [ 211 ]. Microbial resistance can be broadly classified into intrinsic and acquired mechanisms. Intrinsic resistance refers to naturally occurring traits that render certain microorganisms insensitive to specific drugs/treatments, either due to the absence of suitable molecular targets or the low permeability of their cell envelopes. In contrast, acquired resistance arises when microorganisms that were initially susceptible evolve defense mechanisms, such as enzymatic machinery, target modification, reduced uptake, or active efflux, that impair the efficacy of antimicrobial agents [ 212 ]. Although antimicrobial resistance is a natural evolutionary process, it has been drastically accelerated by the excessive and recurrent use of antimicrobials. This practice imposes continuous selective pressure on microbial communities, accelerating the acquisition and dissemination of resistance genes across diverse species and ecological niches [ 213 ]. Consequently, there is a pressing need for novel antimicrobial strategies that are fast-acting, non-invasive, and do not induce resistance, especially in the context of biofilm-associated infections. While ROS-based therapies hold promises for overcoming traditional antimicrobial resistance, their effectiveness can still be challenged by the complex nature of microbial biofilms. These structured communities confer multifactorial protection to embedded microorganisms, significantly reducing their susceptibility to oxidative damage [ 214 ]. A critical element in this defense is the EPS matrix, which serves as a physical barrier and a chemically reactive interface. The EPS limits the penetration of oxidizing agents, such as H 2 O 2 , thus delaying their diffusion and allowing time for microbial adaptation. In  Pseudomonas aeruginosa , for example, oxidative stress has been shown to induce the formation of mucoid variants with increased alginate production, while other exopolysaccharides like Psl and Pel contribute to resistance against UVA light and H 2 O by enhancing matrix density and neutralizing ROS [ 215 , 216 ]. Beyond physical and chemical barriers, biofilms also upregulate enzymatic detoxification systems. Superoxide dismutase (SOD) converts superoxide radicals (O 2 − ) into hydrogen peroxide, which is further degraded by catalases and peroxidases into water and oxygen, reducing the antimicrobial effectiveness. Notably, catalase-deficient biofilms display higher sensitivity to H 2 O 2  compared to wild-type strains [ 214 ]. Also, in multispecies biofilms, interspecies cooperation further enhances resilience, as protective metabolites produced by one species may benefit the entire microbial community. Additional defense mechanisms include transcriptional regulators (e.g., OxyR, BrlR), molecular repair pathways, and efflux pumps such as MexEF-OprN, contributing to oxidants removal and maintenance of intracellular homeostasis [ 213 , 214 ]. Despite the multiple protective strategies biofilms offer, photocatalytic therapies remain a compelling antimicrobial strategy. One of the key advantages lies in the transient nature of light activation, which generates bursts of highly ROS within a short time window, limiting the ability of microorganisms to mount an effective adaptive response [ 163 ]. Moreover, photocatalysts can present low or no toxicity in the absence of light, reducing the selective pressure required for resistance development. Most importantly, the oxidative damage induced by ROS is non-specific and extensive, targeting a wide array of cellular components, often simultaneously [ 18 ]. This multifocal aggression compromises critical cellular functions irreversibly, hindering the activation or coordination of complex defense mechanisms. In other words, the intensity of the damage may overwhelm bacterial homeostasis before stress response pathways, such as the upregulation of catalases, efflux systems, or genetic repair mechanisms, can be fully mobilized. This contrasts sharply with treatments based on single molecular targets, such as antibiotics, where more specific and delayed modes of action increase the likelihood of resistance development through point mutations, enzymatic detoxification, or regulatory adaptations [ 212 ]. Given the protective nature of biofilms against oxidative stress, strategies can be proposed to enhance the long-term antibacterial effectiveness of photocatalytic surfaces. One promising approach involves preventing biofilm formation altogether. Since biofilms confer significant resilience to embedded microorganisms, interrupting the initial adhesion and early accumulation phases is critical. In this context, early-stage photoactivation of photocatalytic surfaces, prior to mature biofilm development, could serve as a preventive strategy, effectively reducing microbial colonization and biofilm establishment. However, a particularly attractive and clinically relevant feature of photocatalytic systems lies in their potential for reusability [ 19 , 217 ]. Unlike conventional antimicrobial coatings that may lose efficacy over time due to drug depletion, photocatalytic surfaces can be reactivated upon demand through light exposure, enabling repeated antimicrobial cycles without the need for exogenous chemical replenishment. This reusability is especially advantageous in the context of biofilm-related infections, which are often chronic and prone to recolonization over the lifespan of an implant [ 218 ]. In such scenarios, the ability to restore antimicrobial activity via simple light irradiation offers a low-maintenance, non-invasive, and sustainable approach for long-term microbial management. This cyclical activation capability may suppress recurrent infections and minimize the selective pressures associated with continuous antimicrobial exposure, reinforcing the potential of photocatalytic coatings as a viable long-term strategy in clinical practice. In this context, considering the mechanisms of photocatalysis, which differ from conventional PDT by not relying on photosensitizers but instead modifying semiconductor materials to achieve a band gap compatible with the irradiation wavelength, recent studies have emerged proposing this approach for antimicrobial applications. Despite the fundamental differences, these investigations have often been categorized under the umbrella of PDT, reflecting a current gap in nomenclature standardization. For instance, a photocatalytically active coating was synthesized by integrating a TiO 2 -graphene (TiO 2 -G) metastructure onto titanium implant surfaces via a hydrothermal method followed by plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD) [ 219 ]. This strategy enabled precise modulation of the semiconductor's band structure, significantly enhancing NIR light absorption and activating TiO 2 's photocatalytic potential under clinically relevant irradiation conditions. In vitro assays demonstrated that under 5 min of 808 nm NIR irradiation, the TiO 2 -G/DOX surface achieved a biofilm reduction of 96.4 % against  S. aureus  and 97.4 % against  E. coli , outperforming the TiO 2 -G surface alone (82.2 % and 82.3 %, respectively). This antibacterial activity was driven by ROS generation and NIR-triggered doxycycline release, which synergistically disrupted bacterial membranes and increased permeability. In vivo, the TiO 2 -G/DOX coating eradicated 99.5 % of bacteria within 24 h post-implantation and significantly reduced inflammation while enhancing new bone formation and M2 macrophage polarization. Similarly, Wu et al. engineered a multifunctional photocatalytic coating by constructing a micro/nano-structured titanate/TiO 2 –X heterojunction directly on titanium surfaces [ 220 ]. This semiconductor modification strategy significantly narrowed the TiO 2  band gap (e.g., down to 0.09 eV), enabling strong NIR light absorption and activation under 808 nm irradiation. In vitro, these heterostructured coatings exhibited antibacterial rates of 98.78 % against  S. aureus  and 98.33 % against  E. coli , attributed to synergistic ROS generation (•OH: ∼49.5 %) and localized heating. Mechanistically, the heterojunctions promoted efficient charge separation, boosting photocatalytic activity under NIR light. In vivo, NIR-irradiated implants showed a 94.45 % bacterial reduction and significantly alleviated inflammation. Further, a nanostructured TiO 2  coating was hydrothermally applied to SLM-printed Ti6Al4V to introduce structural defects and oxygen vacancies, effectively narrowing the band gap and enabling NIR absorption. This photoresponsiveness effect raised the surface temperature to 46.9 ± 0.32 °C after 15 min, leading to membrane disruption and bacterial death, with antibacterial rates of 90 % against  S. aureus  and  E. coli . Although these NIR-induced photocatalytic coating approaches are promising, the use of NIR light for implant-associated infections poses important limitations. Despite its deep tissue penetration, NIR often requires higher power densities and prolonged irradiation to induce effective ROS generation in many photocatalytic systems—raising concerns about potential thermal damage to surrounding tissues. Moreover, the integration of NIR therapy into clinical practice involves additional costs, including the acquisition of specialized laser equipment, maintenance of optical delivery systems, and the need for trained personnel to operate them safely. These factors can limit widespread adoption, particularly in low-resource settings. In contrast, visible-light-responsive coatings present a more cost-effective alternative, as they can be activated by standard surgical and dental-related lighting sources, simplifying implementation while maintaining therapeutic efficacy and safety.

3.1 Photothermal therapy PTT is based on the local increase of temperature to induce bacterial death, relying on two essential components: (i) a light source with an appropriate wavelength and (ii) a photothermal agent (PTA). The most frequently employed light spectrum for PTT is near-infrared (NIR), wherein the first NIR window (NIR-I) spans wavelengths from 700 to 1000 nm, and the second NIR window (NIR-II) ranges from 1000 to 1700 nm [ 112 ]. The utilization of NIR light is primarily attributed to its enhanced penetration into tissues and diminished absorption by water and blood components, such as hemoglobin, facilitating superior biomedical applications. The second pivotal component for PTT is a PTA, which, when exposed to light, can convert light energy into heat through various mechanisms depending on the type of PTA [ 113 ]. The primordial characteristics of PTAs for biomedical applications include higher photothermal conversion efficiency (PCE), photostability, excellent biocompatibility, rapid clearance from the body after use, and facile synthesis and modification [ 114 ]. Among the myriad PTAs reported in the literature, four main types can be identified: noble metals, semiconductors, polymers, and organic molecules. Each PTA employs a distinct mechanism of heat generation [ 113 ]. Noble metal materials, such as gold (Au), silver (Ag), and platinum (Pt), commonly in nanoparticle form, serve as photothermal agents due to the photophysical phenomenon known as local surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) [ 115 ]. In LSPR, light irradiation induces the excitation of free electrons on the metallic surface, leading to the collective oscillation of electrons in the CB. The non-radiative decay process, via intra- and interband transitions, results in the formation of energetic and hot electrons, with particle heating attributed to the phonon-phonon scattering process [ 116 ]. Nevertheless, the photothermal action of noble metallic nanoparticles is intrinsically linked to factors such as size, shape, dielectric constant, wavelength, and light intensity. Semiconductors, including molybdenum disulfide (MoS 2 ), manganese dioxide (MnO 2 ), and titanium dioxide (TiO 2 ), constitute the second class of PTAs capable of generating heat. Here, this process occurs through the generation and relaxation of electron-hole pairs. Light irradiation of semiconductors with energy equal to or greater than the band gap causes electron excitation, leading to their migration to the CB. Subsequently, electronic vacancies or holes are formed in the VB. The non-radiative relaxation of electrons allows the liberated energy, in the form of heat, to affect the crystal structure of the semiconductor [ 117 ]. Consequently, the crystal's thermal energy increases, promoting temperature rise and distribution. In addition to metals and semiconductors, polymers (e.g., polyaniline [ 118 ], poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) [ 119 ] and carbon-based nanomaterials [ 120 ]) are extensively investigated as PTAs due to their advantageous properties, such as biodegradability and high PCE, respectively. Polymers and carbon-based materials as PTAs induce a temperature increase through molecular orbital migration. PTA's electrons in the ground state, within the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO), undergo excitation upon light irradiation, migrating to a higher energy orbital, the lowest occupied molecular orbital (LOMO) [ 121 ]. This transition, coupled with a relaxation process, facilitates energy transfer from the excited electron to the atomic lattice, increasing the material's temperature [ 115 ]. Yet, more recently, small organic molecules have emerged as a new generation of PTAs. For instance, cyanine-based dyes (indocyanine green [ 122 ], Prussian blue [ 123 ], red phosphorous [ 124 ]) offer cost-effectiveness and purportedly higher biocompatibility. For example, Shim et al. [ 125 ] demonstrated that indocyanine green, combined with NIR light (801 nm) for 12 s (24 J cm −2 ), induced a 96.8 % reduction in  Streptococcus gordonii  biofilms cultivated on zirconia disks. Nevertheless, the low PCE, poor photostability, and lack of an in vivo assay remain significant drawbacks to further applications of this PTA class in the prevention and treatment of infections associated with zirconia dental implants. Regardless of the mechanism, the antimicrobial effect induced by PTAs under irradiation is directly correlated with the biological effects of increased temperature. Since human infections are primarily caused by mesophile microorganisms, i.e., organisms that thrive at approximately 37 °C, temperatures exceeding this threshold are regarded to cause cell damage [ 126 ]. PTT-induced damage in microbial cells is intrinsically associated with the denaturation of bacterial cell walls, proteins, and enzymes, culminating in the leakage of cell components and DNA/RNA inactivation [ 127 ]. This effect is primarily attributable to alterations in protein/nucleic acid structure, induced spatial dissociation/rearrangement of protein subunits, or the disruption of chemical interactions between amino acid side chains [ 128 ]. Behzadpour et al. [ 129 ] demonstrated that polypyrrole core–carbon-coated nanostructures increased on average 20 °C within 20 min of exposure to 808 nm wavelength light. The temperature increase resulted in an approximately 80 % reduction in colony-forming units (CFU) of methicillin-resistant  Staphylococcus aureus  ( S. aureus ) (MRSA), with protein and nucleic acid leakage assessed by the Bradford method. Also, Shi et al. [ 130 ] revealed that molybdenum disulfide nanodots, combined with erythrocyte membrane fragments, can alter bacterial morphology. However, just as bacteria are prone to heat damage, host cells are also susceptible. Considering this, Hu et al. [ 131 ] developed a surface charge-adaptive gold nanoparticle (AgNP) capable of adhering and accumulating preferentially in biofilms. The PTT effect in MRSA resulted in a robust bactericidal effect, and in rabbits, the same antimicrobial effect was observed, with minimal heat spreading to healthy tissues and less pronounced inflammatory infiltration after 7 days of treatment. Addressing the need for implants capable of sequentially regulating antibacterial activity and promoting osteogenesis, Chen et al. developed a micropatterned graphene oxide nanocomposite coating on titanium implants [ 132 ]. In vitro, the coating exhibited potent antibacterial effects under NIR light, reducing  E. coli  and  S. aureus  by 96.9 % and 98.6 %, respectively, due to its photothermal effect (reaching 54.3 °C within 10 min) while its micropatterned surface supported cell adhesion, guided growth, and enhanced osteogenic differentiation in the absence of light. This dual-functional design offers a promising strategy for antibacterial implants that effectively combat infection and support bone integration—two critical challenges in long-term implant success. Similarly, to overcome persistent bacterial infections on titanium implants, a multifunctional coating composed of Cu 2-x S and graphene oxide (TGC) was developed, enabling synergistic photothermal and chemodynamic antibacterial action under NIR-II irradiation [ 133 ]. In vitro, the coating exhibited strong photothermal behavior and generated hydroxyl radicals (·OH) via Fenton-like reactions in the presence of H 2 O 2 , leading to 99.2 % and 99.4 % bacterial reduction against  E. coli  and  S. aureus , respectively. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis revealed severe morphological damage and membrane rupture in bacteria exposed to the TGC coating under NIR light. In vivo, the coating maintained photothermal performance and significantly reduced bacterial load in an implant-associated infection model, with 98.75 % inhibition of  S. aureus  and decreased IL-6 expression in peri-implant tissues, indicating effective infection control and attenuation of inflammation. Certain metal ions, such as Cu 2+ , have demonstrated antibacterial properties and the ability to induce chemodynamic therapy (CDT) effects (i.e., ROS generation via a catalytic mechanism). For example, Mei et al. [ 134 ] developed copper-doped polyoxometalate nanoclusters (Cu-POM) as a multifunctional strategy to eradicate biofilm-associated infections on implant surfaces through synergistic chemodynamic and mild PTT ( Fig. 4 a). In vitro, Cu-POM combined with NIR irradiation generated ROS and hydroxyl radicals via Fenton-like reactions, as confirmed by methylene blue oxidation and electron paramagnetic resonance ( Fig. 4 b). This treatment also caused lipid peroxidation, DNA degradation, and up to 53.6 % bacterial death, altering biofilm metabolism with thousands of metabolites upregulated or downregulated ( Fig. 4 c). Beyond direct antibacterial effects, Cu-POM + NIR stimulated macrophage polarization toward the pro-inflammatory M1 phenotype via ROS-mediated pathways. In vivo, the Cu-POM + NIR-treated group exhibited effective temperature rise (∼45 °C), complete wound healing, reduced biofilm burden, suppressed inflammation, and elevated expression of CD86 and iNOS, confirming the reactivation of local innate immunity. Further, to tackle implant-associated infections and promote bone integration, a multifunctional titanium implant (Ti-TF-acBSP) was developed by co-functionalizing the surface with photothermal FeIIITA nanoparticles and immunomodulatory acetylated Bletilla striata polysaccharide (acBSP) ( Fig. 4 d–g) [ 135 ]. In vitro, under NIR irradiation, the coating achieved ∼80 % reduction of  S. aureus  through hyperthermia-induced bacterial membrane disruption, confirmed by morphological deformation, ONPG hydrolysis, and DNA leakage assays. Beyond direct antibacterial effects, acBSP induced macrophage polarization toward the M1 phenotype, enhancing pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion, bacterial phagocytosis, and promoting the secretion of osteoinductive factors such as OSM and VEGF, which stimulated osteogenic differentiation of MSCs. In vivo, the Ti-TF-acBSP coating exhibited excellent photothermal activity, significantly reduced bacterial colonization in a rat femur infection model, suppressed inflammation, and improved new bone formation and implant-bone contact. However, PTT presents some limitations, including potential undesired cytotoxicity to host cells in the vicinity [ 136 ], which is dependent on the temperature attained during the treatment protocol, and a restricted or insufficient investigation efficacy against mature multispecies biofilms.
