Fig. 7 4.1.1 Sol-gel synthesis Sol-gel methods are widely used for the synthesis of photocatalysts, making these valuable for nanoscale TiO 2  material production ( Fig. 7 a). They involve two main stages: hydrolysis and polycondensation. During hydrolysis, metal alkoxides break down in either water or alcohol, with the choice of reaction medium leading to either an “aqueous” or “non-aqueous” route [ 224 ]. Polycondensation follows, involving the bonding of neighboring molecules, forming metal oxide bonds and polymer networks. This process increases the system's viscosity, resulting in a porous gel structure while maintaining a liquid phase, in which the size and cross-linking of colloidal particles depend on the precursor and pH [ 225 ]. Then, substrates are often immersed in the reaction mixture during hydrolysis or condensation, followed by aging, drying, thermal treatments, or a combination to promote crystallization and adhesion. By using such methods, thin films with thicknesses spanning 50–500 nm can be fabricated using diverse coating techniques, such as dip-coating, spin-coating, spray-coating, flow-coating, and capillary-coating [ 225 ]. For instance, aiming to enhance the photocatalytic properties of spin-coated sol-gel anatase-type TiO 2 , Tsuji et al. [ 226 ] implanted Ag-negative ions at different energies and doses to these coatings, followed by annealing. The treated samples demonstrated improved photocatalytic efficiency, where Ag nanoparticles (AgNPs), located at a shallow depth in the coating, significantly improved the photocatalytic efficiency, surpassing that of rutile single crystal TiO 2  due to a lower bandgap. Corroborating such results, Khitous et al. [ 221 ] demonstrated a simple, low-cost method that combines asymmetrically shaped AuNPs, formed via thermal dewetting, with a TiO 2  sol-gel layer applied by spin-coating, enhancing visible-light photocatalysis through improved reaction kinetics and hot electron lifetimes ( Fig. 7 a’). In addition, as an example that the method of synthesis can completely change the photocatalytic efficiency, in a study conducted by Asadi et al., [ 227 ] nitrogen and sulfur co-doped TiO 2  nanoparticles were synthesized through a combination of sol-gel and hydrothermal methods. Their results revealed that materials prepared using the sol-gel approach exhibited significantly enhanced photocatalytic activity compared to the hydrothermal one, probably due to the particle size and surface area differences, making them a promising option for practical applications. Nevertheless, a disadvantage of such a method for biomedical implant application relies on its poor adhesion to metallic substrates, thereby needing special attention towards physical or chemical modification of the substrate to enhance the adhesion strength at the coating-substrate interface [ 228 ]. 4.1.2 Anodization method The anodization method is commonly conducted in an electrolytic solution under constant voltage potential, facilitating the growth of nanostructure surfaces such as nanotubes ( Fig. 7 b). Highly ordered TiO 2  nanotube arrays (TNTAs), prepared via electrochemical anodization, have gained interest due to their aligned porosity, high crystallinity, and oriented nanotubular morphology, which enhance light absorption and charge separation. Considering this, Xiao et al. [ 229 ] constructed a hierarchically ordered Au x /NP-TNTA heterostructure, fabricated through two-step anodization and electrostatic self-assembly, with versatile photocatalytic properties, including pollutant degradation, with enhanced photosensitization from glutathione-capped Au x  clusters (i.e., atomically precise thiolate-protected gold clusters) and elucidated mechanisms offering insights for novel metal-cluster/1D semiconductor applications. Targeting implant applications, Moon et al. [ 222 ] prepared TiO 2  nanotubes (NTs) via anodization followed by crystallization through heating at 400 °C for 3 h in air. Then, to extend the photocatalytic activity of titania beyond the UV range into the visible light spectrum, the authors decorated the NTs with Au ( Fig. 7 b’) or Pt by ion plasma sputtering. Such doping can also be performed by hydrothermal treatment (HT). Typically, the synthesis of photocatalytic coatings using HT occurs by introducing the sample into the vessel containing a liquid medium, followed by annealing at high temperatures and subsequent cooling, allowing for the growth of a coating onto the substrate. Zhang et al. [ 230 ] recently reported on successfully constructing a TiO 2  nanostructure on a Ti surface by HT growth using NaOH solution. Interestingly, to achieve photocatalytic activity under visible light, the authors synthesized a TiO 2 /MoS 2  coating in two HT steps: the first one with NaOH and the second one with MoS 2 , which effectively killed  S. aureus  in vitro and in vivo within 10 min of irradiation. 4.1.3 Magnetron sputtering Photocatalytic coatings can also be produced using magnetron sputtering, offering precise control over plasma parameters and the desired properties ( Fig. 7 c). Sputtering is a well-established process that involves expelling atoms from a target surface when bombarded by energetic particles, leading to the formation of thin films on a substrate [ 231 ]. The ejected atoms have high energy, which enhances their ability to condense and adhere to the substrate. Wong et al. [ 223 ] developed TiO 2 (N)/Ag/TiO 2 (N) sandwich films via magnetron sputtering, embedding an Ag layer between two N-doped TiO 2  layers using two Ti and one Ag target ( Fig. 7 c’). Microbiological experiments showed that in the absence of Ag, microbial cells preserved their integrity with smooth surface morphology, regardless of visible light exposure. However, when Ag was incorporated into the films, it induced roughening of the bacterial surface in the dark, likely due to interactions between Ag and the bacterial cell wall. Upon exposure to visible light, these surfaces underwent more pronounced structural changes, including the development of distinct cracks. In another report, Ueda et al. [ 232 ] deposited pure gold (Au) and a titanium-gold (Ti-Au) alloy film (60 mol% Ti, 40 mol% Au) onto Ti substrates using sputtering, followed by thermal oxidation to create TiO 2  layers. These layers were evaluated for their antibacterial properties against  Escherichia coli , cytotoxicity, and bonding strength to Ti substrates. The most promising results in terms of antibacterial activity under visible-light exposure were achieved with a 38 nm thick sputtered film made of pure Au, evidencing an R-value of 1.8, corresponding to approximately 98 % reduction in  E. coli  viability. Interestingly, Ratova et al. evaluated the photocatalytic and antimicrobial performance of bismuth oxide, bismuth tungstate, and titanium dioxide coatings deposited on glass beads via reactive magnetron sputtering, followed by annealing [ 233 ]. Bismuth oxide coatings showed superior dye degradation and complete inactivation of  E. coli  under visible light within 48 h, attributed to their low bandgap and stable hydrophobic surface, offering both disinfection and antifouling advantages. Nevertheless, bismuth oxide coatings may not present ideal mechanical and chemical stability for implant applications. In contrast, titanium dioxide is widely used in biomedical implants due to its excellent biocompatibility and long-term stability, but it requires modification to be activated under visible light—making doping with Bi 2 O 3  a promising strategy to combine the robustness of TiO 2  with the visible-light responsiveness of bismuth-based systems. 4.1.4 Plasma electrolytic oxidation Plasma electrolytic oxidation (PEO) utilizes a powerful electrical discharge within a system comprising a cathode (a cooled vessel), a working substrate immersed in an electrolyte serving as the anode, and a power supply ( Fig. 7 d). This method offers a cost-effective alternative to vacuum-based plasma technologies and is particularly advantageous for creating robust, uniform coatings on complex-shaped metallic objects, such as biomedical implants and devices, without exposing the entire substrate to high temperatures or requiring sophisticated equipment. Unlike other coating processes, PEO results from a substrate conversion process in tandem with deposition. Its core advantage lies in the generation of high-voltage plasma discharges around substrates of varying shapes, enabling the doping of diverse chemical elements in a single step. This capability allows for the production of biofunctional coatings characterized by thickness, roughness, porosity, and crystallinity, which are beneficial for photocatalytic activity and implant-bone integration. Wu et al. [ 185 ] synthesized TiO 2  porous nanoceramic coatings on titanium substrates using the PEO process that presented photocatalytic activity due to a disordered outer layer with oxygen vacancies, effectively degrading methylene blue, rhodamine B, and lipopolysaccharide (LPS) under visible light ( Fig. 7 d’). Although the authors claimed that the coating could improve Ti implant decontamination, light irradiation of biofilm formed onto the developed coating was not evaluated. On the other hand, we [ 19 ] employed the PEO technique to develop a Bi-doped TiO 2  coating suitable for biomedical and dental implant applications. This coating demonstrated enhanced photocatalytic activity, attributed to Bi doping, resulting in the effective reduction of  S. sanguinis  and  Actinomyces naeslundii  dual-species biofilm, with visible light further amplifying its antibacterial properties, holding potential for peri-implant infection control. 4.2 Critical determinants of photocatalytic implant coating functionality: structural integrity, reusability, substrate-specific interactions, and biocompatibility Following the discussion on synthesis methods, it is crucial to consider how physical and interfacial properties influence the overall functionality and clinical longevity of photocatalytic coatings. These factors directly affect antibacterial efficacy and determine the coating's ability to withstand friction, cyclic loading, and exposure to biochemical fluids during implantation and daily use. Insufficient adhesion between the coating and implant surface can result in degradation or delamination, exposing the underlying material and increasing susceptibility to microbial colonization and biofilm formation, thereby raising the risk of peri-implant disease [ 234 ]. Additionally, the tribocorrosion process may release metallic ions and debris, altering the peri-implant environment, triggering inflammation, and contributing to bone resorption [ 235 ]. Loss of structural integrity also compromises the coating's antimicrobial performance and reusability, as photocatalytic activity depends on stable ROS generation at the coating–tissue interface. Therefore, for clinical translation use, photocatalytic coatings must combine efficient ROS-based antimicrobial activity with strong interfacial adhesion, mechanical and chemical durability, and biocompatibility. 4.2.1 Coating thickness, adhesion and substrate-specific interactions Coating thickness plays a central role in photocatalytic performance and coating stability [ 236 ]. Very thin coatings may lack sufficient active surface for ROS generation, while excessively thick layers can hinder light penetration and promote charge recombination [ 237 , 238 ]. Dundar et al. demonstrated that TiO 2  films with intermediate thicknesses around 200 nm exhibited superior photocatalytic activity, with thicker films showing reduced performance due to optical and transport constraints [ 238 ]. The Sofroniou et al. study further showed that coatings with a thicker TiO 2  surface top layer displayed superior antibacterial performance against MRSA under irradiation compared to thinner or more stratified systems due to improved light penetration and increased nanoparticle exposure at the air–film interface [ 239 ]. These findings highlight the importance of optimizing thickness as a key parameter for achieving efficient and durable photocatalytic performance. Seremak et al. investigated the long-term durability of TiO 2  photocatalytic coatings deposited via low-pressure cold spray, highlighting how coating thickness, crystallinity, and bonding mechanisms influence mechanical stability and photocatalytic performance [ 240 ]. Thicker and more crystalline coatings exhibited superior adhesion (>30 N) primarily due to enhanced mechanical interlocking, whereas thinner, amorphous coatings adhered mainly through chemical bonding at the interface via Ti–O–Al linkages. In this context, it is notable that interfacial adhesion between the coating and the underlying implant substrate significantly affects the stability and long-term performance of biomedical devices. Coatings with insufficient bonding strength may delaminate under physiological loading, compromising the mechanical integrity and functional lifespan of the implant. Achieving reliable adhesion—via chemical bonding, mechanical interlocking, or intermediate layers—is thus critical for the clinical translation of photocatalytic coatings. Furthermore, given that photocatalytic strategies are increasingly applied to various implant substrates, including titanium, zirconia, biodegradable metals, and polymers, substrate–coating compatibility must be thoroughly evaluated. Surface energy, oxide layer chemistry, and thermal expansion mismatch can significantly affect coating uniformity, adhesion, and degradation behavior. For example, heat treatments required for crystallization may degrade polymeric materials or compromise low-melting alloys, while differences in oxide formation depending on the substrate can affect bonding mechanisms. For polymeric implants and devices, sol-gel–derived TiO 2 –ZnO thin films deposited on polycarbonate substrates via an intermediate SiO 2  layer demonstrated high optical transparency, mechanical robustness, and photocatalytic activity [ 241 ]. Pre-treatment of the polymer surface with light irradiation facilitated the formation of surface hydroxyl groups, enhancing interfacial bonding with the SiO 2  layer, overcoming the limitation poor adhesion feature of typical sol-gel coatings. Adhesion performance was rated excellent (grade 0, ISO 2409), even after extended UV exposure and abrasion cycles [ 241 ]. In contrast, ceramic substrates such as zirconia—widely used in dental implantology—present inherent challenges for coating adhesion due to their chemical inertness and low surface reactivity. To overcome these limitations, surface activation techniques like plasma treatment or functionalized interlayers can be employed to increase surface energy and promote film anchorage. Although direct studies on photocatalytic TiO 2 -based films on zirconia are limited, similar strategies are applicable. Notably, Bouras et al. reported that Zr-doped ZnO thin films deposited on ceramic substrates exhibited superior photocatalytic activity compared to those on glass [ 242 ]. This enhancement was attributed to the ceramic-supported films’ rougher morphology, increased crystallite size, and improved charge separation efficiency, collectively promoting greater light absorption and hydroxyl radical generation. Additionally, an innovative approach involved the integration of TiO 2  nanotubes onto nanostructured aluminum surfaces fabricated via tubular channel angular pressing [ 243 ]. These high-strength aluminum substrates were further functionalized with nano-concave arrays, enabling localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) coupling with the TiO 2  nanotubes. The resulting hybrid surfaces showed remarkable mechanical performance, with adhesion forces exceeding 2100 mN in scratch tests, alongside significant antibacterial efficacy against  E. coli  under light activation. Similarly, PEO has emerged as a promising technique for biomedical applications due to its ability to produce strongly adherent, porous, and crystalline oxide layers on metals such as titanium, alloys, and zirconium [ 104 ]. Unlike conventional methods, PEO creates mechanically interlocked coatings and chemically bonds to the substrate through in-situ oxide growth, resulting in superior adhesion and long-term interfacial stability. Another key advantage is the precise control over coating features achieved by adjusting the electrolyte, current density, and processing time. The substrate itself plays a pivotal role in this process. Its thermal and electrical properties influence microdischarge behavior, which governs oxide growth, melting/resolidification, and incorporation of electrolyte species. These factors directly impact coating thickness, crystallite size, and defect formation, all critical for photocatalytic performance. In this context, PEO coatings benefit from substrate-driven modulation of charge carrier dynamics, where structural and chemical features of the oxide influence redox activity. For example, zirconia coatings formed via PEO on zirconium substrates showed increased oxygen vacancy formation with extended oxidation time [ 244 ]. These vacancies not only improved photoluminescence and ROS generation but also reinforced the coating's cohesion and adhesion, which is critical for durable biomedical performance. Further, a typical feature of the PEO process is the occurrence of microdischarges that are influenced by coating thickness: in the early stages, lower-energy microarcs favor the formation of anatase, whereas as the coating thickens, only more intense electric fields can cause a dielectric breakdown, promoting the formation of rutile or anatase/rutile mixtures [ 19 ]. This evolution directly impacts the photocatalytic behavior of the surface. Nagay et al. observed that Bi-doped TiO 2  PEO coatings on commercially pure titanium (cpTi) substrates presenting a mixture of anatase and rutile showed excellent photocatalytic antibacterial performance under visible light due to the optical and high surface area properties of the coating [ 19 ]. This observation aligns with the findings of Pantaroto et al., who demonstrated, through magnetron sputtering, that mixed-phase TiO 2  films on cpTi substrate exhibit superior photocatalytic activity against oral pathogens under UV light compared to only anatase or rutile thin films [ 245 ]. On the other hand, Momeni et al. investigated the effects of adding SiO 2  to nitrogen-doped TiO 2  thin films applied to stainless steel via a sol-gel spray method, aiming to enhance visible-light photocatalytic performance and mechanical stability [ 246 ]. Contrary to prior findings on glass or polymer substrates, the addition of 20 % SiO 2  increased the band gap energy (from 2.93 to 3.09 eV), induced significant crack formation during calcination, and ultimately reduced visible-light photocatalytic activity and hydrophilicity. The reduced activity was attributed to low crystallinity, increased electron-hole recombination from grain boundaries, Fe 2+  ion diffusion from the steel substrate, and a detrimental crack pattern that diminished surface area. Although all films demonstrated strong adhesion in nanoscratch testing, SiO 2 -containing films showed lower mechanical stability, evidenced by force drop-offs and crack formation under stress [ 246 ]. These findings suggest that for steel-based substrates used under visible-light conditions, non-silica TiO 2  coatings may offer superior performance in terms of photocatalytic efficiency, surface integrity, and durability. Importantly, this study highlights the need for a careful balance in dopant type and concentration—while doping is essential to shift TiO 2  activity to the visible-light range, excessive or poorly integrated secondary phases may compromise mechanical and functional properties critical for clinical applications. It is important to highlight, though, that while this section consolidates key factors—particularly coating thickness and interfacial adhesion—that critically influence the performance of photocatalytic coatings and, consequently, ROS generation for antibacterial purposes, it is important to note that most of the available evidence comes from systems not specifically designed for visible-light activation. Nevertheless, these studies offer valuable insights into the structural and interfacial mechanisms that underpin coating performance. Still, investigations that systematically assess these parameters under visible-light-responsive conditions remain scarce. Future research should aim to bridge this gap by evaluating how variations in coating thickness and interfacial strength influence functional durability, antibacterial activity, and oxidative performance under clinically relevant illumination. Experimental strategies may include pull-off and scratch adhesion tests, cross-sectional analysis via SEM or profilometry, and correlating these features with ROS generation and microbial inhibition. Furthermore, extending these evaluations to different implant-relevant substrates will be essential to ensure coating reliability and performance across diverse biomedical applications. 4.2.2 Mechanical properties, wear and corrosion resistance: implications for photocatalytic antimicrobial performance and biocompatibility In photocatalytic coatings intended for biomedical and dental implants, mechanical robustness and corrosion resistance are critical for structural durability and preserving antimicrobial functionality over time. Surface degradation, whether by wear or electrochemical attack, may directly compromise ROS generation, reduce effective surface area, and even trigger adverse tissue responses. Wear resistance is particularly important in load-bearing or micro-movement-prone regions, such as implant-abutment interfaces [ 234 ]. Surface abrasion can erode the photocatalytic layer, removing active crystalline domains (e.g., anatase/rutile TiO 2 ), exposing the underlying substrate, and decreasing antimicrobial efficiency. In such scenarios, the loss of surface integrity would diminish photocatalytic activity and facilitate bacterial adhesion and biofilm formation in damaged regions. Translating to clinical application, wear resistance against mechanical instrumentation, for example, is critical to ensure that photocatalytic coatings remain functional during routine decontamination procedures. In this context, a TiO 2  nanoceramic coating was developed on titanium implants using a PEO-based process followed by annealing and polishing [ 185 ]. The resulting coating featured a dense, nanocrystalline microstructure and an oxygen-vacancy-rich disordered outer layer, with a thickness of about 26 nm, enabling visible-light-driven photocatalysis ( Fig. 8 a). Additionally, the coating maintained its structural integrity after treatment with steel curettes and ultrasonic scalers—procedures that typically damage conventional titanium or TiO 2  coatings ( Fig. 8 b). This superior wear resistance was attributed to the high surface hardness (10.22 ± 2.3 GPa), metallurgical bonding with the titanium substrate, and a microstructure that prevented crack propagation. The coating also demonstrated favorable cell responses, with comparable or superior biocompatibility and osteogenic potential compared to untreated titanium [ 185 ]. In another study, Chung et al. (2009) systematically evaluated TiO 2  coatings deposited via arc ion plating (AIP) onto stainless steel substrates, focusing on how deposition parameters influenced microstructure, mechanical durability, and functional performance [ 247 ]. They demonstrated that increasing the deposition time and oxygen partial pressure promoted the formation of anatase-rich coatings with a compact columnar morphology. These structural features led to a substantial increase in surface hardness (up to 679.6 HV) and strong film adhesion (21.2 N in scratch tests), which in turn improved abrasive wear resistance and corrosion protection in NaCl environments. Mechanistically, the improved adhesion and wear resistance were attributed to cohesive strength within the well-crystallized anatase phase and interfacial pseudo-interdiffusion, while corrosion resistance was linked to the dense, inert nature of the oxide layer that limited electrolyte permeation. Importantly, the authors noted that the same conditions that enhanced mechanical robustness—i.e., thicker coatings with higher crystallinity—also supported greater photocatalytic and antimicrobial activity, likely due to reduced recombination of charge carriers and the formation of ROS at the surface [ 247 ]. Many photocatalytic coatings, especially doped oxides or mixed-phase materials, are semiconducting and can exhibit electrochemical reactivity under physiological conditions. Supporting this perspective, an Ag 2 O/SiO 2 /Ta 2 O 5  nanocomposite coating was developed for orthopedic implants and demonstrated excellent tribological, anticorrosion, photocatalytic, and antimicrobial performance [ 250 ]. The inclusion of Ag 2 O and SiO 2  within a Ta 2 O 5  matrix not only enhanced wear resistance—reflected by improved hardness-to-elasticity ratios and reduced friction—but also significantly mitigated corrosion in Ringer's solution. The coating maintained a stable barrier function over time, with superior electrochemical impedance and lower corrosion currents compared to uncoated Ti–6Al–4V. From a photocatalytic perspective, visible-light activation was enabled by the engineered heterojunction, which reduced the band gap and improved charge separation, as confirmed by DFT calculations. This translated into a higher Rhodamine B degradation rate and near-complete bacterial inactivation under visible light. Importantly, the bactericidal effect was driven by a synergistic mechanism combining reactive oxygen species generation via photocatalysis and Ag +  ion release, offering potent dual-mode antimicrobial protection alongside mechanical and chemical durability. Tribocorrosion—the combined action of mechanical wear and electrochemical degradation—also plays a critical role in the long-term stability of titanium implants, especially in a complex physiological environment [ 251 ]. For instance, it was reported that TiO 2 /SrTiO 3  coating developed on Ti6Al4V alloy exhibited synergistic antibacterial, tribocorrosion-resistant, and wear-resistant properties through distinct yet interconnected mechanisms [ 248 ]. Its photocatalytic antibacterial activity is primarily due to the generation of ROS, particularly superoxide radicals (·O 2 − ), facilitated by a heterojunction structure that enhances UV light absorption and charge separation. Under UV illumination, the bacterial proliferation rate dropped to 3 %, and clear inhibition zones were observed, confirming its potent photocatalytic disinfection. In terms of wear resistance, the presence of a robust thermal oxide layer reduced wear volume loss to 1/8 that of uncoated Ti6Al4V and decreased maximum wear scar depth from 15 μm to 3 μm ( Fig. 8 c). The coating also minimized plastic deformation and abrasive damage. Regarding tribocorrosion, the oxide layer served as a protective barrier that stabilized open circuit potential (OCP) during sliding tests in simulated body fluid (SBF) and maintained surface integrity, preventing substrate exposure and corrosion ( Fig. 8 d–f) [ 248 ]. Therefore, since biomedical implants are susceptible to bio-tribocorrosion phenomena in the oral environment (driven by the synergistic interplay of mechanical wear, chemical reactions, biochemical agents, and microbial activity), it is essential to investigate their mechanical and electrochemical behavior under conditions that closely mimic the clinical setting [ 234 ]. Building upon the discussion of corrosion and tribocorrosion resistance in biological environments, it is essential to consider the additional challenge posed by microbiologically influenced corrosion, which has been reported to compromise the integrity of metallic implants and industrial components in biological or humid environments. In this context, Li et al. designed a multifunctional 2D g-C 3 N 4 /Cu 2 O/Cu photocatalytic coating to address both microbial colonization and microbial corrosion ( Fig. 8 g) [ 249 ]. The coating architecture leveraged an S-type heterojunction to enhance visible-light-driven charge separation while simultaneously suppressing Cu 2 O photocorrosion through the stabilizing presence of Cu 0 . The ultrathin porous g-C 3 N 4  provided abundant nucleation sites, enabling uniform Cu 2 O/Cu deposition and facilitating ROS generation. As a result, the coating demonstrated antibacterial effects against  E. coli  and  S. aureus , achieving nearly complete bacterial elimination within 1 h under light and antibacterial activity even in the dark. Long-term assays revealed outstanding durability and microbial corrosion resistance, as evidenced by significantly reduced corrosion current, pit formation, and pitting depth on 316L stainless steel exposed to  Pseudomonas aeruginosa  ( Fig. 8 h) [ 249 ]. These findings highlight the potential dual-functionality of such coatings in combating both biofilm formation and microbial corrosion through synergistic photocatalytic and metallic mechanisms. Altogether, wear, corrosion, and tribocorrosion processes can lead to localized pH changes, ion release, and surface charge alterations that influence both bacterial behavior and cellular responses [ 251 ]. The breakdown of the passive TiO 2  layer under physical, chemical, and microbial challenges can trigger titanium ion/particle release, which in turn activates inflammatory pathways—particularly through neutrophils, macrophages, and osteogenic cells—culminating in increased pro-inflammatory cytokine production (e.g., IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and RANKL-mediated osteoclastogenesis, thus exacerbating peri-implant bone loss [ 252 ]. In this context, photocatalytic coatings are promising solutions, offering on-demand antibacterial activity through light-triggered ROS generation and acting as protective barriers against tribocorrosion and ion leakage. However, their clinical translation requires careful consideration of substrate compatibility. As mentioned earlier, on titanium substrates, photocatalytic coatings like TiO 2  and its heterostructures can achieve strong chemical bonding and mechanical stability through techniques such as PEO or thermal treatments; in contrast, zirconia and polymers often require surface pre-treatments or interfacial layers to enhance coating adhesion due to their inert or thermosensitive nature. Moreover, the biological safety of these coatings is influenced by their degradation behavior and ion release profiles. While dopants like Ag 2+ , Cu 2+ , or Bi 3+  can promote the shift of TiO 2  to the visible light range and achieve photocatalytic antibacterial effects under irradiation [ 27 , 253 ], uncontrolled leaching of these ions may induce cytotoxicity or inflammation. Thus, attaining durable adhesion, mechanical resilience, and biocompatibility requires tailoring the coating strategy to the specific implant substrate, ensuring that the multifunctional benefits of photocatalytic surfaces are performed without compromising tissue integration or patient safety. 4.2.3 Long-term stability and reusability of photocatalytic implant coatings Beyond initial antimicrobial or photocatalytic efficacy, the long-term durability of implant coatings under physiological conditions is critical for their clinical translation. Aging effects, including structural reorganization, phase transitions, and leaching of functional dopants, may occur due to prolonged exposure to body fluids, pH fluctuations, or oxidative environments. These changes can impact the crystalline structure, surface charge, or electron-hole separation efficiency, thereby altering photocatalytic response. For instance, Seremak et al. investigated the long-term durability of TiO 2  photocatalytic coatings deposited via low-pressure cold spray [ 240 ]. After 1000 h of humid chamber aging, amorphous coatings showed improved adhesion due to increased chemical interactions, while the adhesion of crystalline coatings decreased as passivation layers disrupted interfacial interlocking. Importantly, all coatings maintained stable photocatalytic activity across four methylene blue degradation cycles. Still, crystalline coatings demonstrated higher efficiency and stability due to reduced charge recombination and the formation of the brookite phase, which promoted interfacial charge separation. Despite a decline in dye adsorption after aging—attributed to reduced surface area and active sites—photocatalytic efficiency remained satisfactory, indicating that structural evolution, particularly phase transformation and defect formation, plays a key role in sustaining reactivity over time. The coating's ability to retain its functional performance after repeated irradiation—commonly referred to as reusability—is intrinsically linked to its mechanical stability, chemical durability, and robust interfacial adhesion [ 254 ]. Reusability is a key feature for translating photocatalytic coatings into clinical practice, as it ensures sustained antimicrobial performance through repeated light activation. A relevant example is provided by Nagay et al., who developed a TiO 2 -based coating codoped with nitrogen and bismuth via PEO, enabling activation under visible light [ 19 ]. Their study demonstrated that the coating retained photocatalytic activity after multiple cycles—specifically at 24 and 72 h post-initial irradiation—using the same surface under identical conditions. After each cycle, the samples were rinsed, stored in the dark, and reused, yet continued to exhibit significant dye degradation upon re-irradiation. Translating these findings to dental implant applications, the authors highlighted the potential of this approach for multiple peri-implant decontamination sessions. This sustained functionality demonstrates the importance of coating durability, chemical stability, and preserved ROS-generating capacity for the clinical implementation of reusable antimicrobial surfaces. To ensure that photocatalytic implant coatings remain effective over their intended clinical lifespan, it is essential to conduct studies that integrate assessments of mechanical stability, photocatalytic performance, and biocompatibility after aging. In parallel, future research should explore advanced material strategies—such as smart surfaces with self-healing capabilities, ion replenishment, or stimuli-responsive reinforcement—to counteract degradation while preserving surface functionality. Complementary to these efforts, evaluating the reusability of coatings after recolonization with multispecies biofilms is critical to better simulate the clinical environment and gain insight into the coatings’ regenerative potential under biologically dynamic conditions. Moreover, the long-term chemical durability of doped coatings must be validated to ensure that essential dopants needed to achieve visible-light-triggered photocatalysis are retained within the matrix and do not leach excessively into surrounding tissues, which could compromise both safety and functional longevity. Therefore, together, these considerations emphasize the importance of tailoring both material composition and functional design, paving the way for the next critical step: developing strategies to effectively shift photocatalytic activation from ultraviolet to the visible light region. 4.3 Engineering light-responsive coatings: shifting carcinogenic UV absorbance to more safe visible light wavelengths To develop visible-light-induced photocatalytic coatings, it is crucial to comprehensively understand their mechanism of action, particularly how these coatings interact with light to initiate photocatalytic processes. A key challenge is shifting the activation spectrum from carcinogenic UV light, which poses significant risks to human tissues, to safer visible light wavelengths. This transition requires strategically modifying photocatalyst properties, such as bandgap engineering, through doping or surface properties modification. Equally important is the understanding and application of reliable methods to evaluate ROS generation, as such chemicals are essential for achieving effective photocatalytic antimicrobial and pollutant-degrading performance while ensuring safety in biomedical and environmental applications. In a typical process, photocatalysis begins with irradiation on a semiconductor surface, where photons are absorbed, exciting electrons from the VB to the CB, creating electron-hole pairs. These pairs serve as current carriers within the material and can follow two possible paths: 1) Electrons and holes move to the outer surface of the semiconductor catalyst to facilitate chemical reactions with surrounding substrates, leading to the production of ROS, capable of degrading various contaminants, including inorganic and organic compounds, as well as pathogens; and 2) Electrons and holes may recombine within the semiconductor, resulting in the undesired wasteful release of energy as heat, which can hinder the photocatalytic process [ 24 , 27 ]. The efficiency and redox potential of photocatalysis are influenced by the band gap of the semiconductor, and modifying the intrinsic band structure can enhance the photocatalytic activity. Understanding electronic transitions is key to comprehending and improving photocatalytic mechanisms. In sum, heterogeneous photocatalysis relies on the direct irradiation of UV light onto the semiconductor photocatalyst's surface, initiating a sequence of chemical redox reactions (eq.  (2) ): (2) semiconductor + h v → e − ( CB ) + h + ( VB ) In the above reaction, photon absorption by the semiconductor generates electron-hole pairs in the CB and VB on the surface. These electron-hole pairs then migrate to the semiconductor's surface, where they interact with external elements like dissolved oxygen and water, resulting in the creation of ROS, including hydrogen peroxide, hydroxyl radicals, and superoxide radicals [ 255 ]. Such ROS generation can be identified using various advanced techniques [ 256 ]. In this context, electron spin resonance (ESR) is a highly sensitive method for directly detecting free radicals, while fluorescence detection with specific probes, such as dichloro-dihydro-fluorescein diacetate (DCFH-DA), provides a quantitative assessment of intracellular ROS levels [ 257 ]. Additionally, the degradation of dyes like methylene blue and methyl orange is commonly employed to indirectly evaluate ROS activity [ 257 ]. Nevertheless, when using this assay, researchers should bear in mind that the choice of dye for ROS detection through degradation assays is crucial because the dye's absorbance must align with the wavelength of light used to avoid interference from the dye's photodegradation. If the dye absorbs light in the applied wavelength range, it may degrade independently of the coating's photocatalytic activity, leading to inaccurate results [ 257 ]. Therefore, selecting a dye with minimal absorbance at the light wavelength ensures that the observed degradation is due to ROS generation from the coating rather than the dye's direct interaction with the light source. Beyond ROS detection, the electron-hole transitions responsible for ROS generation can be analyzed through photocurrent measurements, density functional theory (DFT) calculations, and electrochemical methods, offering insights into the material's photocatalytic properties and charge transfer dynamics [ 258 , 259 ]. These techniques provide a comprehensive understanding of the photochemical processes involved. Regarding photocatalyst choice, recent advancements in nanotechnology have led to the development of photosensitive nano-semiconductor materials such as ZnO, TiO 2 , BiO X , and Bi 2 O 3 , expanding the range of photocatalysts that can efficiently operate under UV–visible light, spanning wavelengths from 200 nm to >400 nm [ 27 ]. Among them, TiO 2 , known for its excellent photocatalytic properties, hydrophilicity, stability, and cost-effectiveness, is commonly utilized in photocatalysis [ 23 , 24 , 27 ]. While its native anatase form primarily responds to near-UV light, researchers have explored various doping and composite techniques to extend its photocatalytic activity into the visible light region, enabling the elimination of drug-resistant bacteria in water and even leading to the development of biomedical implant infection treatment strategies, including a) altering the semiconductor's composition through doping to extend the absorption range from UV to visible light; b) introducing defect formation and oxygen vacancies; and c) creating heterojunctions and coupling different semiconductors ( Fig. 9 a). Fig. 9 4.3.1 Doping the semiconductor Doping plays a crucial role in optimizing the performance of semiconductor photocatalysts, which involves intentionally introducing elements or impurities into a semiconductor material. Two major factors influencing doping are the capture of photogenerated charge carriers by doped metal ions to facilitate longer separation of charged species and the ability to free and drift trapped photogenerated charge carriers to the interface [ 27 ]. Doping can involve the introduction of cations (metals) and anions (non-metals) as dopants into crystal structures of semiconductor materials, which can lead to significant variations in the overall band gap and the creation of defects that influence photocatalytic behavior. Doping with metals : By targeting photocatalytic reactions, semiconductors can be doped either with transition or noble metals [ 25 ]. In photocatalytic reactions, where there is a significant concern about the potential recombination of photogenerated charge carriers before they can reach the semiconductor's surface to interact with target contaminants, various strategies have been employed, including the use of transition and inner transition metals (e.g., Zn 2+ , Mn 3+ , Fe 3+ , Sn 2+ , Al 3+ , Ni 3+ , and WO 3 ) as dopants [ 27 ]. These dopants play a crucial role in modifying the crystal structure, suppressing charge carrier recombination, prolonging the lifespan of charge carriers, and expanding the photocatalytic activity from the UV region into the visible region. Additionally, the incorporation of noble and post-transition metals like Ag, Pd, Bi, and Au within the matrix of TiO 2  has proven effective in enhancing photocatalytic efficiency under visible light by acting as electron traps, facilitating interfacial charge transfer, and thereby reducing the likelihood of electron-hole pair recombination [ 25 ]. For instance, Venkei et al. [ 263 ] conducted a study to investigate the interaction between a photoreactive composite coating material and  Streptococcus mitis  ( S. mitis ), a common oral bacterium. They assessed the antibacterial efficacy of nanohybrid coatings containing a physiologically safe 0.001 % Ag content through various in vitro experiments. The findings revealed that the spray-coated photocatalytic Ag-TiO 2  on Ti disks was activated by visible light and displayed significant antibacterial properties against  S. mitis  after 15 min of illumination, indicating its potential related to peri-implantitis control. Similarly, Nagay et al. demonstrated that doping bismuth into TiO 2  coatings via a one-step plasma electrolytic oxidation process effectively reduced the bandgap, enabling activation under visible light ( Fig. 9 b) [ 19 ]. The Bi-doped TiO 2  coating exhibited significant antibacterial activity against dual-species biofilms (almost 2-log reduction) while maintaining cytocompatibility with human gingival fibroblasts, highlighting its potential for implant-related applications and infection control. Doping with non-metals : The incorporation of non-metals, particularly nitrogen, into TiO 2  positively impacts its photocatalytic activity under visible light by narrowing the band gap energy. This doping method, involving the replacement of oxygen with nitrogen, is favored due to the comparable ionic radii of nitrogen and oxygen, and it helps extend the light absorption range of TiO 2  from UV to visible light. Non-metal doping also influences the morphology and electronic structure of the photocatalyst, making it an effective strategy for enhancing photocatalytic performance. Among non-metals (e.g., N, C, S, and F), nitrogen doping in TiO 2  is a noteworthy technique because it reduces the band gap and facilitates the transfer of electron-hole pairs. In the study of Zhang et al., [ 260 ] in which they synthesized nitrogen-doped TiO 2  coatings on reduced graphene oxide using sonochemical and hydrothermal methods, nitrogen doping was found to effectively reduce the band gap of TiO 2 , making it responsive to visible light ( Fig. 9 c). Interestingly, the addition of reduced graphene oxide enhanced the photocatalytic activity and improved adsorption capabilities and mass transfer in photocatalytic reactions. Following this similar concept, Javid et al. [ 264 ] developed N-doped TiO 2  films using a plasma-assisted method that enhanced surface roughness and wettability, improving photocatalytic and antibacterial activity under visible light. Nitrogen doping narrowed the band gap by creating mid-gap states, enabling visible-light activation and enhancing hydrophilicity. Under white light, the films achieved ∼20 % reduction in  E. coli  viability compared to dark conditions, demonstrating a potential strategy targeting antibacterial implant coatings. 4.3.2 Introducing defect formation and oxygen vacancies Intrinsic point defects in TiO 2  include oxygen vacancies (V o ), titanium interstitials (Ti int ), titanium vacancies ( V Ti), oxygen interstitials (O int ), and electronic defects involving electrons located at Ti 3+  ions and electron holes located on lattice sites of O −  ions. These defects are introduced due to disorder within the lattice structure of TiO 2 , resulting in non-stoichiometric variations such as TiO 2-x  (oxygen deficient) or TiO 2+x  (titanium deficient). These defects can act as either electron donors or acceptors, shifting the Fermi level within the band gap and enhancing the photocatalytic activity of TiO 2 . Specifically, oxygen vacancies play a crucial role in initiating redox reactions and improving charge separation, making them highly advantageous for photocatalysis, although their stability can be affected by the presence of reactant molecules. Based on this, Tan et al. [ 265 ] demonstrated that a nitrogen-doped TiO 2  photocatalyst synthesized through co-deposition using Ti isopropoxide and ammonia precursors was able to enhance the utilization efficiency of photo-generated charge carriers, promoting surface defect formation (e.g., oxygen vacancies) and facilitating oxygen circulation between Ti 4+  and Ti 3+  sites, resulting in enhanced NO removal efficiency and photocatalytic stability. Further, Shuai et al. developed a biodegradable PCLGA scaffold incorporating oxygen-vacancy-rich Fe-doped TiO 2  nanoparticles to enhance antibacterial activity via H 2 O 2 -driven Fenton reactions, effectively killing bacteria while maintaining mechanical compatibility with cancellous bone and supporting cell attachment, proliferation, and osteogenic differentiation [ 266 ]. Similarly, He et al. demonstrated that introducing surface oxygen vacancies in a TiO 2 /SrTiO 3  heterojunction significantly enhanced charge separation efficiency by 107 % compared to TiO 2 , highlighting the critical role of oxygen vacancies in improving photoelectrochemical performance ( Fig. 9 d) [ 261 ]. In line with this, Wu et al. [ 185 ] developed a TiO 2  nanoceramic coating via PEO that showed visible-light photocatalytic activity due to the presence of a disordered layer on its outer surface, which was confirmed to contain oxygen vacancies, as evidenced by a blue shift in the Raman spectra and a significant increase in Ti-OH content. Such oxygen vacancies’ introduction was further confirmed not to induce cytotoxicity to MG63 cells. Nevertheless, although the rationale of this concept would be directed at peri-implantitis treatment, the authors did not investigate antimicrobial properties under illumination. 4.3.3 Heterojunctions Heterojunctions are formed by combining two or more semiconductors using specific synthesis methods, providing benefits such as reduced charge carrier recombination, improved photocatalytic efficiency, and extended absorption into a wider range of wavelengths compared to single materials [ 267 ]. The visible-light-induced activity of hetero-semiconductors can be enhanced by coupling different semiconductors to align their energy levels, preventing carrier recombination and facilitating charge transfer between them [ 25 , 27 , 267 ]. This approach is effective in modifying UV-light active photocatalysts by incorporating narrow bandgap semiconductors like Bi 2 O 3  or Cu 2 O into materials such as TiO 2 , resulting in comparable energy levels and redox potentials for the mineralization of various contaminants [ 268 ]. For instance, Jiang et al. [ 250 ] developed and investigated an Ag 2 O/SiO 2 /Ta 2 O 5  nanocomposite applied onto Ti–6Al–4V substrates using a double-cathode glow discharge method for photocatalytic antibacterial purposes. The authors proposed that under visible light, electrons are excited in both Ta 2 O 5  and Ag 2 O and transferred through Ta 2 O 5 /SiO 2  and SiO 2 /Ag 2 O heterojunctions, accumulating in the conduction band of Ag 2 O. This electron accumulation enables the reduction of O 2  and protons to generate superoxide radicals and hydrogen, while holes contribute to hydroxyl radical formation for Rhodamine Blue degradation. The enhanced photocatalytic efficiency of the Ag-containing coating is attributed to its double heterojunction structure and extended electron transfer pathway. Notably, the Ag 2 O/SiO 2 /Ta 2 O 5  coating achieved nearly 100 % antibacterial efficacy against  E. coli  and  S. aureus  after 12 h of visible light exposure, highlighting its potential for implant surface modification. Similarly, a Cu 2 O/UiO-66/Bi 2 MoO 6  composite photocatalyst was developed using a simple chemical mixing method and showed high structural purity, efficient charge separation, and fast electron migration due to a double-Z scheme transfer model ( Fig. 9 e) [ 262 ]. UiO-66 played a key role in mitigating photocorrosion, while the synergistic interaction between Bi 2 MoO 6  and Cu 2 O enhanced redox activity under sunlight excitation. The composite exhibited strong photocatalytic antibacterial effects against  S. aureus, E. coli,  and MRSA. Its bactericidal mechanism is driven by oxidative stress from ∙O 2 −  and ∙OH radicals and the controlled release of Cu +  and Bi 3+  ions, supported by its large surface area that increases contact with bacterial cells. An interesting strategy to achieve photocatalytic activation under visible or near-NIR light involves combining multiple bandgap-engineering approaches, such as heterojunction formation and the introduction of oxygen vacancies (OVs). A representative example is the TiO 2 /Bi 2 WO 6  heterostructure, where TiO 2  nanowires are formed on titanium implant surfaces via alkaline thermal treatment, followed by in situ hydrothermal growth of Bi 2 WO 6  nanocrystals ( Fig. 10 a) [ 269 ]. This configuration narrows the bandgap from 3.28 eV (TiO 2 ) to 2.83 eV ( Fig. 10 b), enhancing light absorption in the visible–NIR range. In vitro studies demonstrated high antibacterial activity, with over 98 % reduction of  E. coli ,  P. gingivalis , and MRSA after 10 min of irradiation ( Fig. 10 e). In vivo, in a rat bone defect model with induced MRSA infection, the TiO 2 /Bi 2 WO 6 -coated implants achieved a 97.81 % reduction in bacterial load ( Fig. 10 c and d) and promoted superior bone regeneration, as evidenced by micro-CT analysis ( Fig. 10 f). Importantly, the introduction of oxygen vacancies played a crucial role by creating defect states within the bandgap that facilitate visible light absorption, promote charge carrier separation, and serve as active sites for surface reactions ( Fig. 10 g). Additionally, the coating enhanced the osteogenic differentiation of bone mesenchymal stem cells (mBMSCs), showing increased F-actin organization and cell spreading ( Fig. 10 h), attributed to the micro-nanostructure and piezoelectric properties of the heterojunction. Although this system was evaluated under NIR irradiation, the bandgap of 2.83 eV falls within the visible light range, suggesting that similar systems may also be activated by visible light alone [ 269 ]. Therefore, this example serves as a valuable reference for the design of future light-responsive coatings aimed at controlling infections and promoting osseointegration using clinically safe wavelengths. Nonetheless, the pursuit of ideal coatings with multifunctional attributes has led to diverse approaches, incorporating various dopants, strategies, and light sources. Furthermore, many evaluations of their antimicrobial efficacy lack substantial evidence or employ biofilm models that do not accurately represent clinical conditions for (infected) biomedical and dental implant applications. 4.1 Synthesis strategies for constructing photocatalytic coatings targeting biomedical implant application Effective photocatalyst development requires a comprehensive understanding of synthesis procedures and the characterization of physicochemical properties essential for their performance under light. Notably, achieving an optimal balance among critical properties, including surface area, wettability, stability, and reusability, is crucial when designing reliable photocatalytic coatings. This is because a larger surface area provides more active sites for photocatalytic reactions, enhancing the chances of successful organic compound degradation or other desired reactions. In addition, proper wettability ensures uniform reactant contact with the photocatalytic surface, optimizing reaction efficiency. At the same time, stability and reusability contribute to long-term and sustainable performance, enhancing the cost-benefit of the approach. Importantly, the chosen synthesis technique significantly influences all these essential factors. Consequently, researchers have delved into a wide array of coating fabrication methods, selecting the most appropriate based on their specific objectives. These methods encompass various wet chemical approaches, including sol-gel, hydrothermal, and solvothermal processes, as well as plasma-assisted methods, all employed to engineer both doped and undoped photocatalytic coatings tailored to meet diverse application requirements ( Fig. 7 ). Fig. 7 4.1.1 Sol-gel synthesis Sol-gel methods are widely used for the synthesis of photocatalysts, making these valuable for nanoscale TiO 2  material production ( Fig. 7 a). They involve two main stages: hydrolysis and polycondensation. During hydrolysis, metal alkoxides break down in either water or alcohol, with the choice of reaction medium leading to either an “aqueous” or “non-aqueous” route [ 224 ]. Polycondensation follows, involving the bonding of neighboring molecules, forming metal oxide bonds and polymer networks. This process increases the system's viscosity, resulting in a porous gel structure while maintaining a liquid phase, in which the size and cross-linking of colloidal particles depend on the precursor and pH [ 225 ]. Then, substrates are often immersed in the reaction mixture during hydrolysis or condensation, followed by aging, drying, thermal treatments, or a combination to promote crystallization and adhesion. By using such methods, thin films with thicknesses spanning 50–500 nm can be fabricated using diverse coating techniques, such as dip-coating, spin-coating, spray-coating, flow-coating, and capillary-coating [ 225 ]. For instance, aiming to enhance the photocatalytic properties of spin-coated sol-gel anatase-type TiO 2 , Tsuji et al. [ 226 ] implanted Ag-negative ions at different energies and doses to these coatings, followed by annealing. The treated samples demonstrated improved photocatalytic efficiency, where Ag nanoparticles (AgNPs), located at a shallow depth in the coating, significantly improved the photocatalytic efficiency, surpassing that of rutile single crystal TiO 2  due to a lower bandgap. Corroborating such results, Khitous et al. [ 221 ] demonstrated a simple, low-cost method that combines asymmetrically shaped AuNPs, formed via thermal dewetting, with a TiO 2  sol-gel layer applied by spin-coating, enhancing visible-light photocatalysis through improved reaction kinetics and hot electron lifetimes ( Fig. 7 a’). In addition, as an example that the method of synthesis can completely change the photocatalytic efficiency, in a study conducted by Asadi et al., [ 227 ] nitrogen and sulfur co-doped TiO 2  nanoparticles were synthesized through a combination of sol-gel and hydrothermal methods. Their results revealed that materials prepared using the sol-gel approach exhibited significantly enhanced photocatalytic activity compared to the hydrothermal one, probably due to the particle size and surface area differences, making them a promising option for practical applications. Nevertheless, a disadvantage of such a method for biomedical implant application relies on its poor adhesion to metallic substrates, thereby needing special attention towards physical or chemical modification of the substrate to enhance the adhesion strength at the coating-substrate interface [ 228 ]. 4.1.2 Anodization method The anodization method is commonly conducted in an electrolytic solution under constant voltage potential, facilitating the growth of nanostructure surfaces such as nanotubes ( Fig. 7 b). Highly ordered TiO 2  nanotube arrays (TNTAs), prepared via electrochemical anodization, have gained interest due to their aligned porosity, high crystallinity, and oriented nanotubular morphology, which enhance light absorption and charge separation. Considering this, Xiao et al. [ 229 ] constructed a hierarchically ordered Au x /NP-TNTA heterostructure, fabricated through two-step anodization and electrostatic self-assembly, with versatile photocatalytic properties, including pollutant degradation, with enhanced photosensitization from glutathione-capped Au x  clusters (i.e., atomically precise thiolate-protected gold clusters) and elucidated mechanisms offering insights for novel metal-cluster/1D semiconductor applications. Targeting implant applications, Moon et al. [ 222 ] prepared TiO 2  nanotubes (NTs) via anodization followed by crystallization through heating at 400 °C for 3 h in air. Then, to extend the photocatalytic activity of titania beyond the UV range into the visible light spectrum, the authors decorated the NTs with Au ( Fig. 7 b’) or Pt by ion plasma sputtering. Such doping can also be performed by hydrothermal treatment (HT). Typically, the synthesis of photocatalytic coatings using HT occurs by introducing the sample into the vessel containing a liquid medium, followed by annealing at high temperatures and subsequent cooling, allowing for the growth of a coating onto the substrate. Zhang et al. [ 230 ] recently reported on successfully constructing a TiO 2  nanostructure on a Ti surface by HT growth using NaOH solution. Interestingly, to achieve photocatalytic activity under visible light, the authors synthesized a TiO 2 /MoS 2  coating in two HT steps: the first one with NaOH and the second one with MoS 2 , which effectively killed  S. aureus  in vitro and in vivo within 10 min of irradiation. 4.1.3 Magnetron sputtering Photocatalytic coatings can also be produced using magnetron sputtering, offering precise control over plasma parameters and the desired properties ( Fig. 7 c). Sputtering is a well-established process that involves expelling atoms from a target surface when bombarded by energetic particles, leading to the formation of thin films on a substrate [ 231 ]. The ejected atoms have high energy, which enhances their ability to condense and adhere to the substrate. Wong et al. [ 223 ] developed TiO 2 (N)/Ag/TiO 2 (N) sandwich films via magnetron sputtering, embedding an Ag layer between two N-doped TiO 2  layers using two Ti and one Ag target ( Fig. 7 c’). Microbiological experiments showed that in the absence of Ag, microbial cells preserved their integrity with smooth surface morphology, regardless of visible light exposure. However, when Ag was incorporated into the films, it induced roughening of the bacterial surface in the dark, likely due to interactions between Ag and the bacterial cell wall. Upon exposure to visible light, these surfaces underwent more pronounced structural changes, including the development of distinct cracks. In another report, Ueda et al. [ 232 ] deposited pure gold (Au) and a titanium-gold (Ti-Au) alloy film (60 mol% Ti, 40 mol% Au) onto Ti substrates using sputtering, followed by thermal oxidation to create TiO 2  layers. These layers were evaluated for their antibacterial properties against  Escherichia coli , cytotoxicity, and bonding strength to Ti substrates. The most promising results in terms of antibacterial activity under visible-light exposure were achieved with a 38 nm thick sputtered film made of pure Au, evidencing an R-value of 1.8, corresponding to approximately 98 % reduction in  E. coli  viability. Interestingly, Ratova et al. evaluated the photocatalytic and antimicrobial performance of bismuth oxide, bismuth tungstate, and titanium dioxide coatings deposited on glass beads via reactive magnetron sputtering, followed by annealing [ 233 ]. Bismuth oxide coatings showed superior dye degradation and complete inactivation of  E. coli  under visible light within 48 h, attributed to their low bandgap and stable hydrophobic surface, offering both disinfection and antifouling advantages. Nevertheless, bismuth oxide coatings may not present ideal mechanical and chemical stability for implant applications. In contrast, titanium dioxide is widely used in biomedical implants due to its excellent biocompatibility and long-term stability, but it requires modification to be activated under visible light—making doping with Bi 2 O 3  a promising strategy to combine the robustness of TiO 2  with the visible-light responsiveness of bismuth-based systems. 4.1.4 Plasma electrolytic oxidation Plasma electrolytic oxidation (PEO) utilizes a powerful electrical discharge within a system comprising a cathode (a cooled vessel), a working substrate immersed in an electrolyte serving as the anode, and a power supply ( Fig. 7 d). This method offers a cost-effective alternative to vacuum-based plasma technologies and is particularly advantageous for creating robust, uniform coatings on complex-shaped metallic objects, such as biomedical implants and devices, without exposing the entire substrate to high temperatures or requiring sophisticated equipment. Unlike other coating processes, PEO results from a substrate conversion process in tandem with deposition. Its core advantage lies in the generation of high-voltage plasma discharges around substrates of varying shapes, enabling the doping of diverse chemical elements in a single step. This capability allows for the production of biofunctional coatings characterized by thickness, roughness, porosity, and crystallinity, which are beneficial for photocatalytic activity and implant-bone integration. Wu et al. [ 185 ] synthesized TiO 2  porous nanoceramic coatings on titanium substrates using the PEO process that presented photocatalytic activity due to a disordered outer layer with oxygen vacancies, effectively degrading methylene blue, rhodamine B, and lipopolysaccharide (LPS) under visible light ( Fig. 7 d’). Although the authors claimed that the coating could improve Ti implant decontamination, light irradiation of biofilm formed onto the developed coating was not evaluated. On the other hand, we [ 19 ] employed the PEO technique to develop a Bi-doped TiO 2  coating suitable for biomedical and dental implant applications. This coating demonstrated enhanced photocatalytic activity, attributed to Bi doping, resulting in the effective reduction of  S. sanguinis  and  Actinomyces naeslundii  dual-species biofilm, with visible light further amplifying its antibacterial properties, holding potential for peri-implant infection control.

4.2 Critical determinants of photocatalytic implant coating functionality: structural integrity, reusability, substrate-specific interactions, and biocompatibility Following the discussion on synthesis methods, it is crucial to consider how physical and interfacial properties influence the overall functionality and clinical longevity of photocatalytic coatings. These factors directly affect antibacterial efficacy and determine the coating's ability to withstand friction, cyclic loading, and exposure to biochemical fluids during implantation and daily use. Insufficient adhesion between the coating and implant surface can result in degradation or delamination, exposing the underlying material and increasing susceptibility to microbial colonization and biofilm formation, thereby raising the risk of peri-implant disease [ 234 ]. Additionally, the tribocorrosion process may release metallic ions and debris, altering the peri-implant environment, triggering inflammation, and contributing to bone resorption [ 235 ]. Loss of structural integrity also compromises the coating's antimicrobial performance and reusability, as photocatalytic activity depends on stable ROS generation at the coating–tissue interface. Therefore, for clinical translation use, photocatalytic coatings must combine efficient ROS-based antimicrobial activity with strong interfacial adhesion, mechanical and chemical durability, and biocompatibility. 4.2.1 Coating thickness, adhesion and substrate-specific interactions Coating thickness plays a central role in photocatalytic performance and coating stability [ 236 ]. Very thin coatings may lack sufficient active surface for ROS generation, while excessively thick layers can hinder light penetration and promote charge recombination [ 237 , 238 ]. Dundar et al. demonstrated that TiO 2  films with intermediate thicknesses around 200 nm exhibited superior photocatalytic activity, with thicker films showing reduced performance due to optical and transport constraints [ 238 ]. The Sofroniou et al. study further showed that coatings with a thicker TiO 2  surface top layer displayed superior antibacterial performance against MRSA under irradiation compared to thinner or more stratified systems due to improved light penetration and increased nanoparticle exposure at the air–film interface [ 239 ]. These findings highlight the importance of optimizing thickness as a key parameter for achieving efficient and durable photocatalytic performance. Seremak et al. investigated the long-term durability of TiO 2  photocatalytic coatings deposited via low-pressure cold spray, highlighting how coating thickness, crystallinity, and bonding mechanisms influence mechanical stability and photocatalytic performance [ 240 ]. Thicker and more crystalline coatings exhibited superior adhesion (>30 N) primarily due to enhanced mechanical interlocking, whereas thinner, amorphous coatings adhered mainly through chemical bonding at the interface via Ti–O–Al linkages. In this context, it is notable that interfacial adhesion between the coating and the underlying implant substrate significantly affects the stability and long-term performance of biomedical devices. Coatings with insufficient bonding strength may delaminate under physiological loading, compromising the mechanical integrity and functional lifespan of the implant. Achieving reliable adhesion—via chemical bonding, mechanical interlocking, or intermediate layers—is thus critical for the clinical translation of photocatalytic coatings. Furthermore, given that photocatalytic strategies are increasingly applied to various implant substrates, including titanium, zirconia, biodegradable metals, and polymers, substrate–coating compatibility must be thoroughly evaluated. Surface energy, oxide layer chemistry, and thermal expansion mismatch can significantly affect coating uniformity, adhesion, and degradation behavior. For example, heat treatments required for crystallization may degrade polymeric materials or compromise low-melting alloys, while differences in oxide formation depending on the substrate can affect bonding mechanisms. For polymeric implants and devices, sol-gel–derived TiO 2 –ZnO thin films deposited on polycarbonate substrates via an intermediate SiO 2  layer demonstrated high optical transparency, mechanical robustness, and photocatalytic activity [ 241 ]. Pre-treatment of the polymer surface with light irradiation facilitated the formation of surface hydroxyl groups, enhancing interfacial bonding with the SiO 2  layer, overcoming the limitation poor adhesion feature of typical sol-gel coatings. Adhesion performance was rated excellent (grade 0, ISO 2409), even after extended UV exposure and abrasion cycles [ 241 ]. In contrast, ceramic substrates such as zirconia—widely used in dental implantology—present inherent challenges for coating adhesion due to their chemical inertness and low surface reactivity. To overcome these limitations, surface activation techniques like plasma treatment or functionalized interlayers can be employed to increase surface energy and promote film anchorage. Although direct studies on photocatalytic TiO 2 -based films on zirconia are limited, similar strategies are applicable. Notably, Bouras et al. reported that Zr-doped ZnO thin films deposited on ceramic substrates exhibited superior photocatalytic activity compared to those on glass [ 242 ]. This enhancement was attributed to the ceramic-supported films’ rougher morphology, increased crystallite size, and improved charge separation efficiency, collectively promoting greater light absorption and hydroxyl radical generation. Additionally, an innovative approach involved the integration of TiO 2  nanotubes onto nanostructured aluminum surfaces fabricated via tubular channel angular pressing [ 243 ]. These high-strength aluminum substrates were further functionalized with nano-concave arrays, enabling localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) coupling with the TiO 2  nanotubes. The resulting hybrid surfaces showed remarkable mechanical performance, with adhesion forces exceeding 2100 mN in scratch tests, alongside significant antibacterial efficacy against  E. coli  under light activation. Similarly, PEO has emerged as a promising technique for biomedical applications due to its ability to produce strongly adherent, porous, and crystalline oxide layers on metals such as titanium, alloys, and zirconium [ 104 ]. Unlike conventional methods, PEO creates mechanically interlocked coatings and chemically bonds to the substrate through in-situ oxide growth, resulting in superior adhesion and long-term interfacial stability. Another key advantage is the precise control over coating features achieved by adjusting the electrolyte, current density, and processing time. The substrate itself plays a pivotal role in this process. Its thermal and electrical properties influence microdischarge behavior, which governs oxide growth, melting/resolidification, and incorporation of electrolyte species. These factors directly impact coating thickness, crystallite size, and defect formation, all critical for photocatalytic performance. In this context, PEO coatings benefit from substrate-driven modulation of charge carrier dynamics, where structural and chemical features of the oxide influence redox activity. For example, zirconia coatings formed via PEO on zirconium substrates showed increased oxygen vacancy formation with extended oxidation time [ 244 ]. These vacancies not only improved photoluminescence and ROS generation but also reinforced the coating's cohesion and adhesion, which is critical for durable biomedical performance. Further, a typical feature of the PEO process is the occurrence of microdischarges that are influenced by coating thickness: in the early stages, lower-energy microarcs favor the formation of anatase, whereas as the coating thickens, only more intense electric fields can cause a dielectric breakdown, promoting the formation of rutile or anatase/rutile mixtures [ 19 ]. This evolution directly impacts the photocatalytic behavior of the surface. Nagay et al. observed that Bi-doped TiO 2  PEO coatings on commercially pure titanium (cpTi) substrates presenting a mixture of anatase and rutile showed excellent photocatalytic antibacterial performance under visible light due to the optical and high surface area properties of the coating [ 19 ]. This observation aligns with the findings of Pantaroto et al., who demonstrated, through magnetron sputtering, that mixed-phase TiO 2  films on cpTi substrate exhibit superior photocatalytic activity against oral pathogens under UV light compared to only anatase or rutile thin films [ 245 ]. On the other hand, Momeni et al. investigated the effects of adding SiO 2  to nitrogen-doped TiO 2  thin films applied to stainless steel via a sol-gel spray method, aiming to enhance visible-light photocatalytic performance and mechanical stability [ 246 ]. Contrary to prior findings on glass or polymer substrates, the addition of 20 % SiO 2  increased the band gap energy (from 2.93 to 3.09 eV), induced significant crack formation during calcination, and ultimately reduced visible-light photocatalytic activity and hydrophilicity. The reduced activity was attributed to low crystallinity, increased electron-hole recombination from grain boundaries, Fe 2+  ion diffusion from the steel substrate, and a detrimental crack pattern that diminished surface area. Although all films demonstrated strong adhesion in nanoscratch testing, SiO 2 -containing films showed lower mechanical stability, evidenced by force drop-offs and crack formation under stress [ 246 ]. These findings suggest that for steel-based substrates used under visible-light conditions, non-silica TiO 2  coatings may offer superior performance in terms of photocatalytic efficiency, surface integrity, and durability. Importantly, this study highlights the need for a careful balance in dopant type and concentration—while doping is essential to shift TiO 2  activity to the visible-light range, excessive or poorly integrated secondary phases may compromise mechanical and functional properties critical for clinical applications. It is important to highlight, though, that while this section consolidates key factors—particularly coating thickness and interfacial adhesion—that critically influence the performance of photocatalytic coatings and, consequently, ROS generation for antibacterial purposes, it is important to note that most of the available evidence comes from systems not specifically designed for visible-light activation. Nevertheless, these studies offer valuable insights into the structural and interfacial mechanisms that underpin coating performance. Still, investigations that systematically assess these parameters under visible-light-responsive conditions remain scarce. Future research should aim to bridge this gap by evaluating how variations in coating thickness and interfacial strength influence functional durability, antibacterial activity, and oxidative performance under clinically relevant illumination. Experimental strategies may include pull-off and scratch adhesion tests, cross-sectional analysis via SEM or profilometry, and correlating these features with ROS generation and microbial inhibition. Furthermore, extending these evaluations to different implant-relevant substrates will be essential to ensure coating reliability and performance across diverse biomedical applications. 4.2.2 Mechanical properties, wear and corrosion resistance: implications for photocatalytic antimicrobial performance and biocompatibility In photocatalytic coatings intended for biomedical and dental implants, mechanical robustness and corrosion resistance are critical for structural durability and preserving antimicrobial functionality over time. Surface degradation, whether by wear or electrochemical attack, may directly compromise ROS generation, reduce effective surface area, and even trigger adverse tissue responses. Wear resistance is particularly important in load-bearing or micro-movement-prone regions, such as implant-abutment interfaces [ 234 ]. Surface abrasion can erode the photocatalytic layer, removing active crystalline domains (e.g., anatase/rutile TiO 2 ), exposing the underlying substrate, and decreasing antimicrobial efficiency. In such scenarios, the loss of surface integrity would diminish photocatalytic activity and facilitate bacterial adhesion and biofilm formation in damaged regions. Translating to clinical application, wear resistance against mechanical instrumentation, for example, is critical to ensure that photocatalytic coatings remain functional during routine decontamination procedures. In this context, a TiO 2  nanoceramic coating was developed on titanium implants using a PEO-based process followed by annealing and polishing [ 185 ]. The resulting coating featured a dense, nanocrystalline microstructure and an oxygen-vacancy-rich disordered outer layer, with a thickness of about 26 nm, enabling visible-light-driven photocatalysis ( Fig. 8 a). Additionally, the coating maintained its structural integrity after treatment with steel curettes and ultrasonic scalers—procedures that typically damage conventional titanium or TiO 2  coatings ( Fig. 8 b). This superior wear resistance was attributed to the high surface hardness (10.22 ± 2.3 GPa), metallurgical bonding with the titanium substrate, and a microstructure that prevented crack propagation. The coating also demonstrated favorable cell responses, with comparable or superior biocompatibility and osteogenic potential compared to untreated titanium [ 185 ]. In another study, Chung et al. (2009) systematically evaluated TiO 2  coatings deposited via arc ion plating (AIP) onto stainless steel substrates, focusing on how deposition parameters influenced microstructure, mechanical durability, and functional performance [ 247 ]. They demonstrated that increasing the deposition time and oxygen partial pressure promoted the formation of anatase-rich coatings with a compact columnar morphology. These structural features led to a substantial increase in surface hardness (up to 679.6 HV) and strong film adhesion (21.2 N in scratch tests), which in turn improved abrasive wear resistance and corrosion protection in NaCl environments. Mechanistically, the improved adhesion and wear resistance were attributed to cohesive strength within the well-crystallized anatase phase and interfacial pseudo-interdiffusion, while corrosion resistance was linked to the dense, inert nature of the oxide layer that limited electrolyte permeation. Importantly, the authors noted that the same conditions that enhanced mechanical robustness—i.e., thicker coatings with higher crystallinity—also supported greater photocatalytic and antimicrobial activity, likely due to reduced recombination of charge carriers and the formation of ROS at the surface [ 247 ].
