Many photocatalytic coatings, especially doped oxides or mixed-phase materials, are semiconducting and can exhibit electrochemical reactivity under physiological conditions. Supporting this perspective, an Ag 2 O/SiO 2 /Ta 2 O 5  nanocomposite coating was developed for orthopedic implants and demonstrated excellent tribological, anticorrosion, photocatalytic, and antimicrobial performance [ 250 ]. The inclusion of Ag 2 O and SiO 2  within a Ta 2 O 5  matrix not only enhanced wear resistance—reflected by improved hardness-to-elasticity ratios and reduced friction—but also significantly mitigated corrosion in Ringer's solution. The coating maintained a stable barrier function over time, with superior electrochemical impedance and lower corrosion currents compared to uncoated Ti–6Al–4V. From a photocatalytic perspective, visible-light activation was enabled by the engineered heterojunction, which reduced the band gap and improved charge separation, as confirmed by DFT calculations. This translated into a higher Rhodamine B degradation rate and near-complete bacterial inactivation under visible light. Importantly, the bactericidal effect was driven by a synergistic mechanism combining reactive oxygen species generation via photocatalysis and Ag +  ion release, offering potent dual-mode antimicrobial protection alongside mechanical and chemical durability. Tribocorrosion—the combined action of mechanical wear and electrochemical degradation—also plays a critical role in the long-term stability of titanium implants, especially in a complex physiological environment [ 251 ]. For instance, it was reported that TiO 2 /SrTiO 3  coating developed on Ti6Al4V alloy exhibited synergistic antibacterial, tribocorrosion-resistant, and wear-resistant properties through distinct yet interconnected mechanisms [ 248 ]. Its photocatalytic antibacterial activity is primarily due to the generation of ROS, particularly superoxide radicals (·O 2 − ), facilitated by a heterojunction structure that enhances UV light absorption and charge separation. Under UV illumination, the bacterial proliferation rate dropped to 3 %, and clear inhibition zones were observed, confirming its potent photocatalytic disinfection. In terms of wear resistance, the presence of a robust thermal oxide layer reduced wear volume loss to 1/8 that of uncoated Ti6Al4V and decreased maximum wear scar depth from 15 μm to 3 μm ( Fig. 8 c). The coating also minimized plastic deformation and abrasive damage. Regarding tribocorrosion, the oxide layer served as a protective barrier that stabilized open circuit potential (OCP) during sliding tests in simulated body fluid (SBF) and maintained surface integrity, preventing substrate exposure and corrosion ( Fig. 8 d–f) [ 248 ]. Therefore, since biomedical implants are susceptible to bio-tribocorrosion phenomena in the oral environment (driven by the synergistic interplay of mechanical wear, chemical reactions, biochemical agents, and microbial activity), it is essential to investigate their mechanical and electrochemical behavior under conditions that closely mimic the clinical setting [ 234 ]. Building upon the discussion of corrosion and tribocorrosion resistance in biological environments, it is essential to consider the additional challenge posed by microbiologically influenced corrosion, which has been reported to compromise the integrity of metallic implants and industrial components in biological or humid environments. In this context, Li et al. designed a multifunctional 2D g-C 3 N 4 /Cu 2 O/Cu photocatalytic coating to address both microbial colonization and microbial corrosion ( Fig. 8 g) [ 249 ]. The coating architecture leveraged an S-type heterojunction to enhance visible-light-driven charge separation while simultaneously suppressing Cu 2 O photocorrosion through the stabilizing presence of Cu 0 . The ultrathin porous g-C 3 N 4  provided abundant nucleation sites, enabling uniform Cu 2 O/Cu deposition and facilitating ROS generation. As a result, the coating demonstrated antibacterial effects against  E. coli  and  S. aureus , achieving nearly complete bacterial elimination within 1 h under light and antibacterial activity even in the dark. Long-term assays revealed outstanding durability and microbial corrosion resistance, as evidenced by significantly reduced corrosion current, pit formation, and pitting depth on 316L stainless steel exposed to  Pseudomonas aeruginosa  ( Fig. 8 h) [ 249 ]. These findings highlight the potential dual-functionality of such coatings in combating both biofilm formation and microbial corrosion through synergistic photocatalytic and metallic mechanisms. Altogether, wear, corrosion, and tribocorrosion processes can lead to localized pH changes, ion release, and surface charge alterations that influence both bacterial behavior and cellular responses [ 251 ]. The breakdown of the passive TiO 2  layer under physical, chemical, and microbial challenges can trigger titanium ion/particle release, which in turn activates inflammatory pathways—particularly through neutrophils, macrophages, and osteogenic cells—culminating in increased pro-inflammatory cytokine production (e.g., IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and RANKL-mediated osteoclastogenesis, thus exacerbating peri-implant bone loss [ 252 ]. In this context, photocatalytic coatings are promising solutions, offering on-demand antibacterial activity through light-triggered ROS generation and acting as protective barriers against tribocorrosion and ion leakage. However, their clinical translation requires careful consideration of substrate compatibility. As mentioned earlier, on titanium substrates, photocatalytic coatings like TiO 2  and its heterostructures can achieve strong chemical bonding and mechanical stability through techniques such as PEO or thermal treatments; in contrast, zirconia and polymers often require surface pre-treatments or interfacial layers to enhance coating adhesion due to their inert or thermosensitive nature. Moreover, the biological safety of these coatings is influenced by their degradation behavior and ion release profiles. While dopants like Ag 2+ , Cu 2+ , or Bi 3+  can promote the shift of TiO 2  to the visible light range and achieve photocatalytic antibacterial effects under irradiation [ 27 , 253 ], uncontrolled leaching of these ions may induce cytotoxicity or inflammation. Thus, attaining durable adhesion, mechanical resilience, and biocompatibility requires tailoring the coating strategy to the specific implant substrate, ensuring that the multifunctional benefits of photocatalytic surfaces are performed without compromising tissue integration or patient safety. 4.2.3 Long-term stability and reusability of photocatalytic implant coatings Beyond initial antimicrobial or photocatalytic efficacy, the long-term durability of implant coatings under physiological conditions is critical for their clinical translation. Aging effects, including structural reorganization, phase transitions, and leaching of functional dopants, may occur due to prolonged exposure to body fluids, pH fluctuations, or oxidative environments. These changes can impact the crystalline structure, surface charge, or electron-hole separation efficiency, thereby altering photocatalytic response. For instance, Seremak et al. investigated the long-term durability of TiO 2  photocatalytic coatings deposited via low-pressure cold spray [ 240 ]. After 1000 h of humid chamber aging, amorphous coatings showed improved adhesion due to increased chemical interactions, while the adhesion of crystalline coatings decreased as passivation layers disrupted interfacial interlocking. Importantly, all coatings maintained stable photocatalytic activity across four methylene blue degradation cycles. Still, crystalline coatings demonstrated higher efficiency and stability due to reduced charge recombination and the formation of the brookite phase, which promoted interfacial charge separation. Despite a decline in dye adsorption after aging—attributed to reduced surface area and active sites—photocatalytic efficiency remained satisfactory, indicating that structural evolution, particularly phase transformation and defect formation, plays a key role in sustaining reactivity over time. The coating's ability to retain its functional performance after repeated irradiation—commonly referred to as reusability—is intrinsically linked to its mechanical stability, chemical durability, and robust interfacial adhesion [ 254 ]. Reusability is a key feature for translating photocatalytic coatings into clinical practice, as it ensures sustained antimicrobial performance through repeated light activation. A relevant example is provided by Nagay et al., who developed a TiO 2 -based coating codoped with nitrogen and bismuth via PEO, enabling activation under visible light [ 19 ]. Their study demonstrated that the coating retained photocatalytic activity after multiple cycles—specifically at 24 and 72 h post-initial irradiation—using the same surface under identical conditions. After each cycle, the samples were rinsed, stored in the dark, and reused, yet continued to exhibit significant dye degradation upon re-irradiation. Translating these findings to dental implant applications, the authors highlighted the potential of this approach for multiple peri-implant decontamination sessions. This sustained functionality demonstrates the importance of coating durability, chemical stability, and preserved ROS-generating capacity for the clinical implementation of reusable antimicrobial surfaces. To ensure that photocatalytic implant coatings remain effective over their intended clinical lifespan, it is essential to conduct studies that integrate assessments of mechanical stability, photocatalytic performance, and biocompatibility after aging. In parallel, future research should explore advanced material strategies—such as smart surfaces with self-healing capabilities, ion replenishment, or stimuli-responsive reinforcement—to counteract degradation while preserving surface functionality. Complementary to these efforts, evaluating the reusability of coatings after recolonization with multispecies biofilms is critical to better simulate the clinical environment and gain insight into the coatings’ regenerative potential under biologically dynamic conditions. Moreover, the long-term chemical durability of doped coatings must be validated to ensure that essential dopants needed to achieve visible-light-triggered photocatalysis are retained within the matrix and do not leach excessively into surrounding tissues, which could compromise both safety and functional longevity. Therefore, together, these considerations emphasize the importance of tailoring both material composition and functional design, paving the way for the next critical step: developing strategies to effectively shift photocatalytic activation from ultraviolet to the visible light region.

4.2.1 Coating thickness, adhesion and substrate-specific interactions Coating thickness plays a central role in photocatalytic performance and coating stability [ 236 ]. Very thin coatings may lack sufficient active surface for ROS generation, while excessively thick layers can hinder light penetration and promote charge recombination [ 237 , 238 ]. Dundar et al. demonstrated that TiO 2  films with intermediate thicknesses around 200 nm exhibited superior photocatalytic activity, with thicker films showing reduced performance due to optical and transport constraints [ 238 ]. The Sofroniou et al. study further showed that coatings with a thicker TiO 2  surface top layer displayed superior antibacterial performance against MRSA under irradiation compared to thinner or more stratified systems due to improved light penetration and increased nanoparticle exposure at the air–film interface [ 239 ]. These findings highlight the importance of optimizing thickness as a key parameter for achieving efficient and durable photocatalytic performance. Seremak et al. investigated the long-term durability of TiO 2  photocatalytic coatings deposited via low-pressure cold spray, highlighting how coating thickness, crystallinity, and bonding mechanisms influence mechanical stability and photocatalytic performance [ 240 ]. Thicker and more crystalline coatings exhibited superior adhesion (>30 N) primarily due to enhanced mechanical interlocking, whereas thinner, amorphous coatings adhered mainly through chemical bonding at the interface via Ti–O–Al linkages. In this context, it is notable that interfacial adhesion between the coating and the underlying implant substrate significantly affects the stability and long-term performance of biomedical devices. Coatings with insufficient bonding strength may delaminate under physiological loading, compromising the mechanical integrity and functional lifespan of the implant. Achieving reliable adhesion—via chemical bonding, mechanical interlocking, or intermediate layers—is thus critical for the clinical translation of photocatalytic coatings. Furthermore, given that photocatalytic strategies are increasingly applied to various implant substrates, including titanium, zirconia, biodegradable metals, and polymers, substrate–coating compatibility must be thoroughly evaluated. Surface energy, oxide layer chemistry, and thermal expansion mismatch can significantly affect coating uniformity, adhesion, and degradation behavior. For example, heat treatments required for crystallization may degrade polymeric materials or compromise low-melting alloys, while differences in oxide formation depending on the substrate can affect bonding mechanisms. For polymeric implants and devices, sol-gel–derived TiO 2 –ZnO thin films deposited on polycarbonate substrates via an intermediate SiO 2  layer demonstrated high optical transparency, mechanical robustness, and photocatalytic activity [ 241 ]. Pre-treatment of the polymer surface with light irradiation facilitated the formation of surface hydroxyl groups, enhancing interfacial bonding with the SiO 2  layer, overcoming the limitation poor adhesion feature of typical sol-gel coatings. Adhesion performance was rated excellent (grade 0, ISO 2409), even after extended UV exposure and abrasion cycles [ 241 ]. In contrast, ceramic substrates such as zirconia—widely used in dental implantology—present inherent challenges for coating adhesion due to their chemical inertness and low surface reactivity. To overcome these limitations, surface activation techniques like plasma treatment or functionalized interlayers can be employed to increase surface energy and promote film anchorage. Although direct studies on photocatalytic TiO 2 -based films on zirconia are limited, similar strategies are applicable. Notably, Bouras et al. reported that Zr-doped ZnO thin films deposited on ceramic substrates exhibited superior photocatalytic activity compared to those on glass [ 242 ]. This enhancement was attributed to the ceramic-supported films’ rougher morphology, increased crystallite size, and improved charge separation efficiency, collectively promoting greater light absorption and hydroxyl radical generation. Additionally, an innovative approach involved the integration of TiO 2  nanotubes onto nanostructured aluminum surfaces fabricated via tubular channel angular pressing [ 243 ]. These high-strength aluminum substrates were further functionalized with nano-concave arrays, enabling localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) coupling with the TiO 2  nanotubes. The resulting hybrid surfaces showed remarkable mechanical performance, with adhesion forces exceeding 2100 mN in scratch tests, alongside significant antibacterial efficacy against  E. coli  under light activation. Similarly, PEO has emerged as a promising technique for biomedical applications due to its ability to produce strongly adherent, porous, and crystalline oxide layers on metals such as titanium, alloys, and zirconium [ 104 ]. Unlike conventional methods, PEO creates mechanically interlocked coatings and chemically bonds to the substrate through in-situ oxide growth, resulting in superior adhesion and long-term interfacial stability. Another key advantage is the precise control over coating features achieved by adjusting the electrolyte, current density, and processing time. The substrate itself plays a pivotal role in this process. Its thermal and electrical properties influence microdischarge behavior, which governs oxide growth, melting/resolidification, and incorporation of electrolyte species. These factors directly impact coating thickness, crystallite size, and defect formation, all critical for photocatalytic performance. In this context, PEO coatings benefit from substrate-driven modulation of charge carrier dynamics, where structural and chemical features of the oxide influence redox activity. For example, zirconia coatings formed via PEO on zirconium substrates showed increased oxygen vacancy formation with extended oxidation time [ 244 ]. These vacancies not only improved photoluminescence and ROS generation but also reinforced the coating's cohesion and adhesion, which is critical for durable biomedical performance. Further, a typical feature of the PEO process is the occurrence of microdischarges that are influenced by coating thickness: in the early stages, lower-energy microarcs favor the formation of anatase, whereas as the coating thickens, only more intense electric fields can cause a dielectric breakdown, promoting the formation of rutile or anatase/rutile mixtures [ 19 ]. This evolution directly impacts the photocatalytic behavior of the surface. Nagay et al. observed that Bi-doped TiO 2  PEO coatings on commercially pure titanium (cpTi) substrates presenting a mixture of anatase and rutile showed excellent photocatalytic antibacterial performance under visible light due to the optical and high surface area properties of the coating [ 19 ]. This observation aligns with the findings of Pantaroto et al., who demonstrated, through magnetron sputtering, that mixed-phase TiO 2  films on cpTi substrate exhibit superior photocatalytic activity against oral pathogens under UV light compared to only anatase or rutile thin films [ 245 ]. On the other hand, Momeni et al. investigated the effects of adding SiO 2  to nitrogen-doped TiO 2  thin films applied to stainless steel via a sol-gel spray method, aiming to enhance visible-light photocatalytic performance and mechanical stability [ 246 ]. Contrary to prior findings on glass or polymer substrates, the addition of 20 % SiO 2  increased the band gap energy (from 2.93 to 3.09 eV), induced significant crack formation during calcination, and ultimately reduced visible-light photocatalytic activity and hydrophilicity. The reduced activity was attributed to low crystallinity, increased electron-hole recombination from grain boundaries, Fe 2+  ion diffusion from the steel substrate, and a detrimental crack pattern that diminished surface area. Although all films demonstrated strong adhesion in nanoscratch testing, SiO 2 -containing films showed lower mechanical stability, evidenced by force drop-offs and crack formation under stress [ 246 ]. These findings suggest that for steel-based substrates used under visible-light conditions, non-silica TiO 2  coatings may offer superior performance in terms of photocatalytic efficiency, surface integrity, and durability. Importantly, this study highlights the need for a careful balance in dopant type and concentration—while doping is essential to shift TiO 2  activity to the visible-light range, excessive or poorly integrated secondary phases may compromise mechanical and functional properties critical for clinical applications. It is important to highlight, though, that while this section consolidates key factors—particularly coating thickness and interfacial adhesion—that critically influence the performance of photocatalytic coatings and, consequently, ROS generation for antibacterial purposes, it is important to note that most of the available evidence comes from systems not specifically designed for visible-light activation. Nevertheless, these studies offer valuable insights into the structural and interfacial mechanisms that underpin coating performance. Still, investigations that systematically assess these parameters under visible-light-responsive conditions remain scarce. Future research should aim to bridge this gap by evaluating how variations in coating thickness and interfacial strength influence functional durability, antibacterial activity, and oxidative performance under clinically relevant illumination. Experimental strategies may include pull-off and scratch adhesion tests, cross-sectional analysis via SEM or profilometry, and correlating these features with ROS generation and microbial inhibition. Furthermore, extending these evaluations to different implant-relevant substrates will be essential to ensure coating reliability and performance across diverse biomedical applications.

Surface degradation, whether by wear or electrochemical attack, may directly compromise ROS generation, reduce effective surface area, and even trigger adverse tissue responses. Wear resistance is particularly important in load-bearing or micro-movement-prone regions, such as implant-abutment interfaces [ 234 ]. Surface abrasion can erode the photocatalytic layer, removing active crystalline domains (e.g., anatase/rutile TiO 2 ), exposing the underlying substrate, and decreasing antimicrobial efficiency. In such scenarios, the loss of surface integrity would diminish photocatalytic activity and facilitate bacterial adhesion and biofilm formation in damaged regions. In this context, a TiO 2  nanoceramic coating was developed on titanium implants using a PEO-based process followed by annealing and polishing [ 185 ]. The resulting coating featured a dense, nanocrystalline microstructure and an oxygen-vacancy-rich disordered outer layer, with a thickness of about 26 nm, enabling visible-light-driven photocatalysis ( Fig. 8 a). Additionally, the coating maintained its structural integrity after treatment with steel curettes and ultrasonic scalers—procedures that typically damage conventional titanium or TiO 2  coatings ( Fig. 8 b). This superior wear resistance was attributed to the high surface hardness (10.22 ± 2.3 GPa), metallurgical bonding with the titanium substrate, and a microstructure that prevented crack propagation. Importantly, the authors noted that the same conditions that enhanced mechanical robustness—i.e., thicker coatings with higher crystallinity—also supported greater photocatalytic and antimicrobial activity, likely due to reduced recombination of charge carriers and the formation of ROS at the surface [ 247 ]. 4.3 Engineering light-responsive coatings: shifting carcinogenic UV absorbance to more safe visible light wavelengths To develop visible-light-induced photocatalytic coatings, it is crucial to comprehensively understand their mechanism of action, particularly how these coatings interact with light to initiate photocatalytic processes. A key challenge is shifting the activation spectrum from carcinogenic UV light, which poses significant risks to human tissues, to safer visible light wavelengths. This transition requires strategically modifying photocatalyst properties, such as bandgap engineering, through doping or surface properties modification. Equally important is the understanding and application of reliable methods to evaluate ROS generation, as such chemicals are essential for achieving effective photocatalytic antimicrobial and pollutant-degrading performance while ensuring safety in biomedical and environmental applications. In a typical process, photocatalysis begins with irradiation on a semiconductor surface, where photons are absorbed, exciting electrons from the VB to the CB, creating electron-hole pairs. These pairs serve as current carriers within the material and can follow two possible paths: 1) Electrons and holes move to the outer surface of the semiconductor catalyst to facilitate chemical reactions with surrounding substrates, leading to the production of ROS, capable of degrading various contaminants, including inorganic and organic compounds, as well as pathogens; and 2) Electrons and holes may recombine within the semiconductor, resulting in the undesired wasteful release of energy as heat, which can hinder the photocatalytic process [ 24 , 27 ]. The efficiency and redox potential of photocatalysis are influenced by the band gap of the semiconductor, and modifying the intrinsic band structure can enhance the photocatalytic activity. Understanding electronic transitions is key to comprehending and improving photocatalytic mechanisms. In sum, heterogeneous photocatalysis relies on the direct irradiation of UV light onto the semiconductor photocatalyst's surface, initiating a sequence of chemical redox reactions (eq.  (2) ): (2) semiconductor + h v → e − ( CB ) + h + ( VB ) In the above reaction, photon absorption by the semiconductor generates electron-hole pairs in the CB and VB on the surface. These electron-hole pairs then migrate to the semiconductor's surface, where they interact with external elements like dissolved oxygen and water, resulting in the creation of ROS, including hydrogen peroxide, hydroxyl radicals, and superoxide radicals [ 255 ]. Such ROS generation can be identified using various advanced techniques [ 256 ]. In this context, electron spin resonance (ESR) is a highly sensitive method for directly detecting free radicals, while fluorescence detection with specific probes, such as dichloro-dihydro-fluorescein diacetate (DCFH-DA), provides a quantitative assessment of intracellular ROS levels [ 257 ]. Additionally, the degradation of dyes like methylene blue and methyl orange is commonly employed to indirectly evaluate ROS activity [ 257 ]. Nevertheless, when using this assay, researchers should bear in mind that the choice of dye for ROS detection through degradation assays is crucial because the dye's absorbance must align with the wavelength of light used to avoid interference from the dye's photodegradation. If the dye absorbs light in the applied wavelength range, it may degrade independently of the coating's photocatalytic activity, leading to inaccurate results [ 257 ]. Therefore, selecting a dye with minimal absorbance at the light wavelength ensures that the observed degradation is due to ROS generation from the coating rather than the dye's direct interaction with the light source. Beyond ROS detection, the electron-hole transitions responsible for ROS generation can be analyzed through photocurrent measurements, density functional theory (DFT) calculations, and electrochemical methods, offering insights into the material's photocatalytic properties and charge transfer dynamics [ 258 , 259 ]. These techniques provide a comprehensive understanding of the photochemical processes involved. Regarding photocatalyst choice, recent advancements in nanotechnology have led to the development of photosensitive nano-semiconductor materials such as ZnO, TiO 2 , BiO X , and Bi 2 O 3 , expanding the range of photocatalysts that can efficiently operate under UV–visible light, spanning wavelengths from 200 nm to >400 nm [ 27 ]. Among them, TiO 2 , known for its excellent photocatalytic properties, hydrophilicity, stability, and cost-effectiveness, is commonly utilized in photocatalysis [ 23 , 24 , 27 ]. While its native anatase form primarily responds to near-UV light, researchers have explored various doping and composite techniques to extend its photocatalytic activity into the visible light region, enabling the elimination of drug-resistant bacteria in water and even leading to the development of biomedical implant infection treatment strategies, including a) altering the semiconductor's composition through doping to extend the absorption range from UV to visible light; b) introducing defect formation and oxygen vacancies; and c) creating heterojunctions and coupling different semiconductors ( Fig. 9 a). Two major factors influencing doping are the capture of photogenerated charge carriers by doped metal ions to facilitate longer separation of charged species and the ability to free and drift trapped photogenerated charge carriers to the interface [ 27 ]. Doping can involve the introduction of cations (metals) and anions (non-metals) as dopants into crystal structures of semiconductor materials, which can lead to significant variations in the overall band gap and the creation of defects that influence photocatalytic behavior. Doping with metals : By targeting photocatalytic reactions, semiconductors can be doped either with transition or noble metals [ 25 ]. In photocatalytic reactions, where there is a significant concern about the potential recombination of photogenerated charge carriers before they can reach the semiconductor's surface to interact with target contaminants, various strategies have been employed, including the use of transition and inner transition metals (e.g., Zn 2+ , Mn 3+ , Fe 3+ , Sn 2+ , Al 3+ , Ni 3+ , and WO 3 ) as dopants [ 27 ]. These dopants play a crucial role in modifying the crystal structure, suppressing charge carrier recombination, prolonging the lifespan of charge carriers, and expanding the photocatalytic activity from the UV region into the visible region. Additionally, the incorporation of noble and post-transition metals like Ag, Pd, Bi, and Au within the matrix of TiO 2  has proven effective in enhancing photocatalytic efficiency under visible light by acting as electron traps, facilitating interfacial charge transfer, and thereby reducing the likelihood of electron-hole pair recombination [ 25 ]. For instance, Venkei et al. [ 263 ] conducted a study to investigate the interaction between a photoreactive composite coating material and  Streptococcus mitis  ( S. mitis ), a common oral bacterium. They assessed the antibacterial efficacy of nanohybrid coatings containing a physiologically safe 0.001 % Ag content through various in vitro experiments. The findings revealed that the spray-coated photocatalytic Ag-TiO 2  on Ti disks was activated by visible light and displayed significant antibacterial properties against  S. mitis  after 15 min of illumination, indicating its potential related to peri-implantitis control. Similarly, Nagay et al. demonstrated that doping bismuth into TiO 2  coatings via a one-step plasma electrolytic oxidation process effectively reduced the bandgap, enabling activation under visible light ( Fig. 9 b) [ 19 ]. The Bi-doped TiO 2  coating exhibited significant antibacterial activity against dual-species biofilms (almost 2-log reduction) while maintaining cytocompatibility with human gingival fibroblasts, highlighting its potential for implant-related applications and infection control. Doping with non-metals : The incorporation of non-metals, particularly nitrogen, into TiO 2  positively impacts its photocatalytic activity under visible light by narrowing the band gap energy. This doping method, involving the replacement of oxygen with nitrogen, is favored due to the comparable ionic radii of nitrogen and oxygen, and it helps extend the light absorption range of TiO 2  from UV to visible light. Non-metal doping also influences the morphology and electronic structure of the photocatalyst, making it an effective strategy for enhancing photocatalytic performance. Among non-metals (e.g., N, C, S, and F), nitrogen doping in TiO 2  is a noteworthy technique because it reduces the band gap and facilitates the transfer of electron-hole pairs. In the study of Zhang et al., [ 260 ] in which they synthesized nitrogen-doped TiO 2  coatings on reduced graphene oxide using sonochemical and hydrothermal methods, nitrogen doping was found to effectively reduce the band gap of TiO 2 , making it responsive to visible light ( Fig. 9 c). Interestingly, the addition of reduced graphene oxide enhanced the photocatalytic activity and improved adsorption capabilities and mass transfer in photocatalytic reactions. Following this similar concept, Javid et al. [ 264 ] developed N-doped TiO 2  films using a plasma-assisted method that enhanced surface roughness and wettability, improving photocatalytic and antibacterial activity under visible light. Nitrogen doping narrowed the band gap by creating mid-gap states, enabling visible-light activation and enhancing hydrophilicity. Under white light, the films achieved ∼20 % reduction in  E. coli  viability compared to dark conditions, demonstrating a potential strategy targeting antibacterial implant coatings. 4.3.2 Introducing defect formation and oxygen vacancies Intrinsic point defects in TiO 2  include oxygen vacancies (V o ), titanium interstitials (Ti int ), titanium vacancies ( V Ti), oxygen interstitials (O int ), and electronic defects involving electrons located at Ti 3+  ions and electron holes located on lattice sites of O −  ions. These defects are introduced due to disorder within the lattice structure of TiO 2 , resulting in non-stoichiometric variations such as TiO 2-x  (oxygen deficient) or TiO 2+x  (titanium deficient). These defects can act as either electron donors or acceptors, shifting the Fermi level within the band gap and enhancing the photocatalytic activity of TiO 2 . Specifically, oxygen vacancies play a crucial role in initiating redox reactions and improving charge separation, making them highly advantageous for photocatalysis, although their stability can be affected by the presence of reactant molecules. Based on this, Tan et al. [ 265 ] demonstrated that a nitrogen-doped TiO 2  photocatalyst synthesized through co-deposition using Ti isopropoxide and ammonia precursors was able to enhance the utilization efficiency of photo-generated charge carriers, promoting surface defect formation (e.g., oxygen vacancies) and facilitating oxygen circulation between Ti 4+  and Ti 3+  sites, resulting in enhanced NO removal efficiency and photocatalytic stability. Further, Shuai et al. developed a biodegradable PCLGA scaffold incorporating oxygen-vacancy-rich Fe-doped TiO 2  nanoparticles to enhance antibacterial activity via H 2 O 2 -driven Fenton reactions, effectively killing bacteria while maintaining mechanical compatibility with cancellous bone and supporting cell attachment, proliferation, and osteogenic differentiation [ 266 ]. Similarly, He et al. demonstrated that introducing surface oxygen vacancies in a TiO 2 /SrTiO 3  heterojunction significantly enhanced charge separation efficiency by 107 % compared to TiO 2 , highlighting the critical role of oxygen vacancies in improving photoelectrochemical performance ( Fig. 9 d) [ 261 ]. In line with this, Wu et al. [ 185 ] developed a TiO 2  nanoceramic coating via PEO that showed visible-light photocatalytic activity due to the presence of a disordered layer on its outer surface, which was confirmed to contain oxygen vacancies, as evidenced by a blue shift in the Raman spectra and a significant increase in Ti-OH content. Such oxygen vacancies’ introduction was further confirmed not to induce cytotoxicity to MG63 cells. Nevertheless, although the rationale of this concept would be directed at peri-implantitis treatment, the authors did not investigate antimicrobial properties under illumination. 4.3.3 Heterojunctions Heterojunctions are formed by combining two or more semiconductors using specific synthesis methods, providing benefits such as reduced charge carrier recombination, improved photocatalytic efficiency, and extended absorption into a wider range of wavelengths compared to single materials [ 267 ]. The visible-light-induced activity of hetero-semiconductors can be enhanced by coupling different semiconductors to align their energy levels, preventing carrier recombination and facilitating charge transfer between them [ 25 , 27 , 267 ]. This approach is effective in modifying UV-light active photocatalysts by incorporating narrow bandgap semiconductors like Bi 2 O 3  or Cu 2 O into materials such as TiO 2 , resulting in comparable energy levels and redox potentials for the mineralization of various contaminants [ 268 ]. For instance, Jiang et al. [ 250 ] developed and investigated an Ag 2 O/SiO 2 /Ta 2 O 5  nanocomposite applied onto Ti–6Al–4V substrates using a double-cathode glow discharge method for photocatalytic antibacterial purposes. The authors proposed that under visible light, electrons are excited in both Ta 2 O 5  and Ag 2 O and transferred through Ta 2 O 5 /SiO 2  and SiO 2 /Ag 2 O heterojunctions, accumulating in the conduction band of Ag 2 O. This electron accumulation enables the reduction of O 2  and protons to generate superoxide radicals and hydrogen, while holes contribute to hydroxyl radical formation for Rhodamine Blue degradation. The enhanced photocatalytic efficiency of the Ag-containing coating is attributed to its double heterojunction structure and extended electron transfer pathway. Notably, the Ag 2 O/SiO 2 /Ta 2 O 5  coating achieved nearly 100 % antibacterial efficacy against  E. coli  and  S. aureus  after 12 h of visible light exposure, highlighting its potential for implant surface modification. Similarly, a Cu 2 O/UiO-66/Bi 2 MoO 6  composite photocatalyst was developed using a simple chemical mixing method and showed high structural purity, efficient charge separation, and fast electron migration due to a double-Z scheme transfer model ( Fig. 9 e) [ 262 ]. UiO-66 played a key role in mitigating photocorrosion, while the synergistic interaction between Bi 2 MoO 6  and Cu 2 O enhanced redox activity under sunlight excitation. The composite exhibited strong photocatalytic antibacterial effects against  S. aureus, E. coli,  and MRSA. Its bactericidal mechanism is driven by oxidative stress from ∙O 2 −  and ∙OH radicals and the controlled release of Cu +  and Bi 3+  ions, supported by its large surface area that increases contact with bacterial cells. An interesting strategy to achieve photocatalytic activation under visible or near-NIR light involves combining multiple bandgap-engineering approaches, such as heterojunction formation and the introduction of oxygen vacancies (OVs). A representative example is the TiO 2 /Bi 2 WO 6  heterostructure, where TiO 2  nanowires are formed on titanium implant surfaces via alkaline thermal treatment, followed by in situ hydrothermal growth of Bi 2 WO 6  nanocrystals ( Fig. 10 a) [ 269 ]. This configuration narrows the bandgap from 3.28 eV (TiO 2 ) to 2.83 eV ( Fig. 10 b), enhancing light absorption in the visible–NIR range. In vitro studies demonstrated high antibacterial activity, with over 98 % reduction of  E. coli ,  P. gingivalis , and MRSA after 10 min of irradiation ( Fig. 10 e). In vivo, in a rat bone defect model with induced MRSA infection, the TiO 2 /Bi 2 WO 6 -coated implants achieved a 97.81 % reduction in bacterial load ( Fig. 10 c and d) and promoted superior bone regeneration, as evidenced by micro-CT analysis ( Fig. 10 f). Importantly, the introduction of oxygen vacancies played a crucial role by creating defect states within the bandgap that facilitate visible light absorption, promote charge carrier separation, and serve as active sites for surface reactions ( Fig. 10 g). Additionally, the coating enhanced the osteogenic differentiation of bone mesenchymal stem cells (mBMSCs), showing increased F-actin organization and cell spreading ( Fig. 10 h), attributed to the micro-nanostructure and piezoelectric properties of the heterojunction. Although this system was evaluated under NIR irradiation, the bandgap of 2.83 eV falls within the visible light range, suggesting that similar systems may also be activated by visible light alone [ 269 ]. Therefore, this example serves as a valuable reference for the design of future light-responsive coatings aimed at controlling infections and promoting osseointegration using clinically safe wavelengths. 5 Shedding light on visible-light-triggered photocatalytic antimicrobial coatings for biomedical and dental implants: an evidence-based review In this section, we provide a comprehensive overview of the existing literature assessing the antimicrobial effects of visible-light-induced photocatalytic coatings to control implant infections. Our research question was:  “What is the current state of the art in research pertaining to antimicrobial visible-light-induced photocatalytic coatings on substrates relevant to biomedical and dental implant applications?” To identify eligible studies, we conducted a systematic search across four electronic databases: PubMed (Medline), Scopus, Web of Science, and Embase until November 30, 2024 (for more methodological details, please see Supporting Information). Our initial search, utilizing specific keywords ( Table S1 , Supporting Information), identified a total of 6,080 records. After duplicate removal, we proceeded to screen 3,754 studies based on their titles and abstracts. Subsequently, we conducted a full-text review and selected studies that met the eligibility criteria for inclusion in this review, totaling 39 studies ( Fig. 11 a)[ 19 , 222 , 223 , 230 , [232] ,  [250] , 263 , 264 , [270] ,  [271] ,  [272] ,  [273] ,  [274] ,  [275] ,  [276] ,  [277] ,  [278] ,  [279] ,  [280] ,  [281] ,  [282] ,  [283] ,  [284] ,  [285] ,  [286] ,  [287] ,  [288] ,  [289] ,  [290] ,  [291] ,  [292] ,  [293] ,  [294] ,  [295] ,  [296] ,  [297] ,  [298] ,  [299] ,  [300] ] Importantly, only studies that aimed to develop or reported coatings suitable for implant applications with antimicrobial assessments were included, regardless of the substrate type. Notably, all included studies were conducted in vitro, with five extending to in vivo experiments using animal models: two in rats [ 277 , 287 ], two in mice [ 230 , 278 ], and one in pigs [ 285 ] ( Fig. 11 b). Ranging from 2008 to 2024 and conducted across various countries, these studies demonstrate the growth of research in this area; however, no clinical trials have been performed to date. Pure Ti was the most commonly used substrate (47 %), with non-metallic substrates like glass and silica chosen for evaluation due to their inertness and transparency, broadening applications ( Fig. 11 c). Among the synthesis methods, hydrothermal treatment was the most frequently employed synthesis method (11 %), followed by magnetron sputtering and immersion techniques (8 % each), with additional methods often relying on temperature to enhance crystallinity ( Fig. 11 d). For microbiological assessments,  S. aureus  and  E. coli  were the most commonly tested bacteria ( Fig. 11 e). These findings highlight the potential of the visible-light-triggered photocatalytic coating method; however, their clinical applicability remains limited due to the scarcity of in vivo studies and their relatively recent introduction in the scientific literature. To delve into the methodological disparities and observed in vitro outcomes among the included studies, a summary of the data from research that conducted photocatalytic, microbiological, and cellular assays is outlined ( Table 1 ). Glass, poly(vinyl chloride), polypropylene, silica wafer, and composites were also used. It is worth noting that while many studies claim the potential suitability of their developed coatings for biomedical implant applications, some have opted for non-metallic substrates like glass or silica. These choices are often made due to the inertness and transparency of such substrates, which makes them appropriate model surfaces as they minimize their influence on the outcomes and expand the potential applications across various fields. However, it is crucial to acknowledge that while these substrates offer advantages for studying general photocatalytic antimicrobial coatings, researchers should carefully assess the specific requirements of their individual studies and applications. Given that the chosen method can substantially influence the properties of the resulting coatings—especially in subtractive techniques—researchers are encouraged to thoroughly examine how their developed coatings perform on substrates pertinent to their intended applications. This is particularly important for materials like Ti and its alloys, which are commonly used for biomedical implant applications. Regarding the synthesis methods ( Fig. 11 d), hydrothermal treatment emerged as the most frequently employed fabrication technique in the reported studies, accounting for 11 % of the cases. It was followed by magnetron sputtering (8 %) and immersion techniques (8 %). Additionally, various other methods such as anodization, electrodeposition, electromagnetic deposition, electrophoretic deposition, plasma spray, pulsed-pressure-metal-organic chemical vapor deposition (pp-MOCVD), spray methods, and plasma-based techniques (e.g., ion plasma, plasma electrolytic oxidation, pulsed DC plasma) were utilized. In certain cases, two-step deposition methods were employed, primarily involving a combination of heat/annealing treatment with other technologies. Overall, it is possible to observe a common factor uniting all the methods employed in these processes: temperature. The structural attributes of semiconductor materials, particularly crystallinity, hold a pivotal role in dictating their photocatalytic efficacy [ 245 ]. The achievement of such properties can be pursued through diverse techniques, with high temperature representing one viable approach. Specifically, crystallinity significantly influences the separation and mobility of charge carriers (electrons and holes) generated during photocatalysis [ 301 ]. In crystalline structures, electrons and holes exhibit greater freedom of movement, reducing the likelihood of recombination, where they combine and neutralize each other's effects. This heightened charge separation substantially enhances the material's effectiveness in initiating and sustaining photocatalytic reactions. In this view, Krumdieck et al. [ 275 ] focused on developing a high-performance, nanostructured TiO 2  coating using an up-scalable pulsed-pressure metal-organic chemical vapor deposition (pp-MOCVD) process, producing the anatase-rutile-carbon (NsARC) composite with enhanced functionality ( Fig. 12 a). By integrating single-crystalline anatase nanostructures, rutile-anatase heterojunctions, and amorphous carbon, the coating achieves superior surface area, effective charge separation, and visible-light activation. The nanomorphology includes segmented mille-feuilles structures of anatase and strobili-like dendritic rutile optimized for visible-light-driven photocatalytic activity ( Fig. 12 b). The proposed mechanism suggests that high precursor flux, rapid pyrolysis, and carbon formation induce the unique mille-feuille anatase structure by stabilizing unstable crystal step edges, while dendritic rutile strobili are formed through fast crystal growth and potential carbon involvement, resulting in polycrystalline branching ( Fig. 12 c and d). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and Raman analysis showed the presence of amorphous carbon and carboxylate groups, with no carbon doping of the TiO 2  matrix, while the anatase phase displayed a rare (220) texture, and the rutile phase was identified as phase-pure. Unlike conventional TiO 2 , NsARC's black coloration, derived from carbon capping, extending light absorption while reducing electron-hole recombination, ultimately demonstrating antimicrobial performance, achieving up to a 99.99 % reduction in viable  E. coli  under UV, 3 to 4-log under visible light, and a 2-log reduction in darkness via carbon-centered radicals, ROS generation, and membrane disruption, highlighting its potential for scalable antimicrobial applications ( Fig. 12 e and f). Fig. 12 5.2 Designing optimal coatings: impact of semiconductors and dopants on the visible-light-driven photocatalytic activity As highlighted, numerous methods, including physicochemical deposition techniques like hydrothermal treatment, spin-coating, dip-coating, and spray-coating, as well as anodization and plasma-based deposition methods, have been employed to immobilize photocatalysts onto solid substrates. Nonetheless, besides the synthesis method, designing visible-light photocatalytic coatings for implant applications requires careful attention to semiconductors, dopants, and substrates. Semiconductors are the primary catalysts, and their selection profoundly influences coating efficiency. Dopants enhance photocatalytic properties, broaden light absorption, and aid charge separation [ 27 ], while substrate choice impacts adhesion, stability, and compatibility with the biomedical implant material. The harmonious integration of these elements is crucial for the success of these coatings in biomedical contexts, where safety, efficacy, and long-term performance are essential considerations. In the comprehensive systematic search on visible-light photocatalytic coatings for biomedical implant applications, TiO 2  takes center stage as the predominant semiconductor, accounting for approximately 60 % of the studies. This prominence relates to its multifaceted advantages, including inherent photocatalytic activity, biocompatibility, chemical stability, widespread availability, cost-effectiveness, ease of synthesis as coatings, and, notably, its tunability [ 36 ]. TiO 2 's structural characteristics can be readily tailored using techniques like doping, facilitating the fine-tuning of its photocatalytic capabilities within the visible-light range. Fig. 13 Overall, in an effort to shift the TiO 2  absorption spectra towards broader wavelengths, researchers most commonly employed Ag as the doping element, followed by nitrogen and carbon. Ag, when deposited on TiO 2 , becomes a particularly fascinating metal because of its inherent antibacterial effect and ability to localize surface plasmon resonance effects [ 283 , 302 ]. This phenomenon not only broadens the absorption spectrum of the material to encompass UV and visible-light regions, but also significantly enhances the photocatalytic properties of TiO 2  when exposed to visible light. Hegemann et al. [ 288 ], for example, explored plasma technology to deposit Ag nano-islets on TiOx films, creating ROS-generating surfaces with antibacterial efficacy, minimal metal ion leaching, and sustained activity over two years of storage in the dark, with restoration under visible light ( Fig. 14 a and b). The proposed mechanism was that AgOx-doped TiOx coatings generate ROS in the dark via oxygen vacancies and doped AgOx ( Fig. 14 c), while under light irradiation, its narrow band gaps supported by oxygen vacancies efficiently generated ROS (•O2−, •OH, singlet oxygen, and hydrogen peroxide) through electron and hole transfer ( Fig. 14 d). Similarly, Bletsa et al. [ 283 ] reported on the development of a visible-light-responsive coating through a one-step process of direct flame aerosol deposition, resulting in a porous nanothin Ag/TiOx particle film that presents photocatalytically active and capable of generating superoxide radicals under visible light. Enhanced by an infusion of a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) polymer solution into the film, the resulting polymer nanocomposite film exhibited superior photocatalytic properties, increased mechanical stability, and repeated eradication of established biofilms, making it ideal for medical device coatings. Overall, the improvement was largely attributed to the synergistic interplay between the surface plasmon resonance from Ag nanoparticles and the inherent defects within the TiO 2  particles. Nevertheless, although promising, it has been proposed that doping TiO 2  with non-metal elements (anions) enhances its photocatalytic performance more effectively than when doped with metal elements (cations). Fig. 14 As observed in the included studies in the systematic review, the dopant nitrogen has been recognized for its ability to reduce the material's band gap and enhance electron-hole pair transfer. Javid et al. [ 264 ] indicated that non-metal dopants like nitrogen, with lower electronegativity than oxygen, shift the 2p-orbital levels of the VB upwards, effectively narrowing the band gap. Such doping contrasts with metal doping, which introduces extra energy states within the band gap. Nitrogen's similar atomic radius to oxygen, low ionization energy, and high stability make it an ideal dopant, as demonstrated by enhanced photodegradation of pollutants like methylene blue in hydrothermally-treated nitrogen-doped TiO 2  coating [ 290 ]. Nevertheless, despite the reported absorption shift from UV to visible light with non-metal doping, this shift remains controversial. In density functional theory, dopants in the TiO 2  matrix either replace a part of the structure or fit into its gaps, thereby creating new energy levels that can extend or sit above the VB [ 27 ]. Hence, the introduction of nitrogen can alter the energy levels of the material in various ways, leading to a range of photocatalytic behaviors. This variability might account for why nitrogen is commonly co-doped with other elements in TiO 2  photocatalysts. In agreement, our systematic review indicates that in instances where TiO 2  is co-doped with multiple elements, nitrogen is consistently a chosen dopant, either with copper [ 284 ], bismuth [ 19 ], or silver [ 223 ]. Co-doping is particularly interesting because it can enhance photocatalytic efficiency compared to single doping. According to Betancur-Henao et al. [ 284 ], in a typical process, when exposed to UV light, electrons in TiO 2  are energized from the VB to the CB, creating h +  holes in the VB. Usually, these electrons and holes quickly recombine, leading to low photocatalytic activity. Adding nitrogen creates a new energy level just above the VB, which helps to activate electrons under visible light by providing a stepping stone to the CB. Ultimately, the electrons excited by light are effectively moved to the CB of CuO, serving as an electron trap, and this process creates a heterojunction between the CuO and TiO 2  semiconductors, enhancing their interactive properties. Besides TiO 2 , various other semiconductors have been documented in the literature for their ability to induce photocatalytic activity under visible light. Among oxides, Singh et al. [ 291 ] presented Mn 2 V 2 O 7  (MVO) as a low-cost, earth-abundant antibacterial photocatalyst. MVO synthesized via solid-state sintering exhibits elliptical domains ( Fig. 14 e) and β-phase crystallinity confirmed by XRD ( Fig. 14 f), with direct and indirect band gaps of 1.7 eV and 1.2 eV, respectively ( Fig. 14 g), enabling efficient ROS generation under exposure to solar and indoor light ( Fig. 14 h). Its distorted honeycomb structure supports simultaneous electron-driven reduction and hole-driven oxidation, producing ROS like •OH and O 2 −  for applications in antibacterial treatments. Overall, with a 1.7 eV bandgap, enabling visible light absorption up to ∼700 nm, its redox potentials align with water's potential, reducing bacterial load by 4 orders of magnitude under ambient or low-intensity solar light, with coatings achieving 76 % bacterial reduction, making it suitable for large-scale applications ( Fig. 14 i–l). 5.3 Exploring the spectrum: recent insights into antimicrobial efficacy in visible-light photocatalytic coatings for implant application As observed in  Fig. 13 , antimicrobial photocatalysis's efficacy is influenced by various parameters, such as the microorganism involved, the photocatalyst's nature and amount, physicochemical features, light intensity, lamp source, and duration of exposure. Given that the primary objective of photocatalysis for biomedical implants is to eliminate microbes, the antibacterial efficacy of the designed photocatalytic coatings was mostly evaluated using in vitro biofilm assays with a single-species model (constituting 62 % of the studies), with a major focus on  E. coli  (featured in 68 % of the studies), and secondarily on  S. aureus  (in 51 % of the studies). In the studies of biofilms on biomedical implants like those used in orthopedic, cardiac, and urinary applications,  S. aureus  and  E. coli  are frequently researched due to their well-known ability to form biofilms in these applications and their resistance to antibiotics. This makes them significant for understanding chronic infections and creating new treatments. However, for dental implants and the oral environment, these bacteria are less typical. Consequently, models based on  S. aureus  and  E. coli  might not fully represent the biofilm activity that actually occurs in peri-implantitis infections. This highlights the need for more studies involving oral biofilm models to advance the dental implant therapy field. Notably, our recent work [ 19 ] was the first to explore visible light photocatalysis as an innovative approach for managing peri-implant infections, specifically targeting bacteria crucial to the development of oral biofilms. Using PEO as the technology of choice, we developed a visible-light-responsive N,Bi-doped TiO 2  photocatalytic coating with characteristics ideal for biomedical implant use, such as suitable roughness, wettability, and cytocompatibility. The coating's antibacterial efficacy was evaluated against two significant early dental implant biofilm colonizers:  S. sanguinis  and  A. naeslundii . We found that the nitrogen and bismuth doping effectively narrowed the TiO 2 's band gap to the visible light spectrum, enhancing its photocatalytic activity under white LED light and offering the potential for reuse ( Fig. 15 a and b). This capability facilitated bacterial elimination of a 24-h biofilm after just 30 min of light exposure, resulting in reductions of up to 1.3 log for  S. sanguinis , 1.0 log for  A. naeslundii , and 0.7 log for the total bacterial population on Bi–TiO 2  surfaces ( Fig. 15 c) without being cytotoxic to human gingival fibroblasts ( Fig. 15 d). Practically, we introduced a versatile coating that can act in both initial stages of dental implant placement as a preventive surface treatment or as a therapeutic intervention for existing infections by applying light at the site. The antimicrobial mechanism is likely attributed to the generation of ROS, which disrupts bacterial cellular components when the coating is irradiated with visible light matching ( Fig. 15 e) its narrowed bandgap ( Fig. 15 e’). This strategy eliminates the need for a photosensitizer, as is common in traditional PDT, thereby simplifying current treatment methods and providing a pathway for future innovations aimed at reducing the challenging high prevalence of implant-related infections. Importantly, this was the sole study among those reviewed that assessed multi-species biofilms. It is also worth noting that additional studies in the systematic review [ 263 , 270 , 279 , 286 ] describe advanced visible-light-triggered photocatalytic coatings specifically for combating dental implant infections. This highlights the increasing research focus on this topic. Clinical implant infections, however, are polymicrobial, involving complex interactions among multiple species, that single- and dual-species models cannot replicate. Furthermore, a notable issue in the reviewed studies is the evaluation of antimicrobial efficacy against planktonic bacteria. While such testing is valuable for initial antimicrobial screening, researchers aiming to treat infections are advised to focus on well-established, robust biofilm models for a more accurate assessment, as these are also more challenging to eradicate. Thus, considering this method's potential, future research should include polymicrobial biofilm models that more accurately resemble clinical conditions, considering variables such as temperature, pH levels, and the availability of nutrients [ 303 ]. Fig. 16 The photocatalytic coatings disrupt the structural integrity of bacteria through mechanisms involving both chemical interactions and ROS-mediated damage, which can vary depending on the bacterial species and the coating's composition. For instance, FE-SEM micrographs of  S. aureus  and  E. coli  treated with a Ti/CQD@α-Fe 2 O 3  coating show significant cell membrane disruption and intracellular leakage ( Fig. 16 h) [ 273 ]. While  S. aureus  cells appeared more deformed in the micrographs,  E. coli  maintained partial integrity due to its complex outer membrane, characteristic of Gram-negative bacteria, which offer resistance ( Fig. 16 h) [ 273 ]. Similarly, SEM analysis of  E. coli  exposed to N-doped TiO 2  sandwich films with Ag revealed distinct morphological changes ( Fig. 16 i) [ 223 ]. Untreated cells displayed smooth surfaces, whereas treated cells exhibited rough textures and unique surface cracks, particularly under visible light. This indicates the synergistic action of Ag and ROS generation in damaging bacterial structures. Building on the demonstrated efficacy of ROS-generating coatings, another Ag-based coating, the Ag 2 O/SiO 2 /Ta 2 O 5  heterojunction, further highlights the potential of Ag and photocatalysis in antimicrobial applications. Regarding photocatalytic activity, the Ag 2 O/SiO 2 /Ta 2 O 5  coating demonstrated superior optical and photocatalytic performance compared to the Ag-free coating [ 250 ]. Enhanced visible light absorption, a reduced band gap (3.0 eV vs. 3.3 eV), and lower photoluminescence intensity indicate improved charge separation and utilization. In RhB dye degradation tests ( Fig. 16 j), the Ag-containing coating achieved a 93.8 % degradation rate with a higher kinetic constant (0.015 min −1 ), outperforming the Ag-free coating's 66.0 % and 0.006 min −1 , highlighting the Ag 2 O phase's role in boosting photocatalytic activity. Interestingly, the authors performed density functional theory (DFT) calculations to confirm the electron transfer in the Ag 2 O/SiO 2 /Ta 2 O 5  heterojunction, with electrons moving from Ta 2 O 5  to SiO 2  and SiO 2  to Ag 2 O, forming transport channels at the interfaces. Charge density and electron localization analyses further reveal strong interface electron transfer, enhancing photogenerated carrier separation. This finding was validated by investigating the antibacterial behavior under both dark and visible light conditions ( Fig. 16 k) [ 250 ]. The Ag 2 O/SiO 2 /Ta 2 O 5  nanocomposite coating exhibited nearly 100 % antibacterial efficacy against  E. coli  and  S. aureus  under visible light, outperforming the antibacterial effect of Ag +  ions under dark conditions. However, a significant issue with the study is the use of 6 h of irradiation, an approach that is impractical for clinical settings, a concern also noted in other included studies. Considering this, future studies should aim for treatments requiring shorter irradiation periods to better align with realistic clinical scenarios. A noteworthy aspect is the combined effect of the coating's intrinsic antibacterial properties, whether from its topography or embedded antimicrobial agents, and its photocatalytic activity, which together significantly enhances microbial eradication. Regarding physicochemical properties, Wasa et al. [ 296 ] reported that a nanostructured TiO 2  coating reduced bacterial viability without illumination probably owing to its nanostructure composed of carbon, besides hydrophilicity and zeta potential factors. Such antimicrobial effect was even more pronounced after 8 and 48 h of light exposure. In terms of antimicrobial components, most of the studies used Ag to aid the bacterial-killing effect of the coating. For example, employing Ag-TiO 2  sandwich films responsive to visible light, a synergistic antibacterial effect has been observed when combining external ROS with Ag [ 223 ]. This is attributed to the complex bactericidal nature of Ag, which disrupts bacterial processes and prompts an atypical production of ROS within the bacteria. Considering that ROS generation is a key antibacterial action of photocatalysts, it makes sense that Ag, in conjunction with the photocatalytic properties of the sandwich films, efficiently eradicates pathogenic bacteria under visible light. Nevertheless, although employing a combination of elements in high concentrations could potentially boost antibacterial properties, concerns over heightened bacterial resistance and potential toxicity to cells should not be neglected. Hence, it is essential to carefully calibrate the balance between achieving effective antimicrobial action and maintaining the biocompatibility of photocatalytic coatings. 5.4 Balancing function and safety of visible-light photocatalytic coatings: cellular responses, ROS thresholds, and irradiation protocols Owing to concerns about toxicity, a growing body of research on antimicrobial photocatalytic coatings has emerged to tackle these issues. Various cell lines and primary cells from animals and humans have been used for testing, including animal-derived cells such as MC3T3-E1 (murine preosteoblastic), MEFs (mouse embryonic fibroblasts), and NIH3T3 (mouse fibroblast-like), as well as human-derived cells such as BMSCs (bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells), NHDFs (normal dermal fibroblasts), HGFs (gingival fibroblasts), and A549 (adenocarcinomic alveolar basal epithelial cells). Overall, only ≈40 % of the included studies looked at how well cells tolerated the photocatalytic coatings, and none of these studies found serious cell damage, indicating that these coatings generally are cytocompatible. However, it is important to note that half of these studies also explored how light treatment affects cells. For instance, He et al. [ 287 ] observed that although C-TiO 2  nanorods enhanced BMSC adhesion and proliferation, outperforming Ti and TiO 2 , due to the presence of hydrophilic groups ( Fig. 17 a and b), under light irradiation, cell viability temporarily decreased due to hyperthermia and ROS generation, but full recovery was achieved once the irradiation ceased ( Fig. 17 c and d). In another piece of research, Moon et al. [ 222 ] observed that both Au–TiO 2  NTs and Pt–TiO 2  NTs are cytocompatible with hMSCs, maintaining cell viability above 70 % of the control after 24 and 48 h of incubation. Additionally, ALP activity and gene expression analysis showed that Pt–TiO 2  NTs, when exposed to 600 nm light, significantly enhanced early osteogenic differentiation markers (ALP, OPN, BSP) compared to 470 nm light, with the most notable effects observed after one week of cultivation ( Fig. 17 e and f). Furthermore, FE-SEM micrographs revealed that 470 nm light caused filopodia detachment due to plasmonic photocatalysis, while 600 nm light promoted filopodia elongation without disrupting cell adhesion ( Fig. 17 g). Fig. 17 Beyond direct effects on cell viability, it is also critical to consider potential cytotoxic and inflammatory responses associated with the coating–implant interface. While titanium substrates offer excellent biocompatibility and support for coating adhesion, degradation of photocatalytic layers may lead to the release of reactive ions or nanoparticles. These species can disrupt redox homeostasis, promote ROS overproduction, and induce macrophages to secrete cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, and IL-6, etc.), potentially activating pro-inflammatory pathways leading to mitochondrial damage [ 304 ]. Moreover, surface modifications induced by the coatings, such as changes in roughness, wettability, and surface energy, may influence not only the adhesion and morphology of host cells but also immune cell activation and inflammatory cytokine release [ 305 ]. In this context, prolonged exposure to light-activated photocatalytic coatings raises important questions regarding cytotoxicity, especially due to the sustained generation of ROS during illumination. ROS can be described as having a dual role, selectively damaging bacterial components while producing a milder effect on mammalian cells. The simpler structure of bacteria, characterized by a rigid peptidoglycan cell wall, vulnerable membranes, and limited DNA repair mechanisms, make them highly susceptible to oxidative stress. In contrast, mammalian cells are equipped with more complex structural defenses, including a phospholipid bilayer and robust intracellular enzymatic systems capable of repairing oxidative damage to DNA. For instance, we [ 19 ] demonstrated that HGFs DNA integrity was preserved even after 30 min of visible light LED irradiation on Bi-doped TiO 2  photocatalytic coatings ( Fig. 15 h), revealing their resilience to moderate ROS levels. Importantly, mammalian cells possess intrinsic antioxidant defenses—such as the glutathione system and catalase/superoxide dismutase pathways—as well as adaptive transcriptional responses involving the NRF2–KEAP1 axis, which regulate redox homeostasis and protect cells from ROS-induced injury [ 306 ]. It is also important to note that ROS generated by photocatalytic reactions—such as hydroxyl radicals (•OH), superoxide anions (•O 2 − ), and singlet oxygen ( 1 O 2 )—have extremely short lifetimes (from nanoseconds to a few microseconds) and limited diffusion distances (typically below 200 nm) [ 307 , 308 ]. This means that ROS exert their effects at or near the material surface, thereby confining their cytotoxic potential to the immediate vicinity of the coating–cell interface. This spatial and temporal limitation significantly reduces the likelihood of deep tissue penetration or systemic toxicity. Nevertheless, occasionally, the duration of light exposure, combined with the specific type of light source, plays a crucial role in determining the extent of cytotoxic effects on cells, as these factors directly impact the production of ROS and thermal effects, which can either damage cellular components or modulate cell behavior depending on the conditions. Researchers have found that shorter irradiation periods of 15–30 min did not affect cell toxicity [ 19 , 277 , 282 , 287 ], whereas prolonged exposure beyond 5–6 h led to a notable decrease in cell viability, potentially due to oxidative stress from extended phototoxicity or excessive ROS production, as well as potential thermal damage [ 232 , 292 ]. This was evident when NIR light reduced cell metabolism after 10 min exposure [ 230 ]. The choice of light source, particularly in the context of photocatalysis for infection treatment, is crucial. While most studies utilize LED, fluorescent, or xenon lamps with UV–vis filters for visible light, xenon lamps have certain drawbacks, such as heat production, emission of harmful gases, and higher costs [ 309 ]. These factors could compromise the practicality, safety, and effectiveness of their use. Conversely, LEDs, with their cooler operation, longevity, energy efficiency, and precise control, are typically more appropriate for medical applications. Beyond direct cytotoxicity, light-activated ROS may also modulate immune responses at the tissue–implant interface. Evidence from PDT in oncology suggests that ROS-induced necrosis and apoptosis can lead to the release of damage-associated molecular patterns and potentially oxidation-associated molecular patterns, which act as endogenous adjuvants to stimulate immune recognition [ 310 ]. Although such immunostimulatory effects are beneficial in cancer treatment, their implications in implant-related applications remain underexplored. In the context of dental and orthopedic implants, a controlled local inflammatory response may be favorable for initial healing and osseointegration; however, excessive or persistent immune activation could compromise tissue integration or lead to chronic inflammation. Interestingly, studies have hypothesized that cell death occurring in peripheral, lower-intensity light regions (“the penumbra”) may involve apoptotic pathways [ 311 ], potentially contributing to subtle immunomodulatory effects not yet fully characterized in implant settings. These emerging observations underscore the need for deeper investigation into the immunological consequences of photocatalytic ROS exposure, particularly under repeated or chronic light activation protocols. Understanding whether ROS-induced damage at sublethal levels generates immunogenic signals—either harmful or beneficial—could provide a new dimension to the design of “immune-informed” photocatalytic implant coatings. Altogether, visible-light-induced photocatalytic coatings generally exhibit a range of outcomes, indicating a complex relationship between the level of antimicrobial action and cell compatibility, especially after light irradiation. This variation might originate from the diverse in vitro techniques without standardization to perform and evaluate the photocatalytic therapeutic impacts of developed coatings. Coating design also plays a role in minimizing cytotoxicity: tuning dopant concentration, ensuring dopant retention within the matrix, and optimizing the surface energy and roughness can modulate both ROS release and host cell behavior. Therefore, future studies should adopt standardized testing frameworks to evaluate cytotoxicity under physiologically relevant light regimens, including long-term assessments, co-culture models with immune cells, and real-time oxidative stress assays, which together will provide a more comprehensive understanding of biocompatibility under irradiation conditions. 5.5 Bridging the gap: the current status of visible-light-triggered photocatalytic implant surfaces in in vivo models While numerous photocatalytic coatings have undergone extensive examination through in vitro analyses, advancing towards clinical reality, only 5 studies [ 230 , 277 , 278 , 285 , 287 ] assessed the in vivo anti-infection impact and biocompatibility of the developed treatments in animal models. Overall, after contamination of the implants with  S. aureus  or  E. coli , the implants were placed in the subcutaneous tissue of rats or mice, light-treated, and explanted after some days to perform histological and/or CFU analyses. These experimental procedures showed that photocatalytic coatings generally performed well under visible light irradiation by ameliorating the inflammatory reaction in the tissues surrounding the coating, besides reducing the number of remnant bacteria, validating the promising results found in vitro. In evaluating implant infections and light treatments, subcutaneous animal models are preferred due to their straightforward access and simplicity, allowing for easy implant placement and monitoring just underneath the skin. These models facilitate the clear observation and continuous monitoring of infections or reactions, which is particularly valuable for directly assessing the effects of light treatments. They offer a uniform setting for consistent studies, minimizing the variability inherent in more intricate or deeper implant sites. For instance, Zhang et al. (2020) [ 230 ] developed bio-functionalized Ti implants with TiO 2 /MoS 2 /PDA/RGD nanorod arrays that can prevent bacterial infections. Under dual light irradiation (660 nm and 808 nm), these nanostructures generated ROS and hyperthermia, which disrupted bacterial membranes, leading to efficient bacterial killing and biofilm eradication ( Fig. 18 a–c). Specifically, in vivo testing using a rat subcutaneous  S. aureus  infection model demonstrated that TiO 2 /MoS 2 /PDA/RGD nanorod arrays effectively inhibited bacterial growth, with minimal infection and inflammation observed compared to Ti controls ( Fig. 18 d ) . Additionally, histological analyses showed no tissue damage or organ abnormalities from the dual light irradiation, confirming the safety and excellent antibacterial properties of the MoS 2 -modified TiO 2  nanostructures due to the synergistic effects of photodynamic and photothermal therapies ( Fig. 18 e). However, it is important to acknowledge that subcutaneous models might not fully resemble the complexities of deeper or more intricate implant scenarios, particularly for dental implants, where the scenario is transmucosal rather than within a closed compartment. This distinction highlights the need to use subcutaneous models in conjunction with other models to gain a comprehensive understanding. This is especially true for conditions like peri-implantitis, where infections are typically caused by polymicrobial biofilms, and a multi-species inoculum would provide a more accurate representation.
